column2: Yanting Shen, Mengqing Yu, Chenyu Huang and Jiawei Yao
column3:
Superiority of High-Dimensional Latent Variable
Representation in Urban Spatial Structure: Evidence from an
Urban Climate Study
column7:
Quantitative descriptions of urban morphology enhance our
understanding of urban systems' operation and evolution.
Traditional methods of urban classification, which rely on
manually defined morphological indicators, often face
challenges such as information loss, spatial mismatches,
and a lack of robustness. To address these issues, deep
learning techniques have been developed for
high-dimensional feature extraction and latent variable
representation, improving the robustness of urban
classification. However, the effectiveness of these methods
in urban-related studies remains uncertain. This study
employs a deep learning approach focused on urban
microclimate research to investigate how the spatial
characteristics of building and vegetation combinations
affect land surface temperature (LST) in urban residential
areas. Using a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) model, we
encode and sample two-dimensional images of plots to
extract compressed feature vectors (CFV). These CFV are
then clustered as the experimental group, while traditional
planar indicators are used to cluster the control group,
with both groups undergoing k-means clustering across 1 to
20 categories. Finally, we apply the XGBOOST algorithm to
train and predict LST for each dataset derived from these
classification methods, evaluating the model's accuracy to
compare classification efficiency. The results show that
the CFV-based classification consistently outperforms
traditional methods in nearly all experiments (by 4%-62%)
and can reliably determine the optimal number of clusters
(5 categories). These findings confirm the significant
advantages of deep learning-based urban morphology
classification and its potential in urban climate research,
providing strong support for advancing precise urban
science studies.

column2:
Tinghao Feng, Yulu Zhang, Xinhui Xu, Zhengcheng He, Wenjing
Li and Philip F. Yuan
column3:
Integrating Regulatory Compliance In AI-Assisted
Architectural Design
column7:
In the new era of human-computer interaction (HCI),
Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted design tools present
opportunities for designers by offering var-ious
interactive choices. Large Language Models (LLMs) have also
shown their potential in generating design responses.
However, these tools are fac-ing a lot of technical
challenges, especially in terms of design compliance within
the architectural design environment. Architects are
responsible for ensuring their design compliance with
constantly updating regulations at dif-ferent design
stages. But due to fragmentation and high specialization of
building regulations, AI-assisted design tools sometimes
struggle to accurate-ly provide compliant responses based
on these unstructured regulatory terms. In this context,
regulatory compliance becomes one of crucial challenges
within AI-assisted architectural design. To address this
challenge, this paper introduces an AI-enhanced design
platform, FU GPT, aims to balance the conflict between
design creativity and regulatory compliance. In the
plat-form, four compliant interactions were proposed to
support the design de-mands from different design stages:
basic architectural knowledge interac-tion, regulatory
interaction, file parsing interaction and image generation
in-teraction. A regulatory knowledge graph (RKG) and a
multi-dimensional vec-tor comparison engine were designed
as compliant foundations to support the compliance of these
interactive modes. The experiment results indicated that FU
GPT could efficiently provide compliant design responses
for archi-tects at different stages within AI-assisted
design workflow.

column2:
Shenzhou Dai, Sihang Liu, Haojun Wang, Yulin Chen and
Zixiong Lin
column3:
A Full-Process Digital Method for Recursive Geometric
Structure and Machining Parameter Generation Targeting the
Reutilization of Curved Timber
column7:
The commercial wood processing industry, driven by North
American construction, generates a substantial amount of
by-products annually, including branches, bark, wood
shavings, and sawdust. Building upon previous practices in
reusing wood by-products, this study focuses on optimizing
the utilization of curved timber generated during the
logging process. A computational method is proposed to
support the fabrication of non-standard wooden products
using robotic arms or collaborative robots for future
applications. This method facilitates the generation and
visualization of structural schemes and construction
parameters for the primary framework. The approach relies
on GHPython components and is implemented through three key
stages: a three-dimensional posture brute-force search
based on fixed angle increments, structural combination
solving using the SymPy computational library, and node
visualization and generation on the Grasshopper platform.
These steps enable the acquisition of manufacturing
parameters for a stable recursive spatial truss structure
while maximizing the utilization of raw materials. The
study significantly enhances computational efficiency and
validates the structural reliability of the generated
framework through finite element analysis.

column2: Hang Xu, Chengxuan Li, Timur Dogan and Patrick Kastner
column3:
Understand Urban Building Energy Consumption with
Explainable Machine Learning Approaches
column7:
Urban decarbonization is a critical goal in addressing
climate change, requiring large-scale Urban Building Energy
Models (UBEMs) to inform effective policy decisions. To
understand the non-linear relationships between individual
building energy demand, complex neighborhood context, and
population factors at an urban scale, this study uses
machine learning-based  models of energy use combined with
rarely-used geospatial data. In our case study area, we
combine building footprints, tax assessments, and
annonymized meter-level energy usage billing data provided
by the local utility. We derive non-geometric information
derived from tax assessment data that incorporates thermal
systems, vintage, improvement records, demographics, and
rural-urban definitions. We include geospatial features,
such as the urban tree canopy (UTC) ratio, to capture
microclimate impacts on building energy demand, driven by
shading and evapotranspiration effects. We compare multiple
machine learning models—including Multivariable Linear
Regression (MLR), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Support Vector
Machine (SVM), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), and Random
Forest (RF)—regarding their Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root
Mean Square Error (MSE), and the coefficient of
determination (R²). The results show that RF outperforms
other models in our datasets. Furthermore. Complex
non-linear relationships and interaction effects are
explored using partial dependence plots (PDPs),
highlighting the significance of UTC in shaping building
energy consumption. These findings help prioritize model
features for data-driven urban building energy modeling and
emphasize the need to incorporate additional microclimate
features in future studies.

column2:
Fang-Che Cheng, Henriette Bier, Ningzhu Wang and Alisa
Andrasek
column3:
Review of Advances in the Robotization of Timber
Construction
column7:
Robotic timber construction has advanced significantly in
the last decade, considerably impacting production
efficiency and sustainability. This paper explores via
literature review the state-of-the-art robotization in
timber construction by identifying various computational
and robotic tools, techniques, and methods that support the
design to fabrication process. It furthermore reflects on
the advantages of robotic production and assembly, and the
limits to adopting these technologies at large scale. It
contributes to understanding current level of robotization
in timber construction and identifying future steps.

column2: Kifah Alhazzaa and Wei Yan
column3:
Transforming Architectural Education: The Impact of VR and
AR on Understanding Building Energy Efficiency
column7:
This study investigates the efficacy of Virtual Reality
(VR) and Augmented Reality (AR) technologies in enhancing
the understanding of building thermal behavior and energy
simulations among undergraduate students. Given the growing
importance of sustainable building practices and the
complexities involved in energy modeling, immersive
technologies like VR and AR offer promising avenues for
education. The research involved 60 participants from
University X, divided evenly into two groups, each exposed
to either VR or AR learning environments specifically
designed to visualize the results of the building energy
simulations. The study aimed to determine which of these
technologies more effectively facilitates comprehension of
the intricate relationships between building components and
their impact on thermal behavior and energy efficiency. The
AR group showed a significant improvement in
post-experiment assessments, with statistical analysis
revealing that AR provides a more intuitive, engaging, and
contextually relevant learning experience compared to VR.
This is likely due to AR's ability to overlay digital
information onto the physical world, allowing students to
interact with and better understand complex concepts in a
real-world context. The research highlights that students'
academic backgrounds, particularly in STEM versus non-STEM
fields, influence the effectiveness of these technologies.
STEM students demonstrated higher learning gains,
underscoring the role of prior knowledge in maximizing the
benefits of immersive learning environments. The findings
suggest that AR can serve as a powerful pedagogical tool in
Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC)
education, bridging the gap between theoretical knowledge
and practical application. This study advocates for the
broader integration of AR and VR technologies in
educational curricula to prepare future professionals for
the challenges of designing energy-efficient, sustainable
buildings.

column2: Michail Georgiou and Odysseas Georgiou
column3:
Adaptive Design and Fabrication of Modular Topological
Interlocking Assemblies
column7:
This paper presents a novel combinatorial topological
interlocking assembly (TIA) framework that integrates
computational design and digital fabrication, to create
lightweight, reconfigurable structures. Departing from
traditional reliance on self-stabilizing modules, the
system employs folded sheet metal components whose systemic
rigidity emerges through composite clustering, enabling
multi-directional growth and bottom-up formation of complex
geometries. By leveraging a single uniform module and
pre-grouped sub-assemblies, the approach aligns with
circular economy principles and streamlines on-site
installation. Finite Element Method (FEM) simulations
guided iterative form-finding, ensuring ro-bust structural
performance. A full-scale mock-up, realized under strict
time con-straints, demonstrates the system’s scalability,
material efficiency, and potential for rapidly deployable,
reconfigurable construction solutions.

column2: Ali Farajmandi and Negar Kalantar
column3:
Parametric Biomimicry: Translating Spiral Seashell
Formation into Robotic 3D Printing
column7:
The architectural marvel of spiral seashells, with their
intricate geometric patterns and structural efficiency, has
long captivated scientists and designers. This research
delves into the biomimetic potential of mollusks and their
shell structures, exploring their application in
computational design and digital fabrication. By analyzing
the natural construction rules of mollusks, including their
growth patterns, classification, and material composition,
the project seeks to translate these biological phenomena
into parametric models using Grasshopper. Advanced
computational strategies, including non-linear 3D printing
techniques and rotational printing, were developed to
fabricate shells inspired by the natural geometry of
seashells. These fabrication techniques are not only
aesthetic but also demonstrate potential solutions to
challenges in architectural sustainability and material
efficiency. The project employs a six-axis robotic arm,
showcasing the benefits of integrating robotics and
computation into modern design practices. Beyond
fabrication, this study addresses the artistic and
ecological significance of seashell geometry, connecting
the natural world with architectural innovation. The
findings emphasize the importance of biomimicry in
advancing architectural and industrial design, advocating
for a harmonious relationship between natural systems and
human ingenuity. This research provides a foundation for
further exploration into non-linear manufacturing and its
implications for sustainable and adaptive design
methodologies.

column2: Lok Hang Cheung, Likai Wang and Juan Carlos Dall'Asta
column3:
Collaborative, conversational architectural design process
between human designers and multimodal AI agents for
early-stage design exploration
column7:
AI applications in architectural design are mostly confined
to individual use and linear design flows, with a steep
learning curve for mastering sophisticated multimodal AI
tools. Although agentic AI systems have shown enormous
potential for enhancing creative collaboration between
designers and AIs, their use in architectural design is
underexplored. This paper proposes a conversational design
framework for an early-stage architectural design process
in a collaborative environment, featuring an
architectural-focus multimodal agentic AI system, com-posed
of two AI bots. AI bot one is the main design partner,
which is flexible in using different tools to respond to
users’ enquiries. In contrast, AI bot two specialises in
design iterations through image generation and editing upon
verbal communications. Leveraging Discord, a common
messaging platform, facilitates the medium for human-AI
collaboration. A case study of two design workshop sessions
with six architecture students is presented. Participants
joined the online platforms with the developed AI system
for 1-to-1 and group design conversation and collaboration
on a university campus pavilion design. The challenges,
opportunities and implications of research, education, and
real-world practice are discussed through observation and
semi-structured interviews with the students.

column2: Erfan Rezaei Azari and Negar Kalantar
column3:
From Flat to Form ; Developing Flexible 3D-Printed Kerfing
Structures Without Scaffolding
column7:
Kerfing, traditionally used in crafting musical
instruments, enhances material flexibility through
strategic cuts. With the advent of digital fabrication and
parametric design, this study introduces a novel
scaffold-free additive kerfing technique for 3D printing.
Instead of subtracting material, this approach deposits
material to enable rigid materials to deform into complex
3D surfaces. Similar to adjustable 3D-printed lattice cores
[1], this research reimagines kerfing for 3D applications
by proposing a framework for generating flat kerfing core
structures that can be efficiently stacked. By focusing on
the x and y axes, print time is reduced, and the resulting
structures offer enhanced energy absorption and
adaptability, with potential applications in vehicle safety
and aerospace [2].
This study presents flexible 3D-printed kerfing structures
that transform from a flat state into complex 3D forms
without the need for scaffolding. The process is driven by
generating a Dual Graph [3] of a 2D mesh, with two
interconnected layers of panels linked through connectors.
Additionally,  the framework allows for the creation of a
2D mesh that deforms into a desired surface when bent,
leveraging an adaptation of Laplace's equation [4].
Results demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness in
producing flexible kerfing structures, optimized through
Rhino and Grasshopper. Material tests using PLA, TPU, and
Onyx [3] highlight distinct performance characteristics,
with tunable flexibility and rigidity achieved by adjusting
layer gaps, connector thickness, and structure height to
meet specific requirements.

[1] M.F. Ashby, The properties of foams and lattices,
Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A:
Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences 364(1838)
(2006) 15-30.
[2] Y.-Y. Sun, Z.-W. Yu, Z.-G. Wang, Bioinspired design of
building materials for blast and ballistic protection,
Advances in Civil Engineering 2016 (2016).

[3] Thulasiraman, K.; Swamy, M. N. S. (2011), Graphs:
Theory and Algorithms, John Wiley & Sons, Exercise 7.11, p.
198,
[4]Minoux, M. (1986). Mathematical programming: Theory and
algorithms. Egon Balas (foreword) (Translated by Steven
Vajda from the (1983 Paris: Dunod) French ed.). Chichester:
A Wiley-Interscience Publication. John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.
pp. xxviii+489. ISBN 0-471-90170-9. MR 0868279. (2008
Second ed., in French: Programmation mathématique: Théorie
et algorithmes. Editions Tec & Doc, Paris, 2008. xxx+711
pp. . ).

column2: David Gerber, Azam Khan, Simon Breslav and Niko McGlashan
column3:
(CI) A Living Lab's Digital Twin for Human Building
Interaction Research and Design
column7:
The project proposes to collaborate and hypothesize the use
of a Living Lab Digital twin technology. I am the developer
of a digital twin of an existing building that will allow
research and generative design from a real world and near
real time data stream. The digital twin includes both 3D
and 4D visualization of GIS down to sensor level of detail
and provides data and meta data from over 3000 data points.
In particular, the Living Lab project has the objective to
drive research and innovation in the field of smart
buildings, smart materials, artificial intelligence,
machine learning, sustainable architecture, regulatory and
certification system compliance, and sensing technology.
Findings and solutions developed within the project can
showcase leading research in the context of a real
environment. This innovative and collaborative approach to
research and development will leverage a real-world
building environment to advance technology, sustainability,
and the overall quality of life for building occupants.

The focus is on developing opportunities to collaborate and
hypothesize use cases from the building being turned into
an instrument of science. The innovation is that we have
developed a research platform, i.e. a Living Lab and
provided access to geometrically related data sets as a
digital twin. The GCS Living Lab project has three
objectives and two use cases.  1) To provide researchers
and their collaborators a research platform where the
building is an instrument of scientific inquiry. This is
enabled through providing access to a digital model and
associated data streams. 2) to provide the public a curated
visualization of the building as a living lab, emphasizing
its unique sustainability characteristics. This is
envisioned as a display in the lobby of the building with a
limited set of interactions for the public to engage with.
3) The project will enable the further development of
generative design methods and the longitudinal data for
novel machine learning methods to be shared.

The strength of our project and potential collaborations is
the development of research projects via access to a new
building and all the data it will generate. What is unique
is the ability to treat the building as a real time data
set for machine learning and as a generative design
feedback loop. What is particularly exciting is to work
across disciplines and areas of interest where finally we
have a real world building as a ttest bed and simulation
engine.

The core reason to write this proposal is to foster
collaborations, those that involve multiple interests,
multiple disciplines, and to devise use cases of the
digital twin beyond the development team. Our gaps are
simply we don't know what we don't know and look forward to
helping others use the data for their own lines of
scientific and design inquiry.	The team currently includes
architecture and engineering faculty, Human Building
Interaction experts, computer scientists, architects,
project manager of the building construction, and design
and computing experts. The team is interfacing with the BMS
and BAS sub contractors and the designers of all
disciplines. The project PI and dev team will be those to
lead this project as an interactive workshop.

We have an operational digital twin that is continuing to
evolve in its capabilities and ecosystem of interested
parties. We are developing the website currently and will
have that up and running shortly. Our focus is on software
development and model and data integrations.

This project is based on over 10 years of building systems
and developing deep research that has been published.

Our goal in putting this proposal is to scale the use of
the system and the number of collaborations interested in
engaging with each other Architecture, engineering,
computer science, and sustainability researchers and
designers who want to engage with the model, the data, and
design computing folks.

The digital twin is near completion and the timeline for
collaborations to be established is this year. This is a
system that has both short term and longitudinal data sets
and collection possibilities. We are actively developing
interest and possible collaborations. We anticipate this to
go on for a long time.

column2:
Xinhui Xu, Yulu Zhang, Wenxuan Wang, Tinghao Feng, Philip
F. Yuan and Zhengcheng He
column3:
Quantifable and unquantifable machine learning model or
architectural preference prediction based on MBTI
column7:
With the explosion of MBTI personality test, architectural
design suggestions based on human personality have been
widely spread. However, this prediction is subjective, and
the results of previous studies on the relationship between
personality and architectural preferences are not complete.
In order to verify this relationship, this research
designed a questionnaire experiment to carry out two
experiments. Firstly, based on the systematic quadruple
model to evaluate aesthetic experiences as quantifiable
standard, then fit the SVM classification model. At last,
finetune the Vision-Language Model according to the
participants' personality characteristics and architectural
preferences for unquantifiable impression, as to imitate
the aesthetic perception ability of different personalities
to buildings and automatically predict the spatial form of
users' preferences. This research has expanded a positive
and innovative way for predicting architectural design
according to personality.

column2: Yutong Wu, Jiani Du, Zhao Zhang and Han Tu
column3:
Beyond Border Vacuums: A Machine Learning Critique of Park
Boundary Vitality in Manhattan’s Contrasting Morphologies
column7:
Jane Jacobs identified key factors such as population
diversity, small block sizes, and building age as essential
contributors to urban vitality and the reduction of
boundary vacuums within her urban theory. Furthermore, she
also argued that enhancing urban vitality promotes
happiness and a sense of belonging among residents.
Traditional methods have struggled to quantify these
concepts, but recent advancements in big data analytics
have enabled more effective assessments of boundary
vitality. To verify Jacobs’ theory quantitatively, this
study used big data, including Points of Interest (POI)
density, to analyze the vitality of park boundaries in
Manhattan and compare the different influential variables
in the Uptown and Downtown districts. The boundaries were
divided into 7,461 uniform grids. Independent variables
such as population diversity, urban form, and building
conditions were considered. POI data revealed that Downtown
exhibited higher vitality than Uptown. Through correlation
analysis and XGBoost regression, key factors, like street
density and land-use diversity, were significant in Uptown
and Downtown. While racial diversity and building
conditions had a more pronounced impact on Uptown.
Moreover, to explore the relationship between sentiments
and urban elements, we assessed positive sentiment through
Google reviews, utilizing VADER sentiment scores. Visual
elements, such as the sky ratio, accounted for 9.54% of the
positive sentiment, while spatial factors, including
housing prices, contributed 15.96%. This research offers a
novel perspective on the relationship between boundary
vitality, public sentiment, and urban elements, supporting
Jacobs' theory while providing quantitative evidence for
human-centered urban design.

column2:
Patrick So, Boyuan Yu, Jianing Luo, Evan Wu, Zhongding Cui
and Provides Ng
column3:
From Craft to Community: A Digital Fabrication Framework
for Participatory Upcycling of Urban Waste
column7:
Sustainable design encompasses social, cultural, and
environmental aspects. A primary challenge is to synthesise
these dimensions into scalable workflows that can integrate
technical innovation with community agency. This paper
presents a participatory framework leveraging digital
fabrication to empower local upcycling capacity,
transforming salvaged wood and discarded plastic into
public furniture. Centered on a case study in Hong Kong’s
dense residential neighbourhoods, the investigation
combines material surveys, Design for Disassembly (DfD),
and CNC fabrication with heat-shrink joints to bridge
community craftsmanship and automated workflows.
Stakeholder feedback from social workers, engineers, and
industry partners refined safety, adaptability, and
scalability of the proposed framework. Results include a
replicable pipeline for community micro-production,
documentation of material constraints, and insights into
balancing structural robustness with participatory
flexibility. By demonstrating how digital tools can help
democratise urban waste upcycling, this proof-of-concept
offers a model for high-density contexts globally to
harmonise environmental resilience with community
empowerment.

column2: Zhixian Li and Sisi Zlatanova
column3:
Heterogeneity in Travel Preferences between Residents and
Tourists: Evidence from Social Media and Street View Imagery
column7:
Understanding the heterogeneous travel preferences of
residents and tourists is essential for the effective
planning and sustainable development of tourist cities.
While previous studies have suggested that travel
preferences are influenced by individuals’ visual
perception, the differences in travel choices between these
groups remain underexplored. Moreover, existing research
often relies heavily on subjective assessments, limiting
the objectivity and scalability of the findings. To address
these limitations, this study integrates social media data
analysis, natural language processing (NLP), and computer
vision techniques to examine the het-erogeneity in
residents' and tourists' emotional responses to urban
environments in Nanjing, China. Specifically, a
Bi-directional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network is
employed to classify sentiments from 20,045 social media
posts, and a deep convolutional neural network is used to
extract semantic fea-tures from 6,008 Baidu Street View
images. The results reveal that both resi-dents’ and
tourists’ sentiments are positively associated with the
presence of “na-ture” and negatively associated with
“enclosure.” Additionally, the “imageability” of the urban
environment exerts a significant positive effect on
tourists’ emotions, but no significant impact is observed
for residents. These findings offer a novel perspective and
methodological framework for investigating the
heterogeneity of travel preferences and provide insights
for the design and development of more inclusive and
appealing tourist cities.

column2: Anat Talmor Blaistain and Dafna Fisher Gewirtzman
column3:
A Quantitative Model for Analyzing Urban Space Symmetry: 
Predicting Spatial Memory in Public Squares
column7:
Interdisciplinary research combining behavioral and
cognitive sciences with computation in the urban field has
been a growing area of interest, particularly in
understanding how people navigate and interact with urban
environments. Wayfinding, the cognitive process of
determining and following a path, involves both route and
spatial learning, where individuals encode spatial
information to find their way through complex environments.
Our approach employs behavioral experiments in virtual
reality (VR), with a focus on wayfinding, to develop robust
analysis and predictive models. These VR-based experiments
allow for precise control over environmental variables and
the collection of detailed behavioral data. Our recent
study explored the influence of symmetry in urban squares
on spatial memory. The findings indicated that less
symmetrical designs made it easier for both young adults
and older adults to remember the locations of targets,
highlighting how symmetry can influence spatial cognition.
Building on these results, our research seeks to bridge a
critical gap in pedestrian network analysis by developing a
quantitative model to evaluate the degree of symmetry in
public urban squares. This model not only assesses current
spatial configurations but also suggests spatial
manipulations that could improve wayfinding and enhance
spatial memory retention. It offers practical insights into
how urban designers can modify existing spaces to foster
better navigational experiences.
In this paper, we delve into the methodology behind the
model's development and demonstrate its application using
both synthetic and realistic case studies, showing how it
can be used to optimize urban design for better pedestrian
experience.

column2:
Sevan Mohammadpour, Angelos Chronis, Oana Taut, Erfan
Rezaei Azari, Cheng Hen Chen and Joshua Oates
column3:
Shadow-Based Path Detection in Rapidly Expanding Urban
Areas: Utilizing shadow detection and graph-based
vectorization to uncover informal road networks in
high-density slum areas
column7:
Shadow detection for path recognition has become a highly
effective method for identifying road networks via
satellite imagery. However, regions with rapid urban
expansion, such as informal settlements, present
significant challenges for traditional mapping approaches.
Resources like OpenStreetMap (OSM) and Geographic
Information Systems (GIS) are often outdated, incomplete,
or limited to high-density areas where government or NGO
initiatives are involved.
Our research addresses this gap by utilizing
high-resolution satellite imagery to detect shadows and
infer paths between structures. We apply AI-based
thresholding to enhance the precision of detected paths.
Dharavi, Mumbai, one of the most densely populated slums,
was chosen for its suitability for comparative analysis and
data validation.
Our methodology includes acquiring high-quality satellite
images, identifying and masking shadows, and then using
skeletonization to extract vector lines representing
central paths. These vectors are refined by constructing a
graph based on node connectivity and edge properties,
merging shorter edges, and adjusting node angles to
optimize the path network. [1],[2]
Results were cross-referenced with data from NGOs and
governmental bodies, such as those involved in the Dharavi
redevelopment projects. Our findings indicate that the
increased detail in path detection is attributed to our
method of splitting satellite imagery into very small
scales, capturing finer shadows and paths. This approach
reveals a more granular network compared to existing
datasets, often uncovering smaller, undocumented pathways.
Additionally, dense clusters of nodes correlate strongly
with connectivity patterns in available data. [3]

references:
1. Mnih, V., & Hinton, G. E. (2010). Learning to Detect
Roads in High-Resolution Aerial Images. Lecture Notes in
Computer Science (LNCS). Springer.
2. Hu, X., Wu, H., & Zeng, Q. (2020). Shadow-Based Road
Detection from High-Resolution Satellite Images Using Deep
Learning. Remote Sensing, 12(9), 1515.
3. Felixx. (2020). Dharavi Redevelopment Project. Felixx
Projects.

column2: Yuhan Li, Iasef Md Rian, Han-Mei Chen and Shu Tang
column3:
Fractal Curve-Based 3D Concrete Printing of Structural
Porous Column
column7:
3D Concrete Printing (3DCP) has gained significant adoption
in construction, especially for load-bearing walls.
However, its application in fabricating columns remains
limited [1], despite the critical role columns play in open
structures with large windows or screens, where traditional
walls are impractical. While solid columns are common,
3D-printed columns using typical truss patterns often lack
the necessary compressive strength [2]. This paper
introduces a novel approach to designing lightweight yet
strong 3D-printed porous columns using fractal geometry.

Fractal curves, with their continuous and space-filling
properties, offer a design solution by enabling controlled
porosity. This not only supports uninterrupted, pause-free
printing but also optimizes the balance between strength
and weight reduction. The study has two key objectives:
first, to apply fractal-based space-filling curves in
developing parametric models for porous columns with
optimized structural performance; second, to balance
reduced material usage with compressive strength and
potential insulation benefits due to increased porosity.

This study adopts a performance-based, fabrication-aware
parametric design approach. The Iterated Function System
(IFS) algorithm will generate space-filling fractal curves
based on the Hilbert system. These models will be tailored
to accommodate the constraints of 3D printing nozzle sizes
and concrete mixtures. Structural simulations using ABAQUS
will validate the designs before printing, followed by
compression testing of the printed column prototype.
Additionally, the research will investigate reinforcing the
3D-printed columns with steel bars to enhance real-world
applicability. This work aims to introduce a new approach
in 3DCP, enabling open, wall-less structures framed by
3D-printed columns and glass facades.

References:
[1] Bos, F. P., Menna, C., Pradena, M., Kreiger, E., da
Silva, W. L., Rehman, A. U., ... & Mechtcherine, V. (2022).
The realities of additively manufactured concrete
structures in practice. Cement and Concrete Research, 156,
106746.
[2] Tabacu, S., & Ducu, C. (2020). Numerical investigations
of 3D printed structures under compressive loads using
damage and fracture criterion: Experiments, parameter
identification, and validation. Extreme Mechanics Letters,
39, 100775.

column2:
Dongming Xu, Weirun Lin, Xinyi Shen, Sherif Eltarabishy and
Davis Adam
column3:
Intelligent Spatial Planning:  A Multidimensional Study on
Swiss Residential Design Using Large Language model (GPT-4)
column7:
This study examines GPT-4's application in architectural
design, focusing on its capability in spatial planning.
Using the Swiss Dwellings dataset, we assess GPT-4’s
ability to understand and generate spatial relationships
and floor plans across three experimental stages. The
research evaluates three aspects of residential design:
compliance with design rules, spatial organi-zation, and
floor plan generation using adjacency matrices. Results
indicate GPT-4 can produce basic layouts for small
apartments and organize spatial relationships to a degree.
However, its performance decreases with greater design
complexity, showing inconsistencies in intricate layouts.
Iterative interactions and corrections improve GPT-4's
accuracy, highlighting its po-tential for refinement
through feedback. This study identifies GPT-4's strengths
and limitations in architectural design, offering guidance
for fu-ture applications and development.

column2: Giancarlo Di Marco, Davide Lombardi and Theodoros Dounas
column3:
The industrialisation of 3D Concrete Printing through
blockchain: Architecture, Engineering and Computer Science
column7:
After more than one century of continuous use of reinforced
concrete, the Architecture Engineering Construction
Operations (AECO) industry can count on highly reliable
expertise and regulation frameworks to foresee and
determine the performance of any structural element.
Recent studies have highlighted the advances brought by new
fabrication technologies such as 3D Concrete Printing
(3DCP); however, they are yet to be fully explored and
implemented by the industry, whose reluctancy is based on
the lack of empirical data and, therefore, of approved
regulatory benchmarks and construction codes.
This clear knowledge gap provides the ground for an
investigation that links the physical and the digital
space, bridging between the fabrication of 3D-Printed
Concrete (3DPC) elements and the Web3 technologies for the
validation of the empirical experimentation tests.
Our research lies at the intersection of Architecture,
Engineering and Computer Science, and aims to contribute to
defining a regulatory framework for using 3DCP in the AECO
industry through the progressions made in determining the
mechanical properties of 3DPC under various conditions and
production technologies. By using two research labs, one
located in Europe and the other in Asia, we use robotic
concrete 3D printing and Decentralised Ledger Technologies
(DLTs) to address the following research questions: can the
structural performance of (reinforced) 3DPC be
standardised? Can DLTs act as a reliable infrastructure
tool for supporting the creation of a robust regulatory
framework for the industrialisation of 3DCP?

column2: Caner Baydur, Provides Ng and Esra Nartkaya
column3:
Historical Soundscape with Metaverse: An Audio-visual
Experiment on the Adaptive Reuse of Heritage Architecture
column7:
Thisstudyexplorestheintegrationofsoundscapedesigninto the
adaptive reuse of heritage sites. Leveraging multiplayer
immersive technologies in metaverse, the research aims to
design an experiment framework that can engage different
stakeholders to co-create an audio- visual experience for
heritage sites. With the help of metaverse, how to set up
an experiment to understand the influence of soundscape
elements on visitor experiences in heritage spaces? The
methodology includes field research involving sound
recordings and categorisation, photogrammetry
documentation, followed by an initial experiment in
metaverse recon- structing audio-visual scenarios. A site
in Safranbolu (a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Türkiye) was
chosen as a case study, which currently emphasises
visual-oriented preservation, making it ideal for a compar-
ative study between audio-visual and visual-only
conservation, yielding insights on soundscape design
applicable to a variety of heritage contexts.

column2: Tai Shobuya, Yuval Kahlon, Yukiharu Iioka and Haruyuki Fujii
column3:
How do AI-based Suggestions Support Designing in Immersive
Environments? Using Generated Images as Visual References
for Architectural Design in Mixed Reality
column7:
Recent advancements in Generative Artificial Intelligence
(GenAI) and Mixed Reality (MR) are reshaping design
workflows, yet their integration into architectural
processes remains limited. This study investigates the
potential of an AI recommendation system (AIRS) to
facilitate ideation and enhance creativity and efficiency
in the conceptual design phase. By employing Stable
Diffusion (SD) within a Voxel-based MR freehand Sketching
Environment (VSE), the system provides
similarity-controlled visual references, aiming to
stimulate ideation and accelerate iterations of
prototyping. A two-stage experiment involving 10
participants was executed, to assess the system’s impact on
creativity, efficiency, and user experience. Participants
completed two design tasks, one with the system and one
without, resulting in 20 furniture prototypes. Quantitative
and qualitative feedback reveal that the AIRS can enhance
creativity by encouraging idea exploration, helping to
overcome design fixation and materialize abstract concepts.
It also improved workflow efficiency, supporting rapid
prototyping and iterative design refinement. The outputs
indicated that near-field stimuli helped detail concepts,
while far-field stimuli inspired reinterpretation and
unconventional approaches. However, challenges such as
inconsistent alignment with user expectations, technical
limitations in the VSE, and ergonomic constraints were
identified. Recommendations for future development include
increasing the number and accessibility of generated
images, incorporating contextual information for better
relevance, and expanding the system to virtual reality
environments, for greater flexibility and scalability.
These enhancements can aid to unlock the potential of
integrated GenAI and MR systems into architectural
workflows, boosting creativity and efficiency in designing.

column2: Yiming Liu and Christiane M. Herr
column3:
Performance-based Urban Environmental Restoration: A
Multi-Layer Cellular Automata Model for Ecological Design
Simulation in High-Density Cities
column7:
Abstract:

High-density built-up areas have fragmented natural
habitats, negatively impacting the environment and human
health. In this context, new design strategies for creating
sustainable and resilient built environments are needed,
where building facades reconnect natural and urban
environments[1]. As complex multi-layered systems,
ecological façades are influenced by various environmental
factors that change over time. However, existing ecological
façade research has typically focused on static analyses of
specific environmental situations [2]. To address this
challenge, we propose a multi-layered Cellular Automata
(CA) model capable of generating ecological
performance-oriented façade forms.

Previous ecological research has employed CA models, which
are characterized by local relationships driving dynamic
global changes, as digital representations of ecosystems to
help understand and predict the complex behaviours of
natural systems. Customized CA models have also been used
as generative strategies for the design of liveable
microbial habitats on building façades [3].

The multi-layered CA model presented in this paper supports
the interactive evaluation and generation of ecologically
responsive urban environments. Firstly, environmental
factors such as solar radiation and wind pressure are
embedded into the ecological model as constraints and
influencing factors. Then, by combining these environmental
data with the existing ecological model, potential growing
spaces for plants are generated and analysed in comparison
with the existing environmental conditions to assess their
ecological viability. The innovation and contribution of
CA-based design support system is its ability to integrate
the mapping of multiple environmental input parameters with
the bottom-up dispersion and growth dynamics found in
various aspects of natural ecosystems.

References

Grobman, T.E. Hauck, J. Joschinski, F. Ludwig, A. Mimet, K.

integrating ecology, architecture and computational design,
People and Nature 5 (2023) 4–20.
https://doi.org/10.1002/pan3.10411.
[2]	S.U. Selvan, L. Windorfer, A. Calbi, S.T. Saroglou, E.

ENVELOPES, in: ACCELERATED DESIGN - Proceedings of the 29th
International Conference of the Association for Computer
Aided Architectural Design Research in Asia (CAADRIA) 2024,
Singapore, 2024: pp. 535–544.
[3]	C.M. Herr, C. Li, Articulating Facade Microbiomes at
Human Scale: A Cellular Automata Driven Bioreceptive Facade
Design Approach to Communicate a New Dimension of Urban

column2: Ilayda Memis, Frank Petzold and Gerhard Schubert
column3:
Architectural Interfaces for Shared Spaces – A Multi-User
Perspective on Intelligent Environment Interactions
column7:
Current examples of intelligent environments aim to
automate certain functions in buildings to relieve humans
of redundant tasks. However, not having any information
about the changes in the environment promotes the feeling
of being controlled. Recent developments in the
human-building interaction field focus rather on
human-centered designs, which offer people more control
over these systems. The interfaces that are created to
provide control are usually de-signed with one user in
mind. Most of the research on Human-Computer Interac-tion
(HCI) also focuses on the interaction between one person
and one interface. However, in cases where the space is
inhabited by many people, this system of control and its
communication becomes more complex. Therefore, there is a
need for interfaces that represent environment-related
information within a shared ar-chitectural space. This
argument applies to cases where multiple people would
prefer to control their immediate environment, including
shading, heating, and ventilation, as well as wayfinding in
crowded environments, such as conferences, fairs, and
concerts. Instead of distributing this information to
individual cell-phones, it can be embedded within
architectural space, as envisioned in ubiqui-tous computing
systems. This means that the architectural space itself
becomes the interface, allowing for a more seamless and
integrated interaction and offer-ing more social and
collective experiences. This paper will provide the theory
and necessary literature demonstrating the need for and the
potential of architec-tural interfaces for shared spaces. A
framework for a potential system will be proposed regarding
HCI and ubiquitous computing research from an architectural
perspective.

column2: Adam Sebestyen, Albert Wiltsche and Ozan Özdenizci
column3:
(CI) From CAAD to Deep Learning: Developing 3D Data
Representation for Generative Neural Networks
column7:
Our proposal explores the development of 3D data
representation techniques for generative neural networks in
architectural design.  Current AI tools like DALL·E 3 and
MidJourney produce 2D pixel-based outputs, limiting their
utility for architects.  Existing research towards 3D AI
CAAD tools face challenges such as inadequate 3D data for
training and the absence of a standard 3D data format. Our
research aims to address these issues by converting CAAD
geometries into a format suitable for neural networks and
vice versa, using NURBS and BSpline techniques.  This
approach promises precise and efficient handling of complex
shapes, overcoming the limitations of current voxel, SDF,
or Mesh representations.  The ultimate goal is to develop a
Grasshopper plug-in that automates these conversions,
facilitating the generation of detailed 3D architectural
designs. The proposal seeks collaboration to refine these
methods and gather feedback from practitioners on the
utility and effectiveness of the proposed workflow.

column2:
M. Hank Haeusler, Azia Carothers, Cristina Ramos Jaime,
Ivana Kuzmanovska and Christopher Bamborough
column3: Consolidated Empirical Bio-material Repository
column7:
This paper introduces mycelium-based composites as
innovative, low-emission materials with potential
applications in the built environment. With global
ecological concerns escalating, the quest for sustainable
build-ing materials is paramount. Focusing on
mycelium-based heat-pressed pan-els as a prototype for
future bio-local, low-emission building materials, this
paper outlines steps toward practical implementation while
examining key factors influencing the mechanical properties
of mycelium-based compo-sites. By consolidating existing
knowledge (68 papers) using bibliometric methodology, the
paper considers the variables at each of the four key
phases of developing and testing mycelium-based materials,
namely material selection and preparation, environmental
control and optimisation, material processing and
treatments and structural behaviour testing. Without
standardisation in material development and testing
methodology ensuring reliable and consistent results,
mycelium-based composites may fail to meet future
compliance criteria, essential for substituting
carbon-intensive materials. Our literature review informs
the formulation of a best practice frame-work and
underscores the importance of consistent fabrication for
structural behaviour analysis. Our study not only enhances
understanding of mycelium's architectural potential but
also establishes a groundwork for standardized utilization
in the architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC)
sector. By offering a coherent approach to material
development and predictive performance assessment, this
research contributes to advancing low emission building
materials and fostering sustainability in the built
environment.

column2: Xuyou Yang and Immanuel Koh
column3:
AI2D-Architecture: a Benchmark for Evaluating Multimodal
Large Language Models in Architecture
column7:
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs), e.g., GPT-4o
(OpenAI, 2024) and Stable Diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022)
have demonstrated extraordinary performance in many tasks.
Various benchmarks, e.g. MathVista (Lu et al., 2023) and
AI2D (Kembhavi et al., 2016) benchmark for evaluating
mathematical reasoning and understanding of science
diagrams of MLLMs respectively, have also been developed to
assess MLLMs’ ability in specific domains or tasks. Despite
the growing number of benchmarks, little attention has been
given to developing one that evaluates how MLLMs perform in
architectural tasks, even as MLLMs’ applications in the
architecture domain are rapidly expanding.

This research develops a benchmark, AI2D-Architecture, to
evaluate the MLLMs’ ability to understand architectural
diagrams. Diagram is the fundamental technique and
procedure of architectural knowledge (Somol, 2010). As both
an explanatory or analytical device and a generative device
(Eisenman, 1999), it  visually mediates disordered and
complex information (Fraser, 2012). Comprehending
architectural diagrams is crucial for adapting MLLMs to
architectural tasks, and a suitable benchmark is essential
for evaluating this ability.

Specifically, a testing set consisting of various
architectural diagrams and questions is carefully
organised. Then, the benchmark is tested with a wide range
of MLLMs. Quantitative results are obtained, demonstrating
that these MLLMs perform very differently on
AI2D-Architecture, and MLLMs with high performance on other
benchmarks may not perform well on the proposed benchmark. 
It implies that AI2D-Architecture can reflect MLLMs’
ability to understand architectural diagrams. As a
preliminary study, it exemplifies one possibility for
evaluating the application of artificial intelligence in
architecture.

column2:
M. Hank Haeusler, Ivana Kuzmanovska, Christopher
Bamborough, Mark Burry, Jane Burry, Michael Ostwald, Blair
Kuys, Sisi Zlatanova and George Shinkle
column3:
(CI) Collaborative Pathways to Sustainable Digital
Innovation in AEC
column7:
The Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC)
sector faces the immense challenge of helping nations meet
their net-zero targets by 2050. Simultaneously, the global
population is projected to increase by 2 billion, reaching
9.7 billion by 2050, requiring thriving built environments.
Addressing these challenges demands significantly increased
professional efforts and necessitates collaboration between
academia and practice in innovative ways.

As some of Australia’s and the world’s leading
Architecture, Design, and Engineering (ADE) practices and
professional bodies, we have responded by establishing the
ARC Centre for Next-Gen Architectural Manufacturing
(Arch_Manu ITTC), an Industrial Transformation Training
Centre, funded by the Australian Research Council with
AUS$16M. Our mission is to transform the national ADE
professions to meet Australia’s immediate strategic needs,
specifically addressing productivity and climate goals
through digital transformation.

We leverage partnerships between academia (UNSW Sydney,
Swinburne University of Technology, Adelaide University,
Bartlett UCL London, CITA Copenhagen, IAAC Barcelona), with
expertise in architecture, computer science, engineering,
construction management, business and management, and IT
systems, along with industry (Architectus, Cox, Bollinger
Grohmann, Grimshaw, Tzannes), and peak bodies (Australian
Institute of Architects, Association of Consulting
Architects Australia, Architects Accreditation Council of
Australia, and NSW Registration Board). Together, we bring
world-leading researchers, visionary practitioners, and
talented graduates to integrate cutting-edge research into
practice.

Our program, which includes 28 industry-embedded PhDs,
national and international placements, short courses, and 3
postdoctoral projects, will build digital knowledge,
skills, and capacity within the Australian AEC sector
across three themes: Synthesis, Management, and Analytics.

A centre of this scale offers the opportunity to rethink
the academic/industry research nexus and contribute
globally to the question: How can industry-embedded PhDs be
conducted collaboratively to achieve sustainable digital
innovations in the AEC sector?
Our research into this novel academic/industry nexus draws
on insights from Chief Investigator Prof. Mark Burry, who,
in the early 2000s, conducted six embedded PhD research
projects with industry partners at SIAL/RMIT University in
Melbourne. A second iteration followed in the mid-2010s
with the EU-funded InnoChain network, a large-scale
research initiative into the digital
design-to-materialisation chain, which included robotic
manufacturing and involved six leading academic
institutions and 14 pioneering industry partners. Three
Partner Investigators in our Centre (Areti, Sheil,
Ramsgaard-Thompson) were leaders of the InnoChain network.
Both the SIAL/RMIT and InnoChain initiatives embedded PhD
candidates with individual industry partners for the
duration of their studies. Both have contributed to the
development of embedded PhD research in the CAAD community.

Arch_Manu aimed to alter this approach and thus offer a
point of difference and contribution to knowledge by
understanding the research by the individual PhD students
and by the centre as a group – to precise as a network of
academics (26 in 6 institution) with a network of PhD
students (28) and a network of industry and peak body
partners (9). Hence, we outlined a different format for
engaging with partners through the following three
engagement frameworks.
1) Intranet - For the sake of easy and streamlined
communication and sharing, we have developed an intranet
through which announcements, events, partner engagements,
and sharing of documents will be coordinated.
2) Partner engagement and interaction - We have developed
three avenues for partner engagement and interaction: the
engagement request cycle, and the hackathon cycle, which
will both be described below: a) Engagement request cycle.
The research is industry-led and we expect that Arch_Manu
PhD researchers will spend a portion of candidature
embedded within our partner organisations. Unlike typical
embedded PhD models, we will be trialling a different
approach with our PhD program. Each PhD candidate will have
the opportunity to engage with all of the Partner
Organisations affiliated with the Centre, if appropriate
and desirable for the required research outcomes. Partner
engagement will be managed through a formal research
engagement request process, triggered by the submission of
a form on the intranet. The requests can be submitted by
PhD candidates or by Partner Investigators, and they can
range in scope and complexity from entire projects, to
small, targeted research activities, or through to simple
requests for specific data or interviews. Requests will be
reviewed and approved by the Arch_Manu Executive Committee.
Once approved, the Centre management team will facilitate
an initial meeting with relevant stakeholders to define and
agree on project objectives, timeline and deliverables. b)
Hackathon Cycle. To encourage development of solutions in
the short term (low hanging fruit, so to speak), Arch_Manu
ITTC will be running a series of Hackathons. They will be
open to participation from all CIs, PIs, and PhDs, as well
as nominated partner representatives. c) Data requests. To
provide data required for research mainly in management and
analytics.
3) PhD Handbook - With three different Australian based
universities with different PhD requirements and the aims
and KPIs of Arch_Manu we developed a PhD handbook.

The Centre commenced in early 2024, with 50% of PhD
students enrolled (the rest to follow by early 2025), two
hackathons completed, data requests underway, and the first
PhD students embedded. We are now able to report and
discuss initial findings.

We propose that we have developed a novel interdisciplinary
research approach that interfaces with multiple CAAD
topics. Through this proposal, we invite collaboration with
like-minded teams to initiate discussions and share
findings during the CAAD Futures 2025 conference.

In conclusion, the Arch_Manu industry engagement model
differs significantly from traditional industry PhD models,
which pair candidates with a single industry partner for
the entire duration of their studies. By offering flexible
collaboration opportunities across the Centre, we hope to
achieve mutually beneficial outcomes. We believe that we
have a rare opportunity to align 28 PhD research projects
with the immediate needs of industry and, in doing so,
drive meaningful change. To achieve this, we must work
together towards shared goals. We hope to outline the
Arch_Manu philosophy and approach, and discuss it at CAAD
Futures 2025.

[1] https://archmanu.com/, accessed Sept 2024.
[2] https://innochain.net/about/, accessed Sept 2024.

column2: Qi Wang, Zhiyong Dong, Maowei Jiang, Peter Búš and Yusong Hu
column3:
MR-RL-Robot: A Smart System for Enhanced Construction
Safety and Efficiency
column7:
Worker safety and operational efficiency remain critical
challenges in the architecture, engineering, construction,
and operations (AECO) industry, particularly within dynamic
and hazard-prone environments. This study presents an
integrated system that combines mixed reality (MR),
reinforcement learning (RL), and robotic automation to
enhance safety management and optimize prefabricated
component assembly. The proposed approach incorporates
real-time risk zone detection, multi-sensor MR-based
guidance, and a cable-driven robotic agent trained via
reinforcement learning to autonomously navigate obstacles,
grasp components, and execute precise placement tasks. The
system operates entirely offline, utilizing local
processing and sensor fusion, including eye tracking, hand
gesture recognition, and spatial mapping, to ensure
reliability without dependence on external networks. A
fail-safe mechanism automatically halts robotic actions in
high-risk areas, while multi-sensor confirmation reduces
false positives and mitigates user alert fatigue.
Experimental evaluation was conducted through a comparative
study between a conventional 2D drawing-based workflow and
the proposed MR–robotic system. Results indicate that the
system reduced high-risk zone intrusions by 85.7%, low-risk
zone entries by 81.3%, and manual intervention prompts by
83.1%. Furthermore, task completion time was reduced by
38%, from an average of 21.6 minutes to 13.4 minutes. These
results demonstrate the system’s effectiveness in improving
on-site safety, reducing human oversight, and accelerating
construction processes. The findings underscore the
potential of MR-guided, RL-enabled robotic solutions to
advance automation practices in prefabricated construction
and contribute to safer, more efficient building
environments.

column2: Ayodh V. Kamath
column3:
Quantitative Information Processing in Making Grammars:
Applications in Intangible Cultural Heritage Practices
column7:
Making computations simulate the process of making things
as the iterative application of the rules of a making
grammar. Applying fundamental concepts from information
theory to making grammars, this paper develops a method to
quantify the information processed in making computations.
This method is then tested as a tool for learning,
recording and propagating intangible heritage practices
(IHPs) in an autoethnographic investigation of making
grammars.
Kolam making is an IHP of ritual drawings at the entrances
to houses, temples and other buildings in South India.
While kolams have been an ongoing subject of generative
design research for at least five decades (Siromoney,
Siromoney, and Krithivasan 1974; Jablan 2001; Ascher 2002;
Demaine et al. 2007; Subramanian, Saravanan, and Robinson
2007; Knight and Sass 2010), most of this research has
focused on the procedural generation of completed kolam
patterns rather than the processes and practices by which
kolams are made. While recent research has recognised this
lacuna, it has been limited to the development of making
grammars from indirect observations of kolam practitioners
(Knight 2018). This paper autoethnographically tests the
author’s use of making grammars as a tool to both learn
kolam making, and simultaneously to record and analyse the
learning process qualitatively and quantitatively.
Thus, paper develops a method to quantify the information
processed in making computations, and applies this method
to understand the utility of making grammars in learning,
recording and propagating IHPs, including discussing the
impact of materiality and individual subjectivity on making
computations.

References:
Ascher, Marcia. 2002. Mathematics Elsewhere: An Exploration
of Ideas Across Cultures. Princeton: Princeton University
Press.
Demaine, E. D., M. L. Demaine, P. Taslakian, and G. T.

Journal of Mathematics and the Arts 1 (2): 125–32.

Mathematical Connections in Art, Music, and Science,
233–46. Winfield, Kansas.
Knight, Terry. 2018. “Craft, Performance, and Grammars.” In
Computational Studies on Cultural Variation and Heredity,
edited by Ji-Hyun Lee, 205–24. Singapore: Springer
Singapore.
Knight, Terry, and Lawrence Sass. 2010. “Looks Count:
Computing and Constructing Visually Expressive Mass
Customized Housing.” AI EDAM 24:425–45.

1974. “Array Grammars and Kolam.” Computer Graphics and

column2: Qianrong Li and Chenyu Zhang
column3:
A Study on the Factors Influencing the Willingness to Use
AIGC Creative Tools in Architectural Design
column7:
In architectural design, Artificial Intelligence Generated
Content (AIGC) technologies are increasingly being
integrated into design tools to enhance architects'
creative expression and design efficiency. However, the
acceptance and willingness of architects to adopt these
AI-driven tools are influenced by various factors,
particularly the quality of the interactive experience.
This study examines the key factors affecting architects'
willingness to use AIGC tools, focusing on interaction
quality, information quality, system performance, and
aesthetic performance. Grounded in the Technology
Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Stimulus-Organism-Response
(SOR) theory, and incorporating Perceived Value Theory, the
research develops a conceptual model encompassing seven
variables: interaction quality, information quality, system
performance, aesthetic performance, perceived usefulness,
perceived ease of use, and usage intention.
A total of 350 valid responses were collected via an online
questionnaire, and empirical analysis was conducted using
Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). The analysis was
carried out in two stages: first, evaluating the
reliability and validity of the measurement model, and
second, testing the hypotheses within the structural model.
The results demonstrate that the measurement model is
highly reliable and valid, with most hypotheses being
supported. Interaction quality, information quality, system
performance, and aesthetic performance are identified as
critical factors influencing architects' willingness to
adopt AIGC tools. Additionally, perceived usefulness and
perceived ease of use mediate the relationship,
significantly affecting usage intention.
This study provides empirical evidence supporting the
application of AIGC tools in architectural design and
offers recommendations for optimizing user experience and
system performance to encourage greater adoption.

column2:
Mehmet Onur Senem, Salih Özdemir, Orkan Zeynel Güzelci and
Sema Alaçam
column3:
A Magnetic Robotic End Effector for Pin Formation and
Concrete Reinforcement: An Innovative Design-to-Production
Approach
column7:
The study introduces a Design-to-Production Framework
(D2PF) for a 6-axis robotic arm equipped with a magnetic
end effector, aiming to explore the formation of metal pins
into desired shapes under the influence of magnetic forces.
The process is applied in an experimental setup where
magnetic-sensitive metal pins are used as reinforcement in
concrete blocks. The research investigates the relationship
between the initial geometry, robotic movements, and the
structural outcomes.
Three experiments were conducted, each involving the
formation of concrete blocks, with varying reinforcement
configurations: no reinforcement, spiral, and circular
arrangements of pins. These blocks were tested using a
3-point bending test to assess their structural strength.
The results demonstrated that blocks reinforced with spiral
and circular pin formations showed significantly improved
tensile strength compared to those without reinforcement.
In particular, the spiral reinforcement exhibited the
highest tensile strength and resistance to cracking, with
the block continuing to bear loads even after initial
failure.
The study concludes that robotic-assisted magnetic pin
formations can improve the structural properties of
cement-based materials, mimicking the behavior of
reinforced concrete. The results suggest potential
applications in scaled-up versions of this system for
larger structures. Limitations were noted, such as the need
to optimize magnetic force and control the height of the
robotic tool path. Future research may focus on material
variations, scalability, and the integration of this
technology into recycling processes for metal-laden
construction waste.
