column2:
Peter Russell, Marc Aurel Schnabel, Henri Achten and Urs
Hirscheberg
column3:
(CI) Bespoke Built Environment Education – enabling
emerging profiles in the AEC industry
column7:
Outlook
The situation facing humanity, but especially the
architecture, engineering and construction industry (AEC),
is complex, to say the least. Independent of the COVID-19
pandemic, the combination of overlapping global challenges
has added unprecedented pressure on the industry to respond
with improvements that are not just incremental, but
ground-breaking.

To demonstrate, consider three factors: human population
growth, carbon emission targets and the quality of human
life.
1. The population of the planet is expected by 2050 to
reach approximately ten billion people. This is an
additional 2.5 billion people to today’s 7.5 billion
population (or an additional 1/3). In order to maintain our
current standards of living, this means we need to do more
with less and be more efficient in our processes as a whole
(this translates to an efficiency of 75% / person).
2. The carbon emission targets of the COP21 Paris accord
foresees a reduction to 1990 levels of carbon output. This
means that from current CO2 levels, society as a whole will
need to reduce its impact by a factor of four (25% /
person).
3. Each individual on the planet is striving for a better
quality of life. This often means consumption, whether it
is food, a communication device, personal mobility, or a
part of the built environment to call one’s own. As the
population collectively grows wealthier, there is a
pressure to produce and consume more. Nonetheless, the
resources available are limited and estimates are that we
need to produce the same quality with half the output (50%
/ person).

Each of these issues would be daunting on its own.
Combined, they form a formidable, if not existential
challenge. By combining the efficiencies described above,
we can calculate that:
0,75 [more people] x 0,25 [less CO2] x 0,50 [resource
efficiency] = 0,094 =
the need to be 10+ times more efficient!

Essentially, the AEC industry needs to be able to reduce
its impact on the environment by a factor of ten (one
magnitude). This is not simply a wish to do the right thing
where we encourage everyone to 'do their best'. The AEC
industry consumes almost 40% of the world’s physical
resources, consumes approximately 40% of the energy, and
produces around 40% of the carbon emissions.

In addition to the calculations of net CO2, the creation
and stewardship of the built environment must also consider
issues such as poverty, health, governance, and
inclusivity. The UN sustainable development goals [UN 2015]
encompass the range of humanity’s challenges, and many of
them are stongly related to a well-termpered built
environment. That is to say, re-designing and
re-engineering the design and engineering of the built
environment is an existential mission. The future of the
human (and non-human) habitat depends on it.

The imperative to improve means an imperative to be digital.
Achieving the construction industry’s major social
objectives (CO2 reduction, safety, water, circularity,
construction volume, etc.) will require better tools,
better methodologies, better information, and better
processes. These tools will certainly be digitally based.
In essence, the AEC industry needs a wholehearted digital
paradigm shift. The digital revolution in architecture and
engineering will be disruptive, but just as in other
industries, disruption creates opportunities.

It is already evident that the digital revolution has
reached the doorstep of the construction industry. This is
an opportunity: the digital processes developed elsewhere
are ideally suited for the construction industry’s methods
of customised production. However, these processes require
completely different ways of working and thinking: shared
knowledge instead of owned knowledge, circular
communication instead of linear transmission, common
responsibility as opposed to limited liability, and
continued involvement even after delivery.  It also
requires equality between the various partners in the
design and project delivery chain. Existing boundaries
between professions are blurring, which means that current
forms of quality assurance will no longer suffice. It calls
for different roles, renewed involvement of the client and
a different definition of the collective and individual
assignments. Above all, it calls for skills that are
currently not or rarely offered in higher education and
vocational programmes, and certainly are scarce in practice.

This shift has resulted in new ways of working, requiring
additional professional skills and new optics on the design
and construction tasks. The skill-set necessary at any
point in a construction project often becomes a dynamic
balance of a variety of roles and functions and the
composition of those functions requires a combination of
skills in an interdisciplinary team. And it is clear:
achieving a tenfold increase in efficiency and
effectiveness will need strong integrated interdisciplinary
teamwork.

This means that any team and its members need to be versed
in a broad range of overlapping skills to work efficiently
as an interdisciplinary team. It requires team members that
can work together on complex issues, understanding each
other’s methodologies and knowledge.
 
The consequence for education and professional profiles
Traditionally, we have educated professionals in the AEC
industry with a so-called ‘T-Profile’. The ‘T’ refers to a
broad range of knowledge with some depth and deeper
knowledge in a narrow range or field. This kind of
education makes up almost all of the current professional
education in the AEC industry.

Interdisciplinary teamwork requires a different kind of
knowledge: a PI (or π) profile. [Burry, White 2020] This
means that professionals have an additional depth of
knowledge alongside their traditional field-specific ones.
This additional set of knowledge serves as an overlap on
interdisciplinary teams. It means that the insights from
one professional can be transferred and multiplied with the
next. In fact, there is a strong case for an ‘m’ profile,
where three legs of knowledge create a stable platform for
decision-making.

Therefore, the future of the profession depends on
educating the next generation of professionals with
multiple profiles (from 'T' to 'π' or m-profile). It will
mean revising if not redesigning the curriculum of
professional architecture and engineering education. This
will not be easy, given that both are protected
professions, with professional associations granting access
to the profession based on a set of pre-defined educational
criteria. Nonetheless, the imperative to change is clear
and if the work of revising the curriculum will take a long
time, then it needs to start now.

In terms of professional development, the introduction of
new skills both in education and in the market needs to
speed up. One of the knock-on effects of the COVID-19
pandemic has been to acclimatise both higher education and
continuing education to online delivery of content. This
means that the mental hurdle to formatting content suitable
for remote study has already happened. This increases the
opportunities for wider dissemination in terms of
demographics, location and specific knowledge domains.

In terms of tertiary education, this opens the possibility
to share content across knowledge domains. This is key to
developing the PI-profile is not a single two-domain
combination of knowledge, but as varied as there are people
with their own interests, skill sets and motivations. In
short, enabling a PI-Profile education will need the widest
available options in order to facilitate highly motivated
graduates for our industry. In parts of the world where
tertiary education is a privilege, the decoupling of
knowledge delivery from siloed field-specific domains can
enable micro-degrees and the ability to acquire credentials
through the accumulation of tailored, bespoke curricula
from a variety of educational institutions.

In terms of continuing education, this opens the
possibility to finally address a bugbear of the industry:
flat productivity growth. In other industries (electronics,
automotive, etc.), productivity growth has increased
between 25% to 35% over the past twenty years. In the AEC
industry, it has been flat and even negative in some
regions.  Providing a range of content for
life-long-learning will allow individuals to update their
own domain-specific knowledge and expand theirs to include
other domains. This has the prospect of ensuring that
previous as well as recent graduates remain relevant to the
industry. This also will be needed to ensure that the
changes in the industry can and will be embedded in
professional practice, organisations, and institutions.

Managing educational complexity
Education is evolving. Digital technologies have also
entered design pedagogy. Initially as a ‘nice to have’
option and now, under pressure from the SARS-COVID2
pandemic, on a massive scale, the past year has brought a
wealth of experience. For example, the Digital Futures 2020
conference in July 2020 was attended by thousands of
lecturers and students from all over the world providing
both direct knowledge (how the workshops were delivered)
and meta knowledge (how we see the future of the
university). This experience demonstrates that revising
education is possible. The pandemic has simply shone a
light on this fact.

Normally, developing a new curriculum, implementing it, and
having the first cohort of students graduate from it,
requires 6 to 8 years. The demands of the profession, the
industry, society and the planet cannot wait that long.
Educational revision needs to be much quicker, more
productive, more responsive and more ingenious. In short,
we need to rethink how we think of the curriculum and we
likely need help in doing so. This is especially so with
the mandate to create individual PI-Profile curricula,
tailored to each individual student.

Bespoke Education
Managing the complexity of creating tailored individual
curricula is essentially the problem of managing complex
information, albeit a special kind: the description of
courses and content that make up a professional education.
If one considers a curriculum description as a kind of
story, then it is clear that there are tools to help with
this process. Machine learning processes already are able
to produce natural language, especially when limited to a
specific domain. The GPT language prediction models from
the open.ai consortium have already provided reasonable
basis texts that come close to being indistinguishable from
human produced ones. By using a data set of previous
design,  and other curricula, it is possible to produce
frameworks for individual curricula, which, after review by
scholars, can be accepted for implementation.

Thus, a combination of artificial intelligence and
scholarly curation could alleviate the burden of managing
the complexity and perhaps even produce heretofore unseen
combinations of PI-profile and m-profile curricula. This
combination will also guarantee the quality from the
various perspectives: the individual candidate and their
ambitions, the needs of the profession, and the societal
expectations to solve the global challenges facing this
generation.

The goal of this Catalytic Interfaces session is to issue a
statement on the need for architectural education reform
that is free from the previous century’s view of what
architects and their brethren should know or need to know.
If possible, we will launch a working group to pursue a
path toward bespoke architectural and urban system
education.

References
Burry, J. and White, M. (2020), From ‘T’ to ‘π’ (pi)-shaped
people: Better Urban Practice through Dual Depth in
Architecture and Planning Education. Archit. Design, 90:
114-121.

United Nations Sustainable Development Goals 2015 >
https://sdgs.un.org

column2:
Alexander Urban, Moritz Koegel, Lukas Fink Pielsticker,
Alexander Karaivanov, Nicolaj Kirisits and Zeynep Aksöz
Balzar
column3:
Resonant Blech: Emergent Soundscapes Through Human-AI
Interaction
column7:
Resonant Blech is an interdisciplinary project exploring
the intersection of architecture, sound, and artificial
intelligence (AI), transforming architectural objects into
autonomous sonic entities. The project employs a modular
system of lightweight, curved-crease folded steel
structures, capable of interacting with their surroundings
via resonant feedback sounds.

The central research question investigates how AI can be
embodied in an architectural context by autonomously
controlling sound feedback loops that resonate through the
structure. Based on this motivation, the project explores
how these sculptural objects facilitate sound-based
interactions through feedback loops at their inherent
eigenfrequencies.

The goal is to generate dynamic, polyphonic spatial
compositions in collaboration with human performers. The
challenge lies in using AI to control multiple feedback
loops, generating a spatial soundscape that adapts to its
environment. The AI manages signal routing, frequency
filtering, and amplitude adjustments, enabling a fluid
interaction between the structure, its surroundings, and
performers.

Structurally, a modular system of curved-crease folding
objects has been developed. Based on digital folding
simulations and prototypes, the design enables pronounced
resonances while maintaining structural stability. The
modules can be assembled in various configurations to adapt
to performance spaces, with each setup producing unique
sound spatiality and timbre.

This research demonstrates that AI can effectively generate
sound within a modular architectural framework,
transforming built environments into interactive,
performative instruments that offer immersive sensory
experiences.

column2: Zimu Bao, Zilu Wang, Hanzhe Bao and Sky Lo
column3:
Digital Twin for Road Traffic Networks:  A Colour
Recognition Approach to Mapping and Simulation
column7:
Digital twin technology has emerged as a transformative
solution for creating dynamic, real-time connections
between physical and virtual environments. This paper
presents a novel system for developing digital twins of
road traffic networks using a low-cost approach based on
colour recognition and the Internet of Things (IoT). The
system enables users to assemble modular physical road
models, which are mapped into virtual counterparts using a
mobile car equipped with a colour sensor. As the car
navigates the physical road model, the sensor captures
surface colours, transmitting the data to a microcontroller
that processes and sends it to a computer for further
analysis. The computer interprets the data to generate an
accurate, interactive virtual road model.The virtual model
integrates seamlessly with virtual reality (VR) technology,
allowing users to explore the road network from a
first-person perspective while supporting bi-directional
interaction—adjustments made in the virtual environment are
dynamically reflected in the physical model. This approach
reduces system complexity and costs while maintaining high
accuracy in physical-to-virtual mapping. At this stage, the
research focuses on validating the feasibility of using
colour recognition for physical-to-virtual mapping in road
traffic networks.Key findings demonstrate the potential of
the system to achieve seamless transformation between
physical and virtual models, laying the groundwork for
future applications. This paper explores the design,
implementation, and verification of the proposed system,
contributing to the development of digital twin
technologies that are user-friendly, cost-effective,
responsive, and reliable.

column2: Quan Zhou, Yize Li, Zejian Li and Immanuel Koh
column3:
ConStructGNN: A Graph Neural Network Framework for Adaptive
3D Architectural Layout
column7:
This study proposes a workflow, ConStructGNN, that
integrates geometric, semantic, and topological information
to address the challenges of 3D spatial layout during the
architectural conceptual design stage. ConStructGNN employs
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to predict spatial features
and infer layout rules. In the preprocessing phase, a
node-edge graph automatically extracts spatial elements
from building models and encodes them into graph datasets
with 3D nodes and topological relationships. Leveraging
this structured representation, ConStructGNN facilitates
designers to create conceptual layout plans by defining 3D
graphs, which serve as intuitive abstractions of spatial
logic, similar to bubble diagrams in early design stages.
To verify their accuracy, spatial consistency is assessed
using Hausdorff distance to compare predicted and input
graphs. Experimental results on representative cases show
that ConStructGNN achieves a spatial similarity exceeding
95%, demonstrating its effectiveness in generating
consistent architectural spatial layouts and improving the
efficiency of conceptual design.

column2: Siyue Zhang and Sky Tian Tian Lo
column3:
Enhancing Hong Kong Architectural Education Through XR: 
Geo-Location and 3D Pin Pointers for Real-Time Information
Visualization
column7:
Traditional architectural education in Hong Kong relies on
static textbooks, limiting students' ability to connect
theoretical knowledge with real-world architectural
experiences. Research has shown that immersive engagement
with architectural spaces enhances student comprehension
and fosters deeper connections to historical content (Hein
& Dooren, 2019). Additionally, static media constrain
students' ability to visualize spatial concepts, making the
translation from two-dimensional to three-dimensional
understanding difficult (Karnam et al., 2020). XR (Extended
Reality) technologies, which include AR and VR, offer
solutions by enabling students to interact with 3D
environments, improving learning outcomes and motivation
(Diao & Shih, 2019). XR’s ability to link virtual content
with real-world architecture makes it particularly
effective for architectural education, where students must
grasp both theoretical and spatial aspects.

This study focuses on developing an XR-based teaching
platform tailored to the architecture of Hong Kong. The
platform superimposes historical and cultural information
onto real buildings, allowing students to interact with
both historical and modern architecture in real-time. A
comparative experiment will be conducted using a Hong Kong
architecture textbook to evaluate the platform’s
effectiveness in enhancing learning efficiency, engagement,
and comprehension compared to traditional methods.

This research aligns with the theme of the CAAD Futures
2025 conference, "Catalytic Interfaces," by demonstrating
how XR can act as a transformative computational tool in
architectural education. The study addresses current and
future challenges in education, fostering interdisciplinary
collaboration between architecture, education, and
technology, and advancing the use of XR in architectural
research and practice.




References:

Diao, P., & Shih, N. (2019). Trends and Research Issues of
Augmented Reality Studies in Architectural and Civil
Engineering Education—A Review of Academic Journal
Publications. Applied Sciences.
https://doi.org/10.3390/APP9091840.

Hein, C., & Dooren, E. (2019). Teaching history for design
at TU Delft: exploring types of student learning and
perceived relevance of history for the architecture
profession. International Journal of Technology and Design
Education, 30, 849 - 865.
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10798-019-09533-5.

Karnam, D., Mashood, K., & Sule, A. (2020). Do student
difficulties with vectors emerge partly from the
limitations of static textbook media? European Journal of
Physics, 41. https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6404/ab782e.

column2: Xiaoxin Lu, Hanzhe Bao and Tiantian Lo
column3:
Enhancing Urban Vitality through Interactive XR
Installations: Fostering Engagement and Environmental
Awareness
column7:
Urban environments are essential to contemporary life;
however, their vitality is increasingly compromised by the
dominance of digital technologies. As traditional functions
of urban spaces shift online, it is critical to reassess
the elements that contribute to their appeal and develop
effective strategies for revitalization. This research
project explores the creation of interactive installations
at strategic points within urban road networks, utilizing
Extended reality (XR) technology to foster meaningful
interactions between individuals and their spatial
contexts. Designed to encourage engagement through
recyclable plastic bottles, these installations gamify the
interaction, promoting environmental awareness alongside
public participation in urban planning processes. Through a
series of case studies, we employed XR to visualize and
manipulate spatial data, enabling real-time user engagement
with their environment. Our findings demonstrate that these
installations enhance accessibility to spatial information
and deepen connections between citizens and their urban
surroundings, with participants reporting increased spatial
awareness and agency in urban discussions. The theoretical
framework established in this research, along with its
preliminary validation, aims to provide insights into
global urban revitalization efforts and facilitate the
evaluation of future design initiatives.

column2: Yufan Meng, Yetong Huang, Zhenyu Wang and Fang Zheng
column3:
Stepwise Generation Method for Competition-Level Floor
Plans of Medium and Large-Scale Gymnasiums Based on Rule
Constraints and Diffusion Models
column7:
Intelligent generative algorithms are increasingly
demonstrating substantial potential in architectural
design. However, their applications remain relatively
limited, primarily focusing on image-based generation of
residential layouts and architectural renderings, with
fewer implementations in spatial generation for
architectural space. Sports architecture, characterized by
complex circulation and a large number of spatial elements,
involves a substantial work-load in floor plan design,
highlighting the urgent need to enhance human-computer
interaction. This study takes the competition-level floor
plans of large and medium-sized stadiums as experimental
objects, introducing a hybrid intelligent generative
algorithm that combines rule-based constraints and deep
learning. A two-stage stepwise generation framework is
constructed to incorporate multi-objective optimization
algorithms for functionality, layout, and circulation
within stadium floor plan designs. This approach broadens
the application scenarios of intelligent generative
algorithms in the design of complex public building spaces,
enhancing the scientific rigor, objectivity, and
multi-objective optimization capabilities of the design
process.
The proposed two-stage segmented generation method exhibits
significant po-tential in improving the detail expression
and functional diversity of floor plan layouts. By
integrating stepwise manual intervention, this approach
substantial-ly reduces the reliance on manual design
efforts and subjective expertise, ena-bling architects to
focus more on creativity and high-level design decisions,
thereby improving overall efficiency. Meanwhile, this study
establishes a two-stage evaluation framework comprising
'loss rate screening during the training phase' and
'spatial semantic recognition accuracy assessment', which
collective-ly enhance the controllability and reliability
of the generative outcomes.
 Nevertheless, the current approach still presents
 limitations in supporting the model's capacity to learn
 complex spatial-semantic relationships. Future re-search
 could focus on expanding high-quality annotated datasets,
 refining the hierarchical structure of prompt expressions,
 and further improving the auto-mated evaluation system.
 These efforts will contribute to building a more robust
 theoretical foundation and practical framework for the
 intelligent generation of architectural floor plans in
 high-complexity design scenarios.

column2: Siwen Cao, Hao Sun and Ziyu Tong
column3:
BPMN-based building project lifecycle analysis with a core
of BIM: Taking a campus project as an example
column7:
Building Information Modeling (BIM) as a management method
is expected to play an essential role in project
management. China has put forward the practice of “one
model to the end” for the data circulation problem to
ensures the seamless flow of data in the project lifecycle.
However, frequent conversions and re-modeling across
project phases hinder effective data exchange, impacting
efficiency, accuracy, schedules, and costs.
BPMN (Business Process Modeling Notation) has been adopted
for BIM process modelling. However, existing studies mostly
focus on stakeholders and their task allocation, and the
potential of BPMN has not been fully explored for
model-centered BIM processes.
This study takes a campus renovation and expansion project
in Suzhou, China as an example. and BPMN was utilized to
sort out the BIM application flow in each phase of the
project, which was divided into several lanes, including
task flow, stakeholder flow, document flow, BIM model flow,
and drawing flow, to identify the bottlenecks in data flow.
The core of this study is to take the BIM model flow as an
independent swim lane to clearly track model changes to
identify delivery breakpoints. Based on the problems, this
study proposes optimization strategies to improve the
efficiency and accuracy of BIM application in the whole
life cycle of a construction project, and to realize the
“one mode to the end” BIM application process, which
provide realistic reference value for promoting the
in-depth application of BIM technology and the digital
transformation of the construction industry.

column2: Dexi Wang and Tsung-Hsien Wang
column3:
A ML-Based Building Energy Performance Evaluation Toolkit
for the Early  Conceptual Design Exploration: Learning from
Energy Performance  Certificates Database
column7:
The construction industry hugely impacts the ecological
environment, with its energy consumption being a
substantial portion of the overall societal energy usage.
Every building commences at the early-stage of design,
during which the available information is too limited to
carry out dynamic simulations but the decisions made are
most impactful.

This study concentrates on combining architectural design
with computer technology to develop a Machine Learning (ML)
based toolkit. The toolkit is advantageous for rapidly
predicting a building’s energy consumption and
environmental impact with relatively little data input.

Based on the Energy Performance Certificates (EPCs)
database, the toolkit examines a substantial quantity of
residential buildings in Sheffield and subsequently trained
the ML model to fit. The Python-based toolkit can be used
on any computer to predict building’s energy consumption,
carbon dioxide emissions, and suggest potential improvement
recommendations with limited user input.

This study admits certain limitations and deficiencies in
the procedure, but it effectively demonstrates the
potential of integrating emerging technologies like
computer technology and ML with architectural design to
address architectural challenges.

column2:
Xinyue Xia, Haojie Fan, Shunuo Li, Huangyan Zheng, Haoyi Xu
and Sining Wang
column3:
Robotic fabrication and in-situ 3D printing for a hybrid
natural timber-bamboo structure
column7:
With advanced fabrication and computational design methods,
non-standard building structures made from natural
materials such as wood and bamboo are attracting the
attention of architectural researchers. As current studies
primarily focus on the design and fabrication of
single-material systems, this work explores a robotic
fabrication and in-situ 3D printing workflow for a hybrid
natural timber-bamboo structure. It encompasses three major
research components: 1) the scanning and virtual recreation
of collected raw materials; 2) the design of a hybrid
structural system based on the materials’ natural geometric
features and structural performance; 3) a bespoke digital
fabrication process that addresses robotic drill-ing and
in-situ 3D printing for non-standard timber-bamboo joints.
The proposed workflow is illustrated through the creation
of a full-scale structural prototype, along with its future
architectural applications.

column2: Hangchuan Wei, Richard Beckett and Marjan Colletti
column3:
Environmental-driven Making: Clay 3D Printing Instructed by
Airflow Data
column7:
Digital fabrication is often regarded as a distinct
materialization process, separate from design, resulting in
a disconnection between digital models and their physical
making. This paper introduces a generative framework for
environmental-driven making using ceramic 3D printing
(3DP). The study examines the plastic deformation of 3DP
ceramic and integrates computational fluid dynamics (CFD)
simulation data to regulate deformation within the design.
This approach generates surface textures with different
roughness that can potentially influence the
bio-receptivity, through which it creates niches for
microbial colonization while also contributing to aesthetic
considerations. The framework is developed primarily using
Houdini, where CFD data continuously informs the generation
of geometry, tool paths, and 3DP instructions. A customized
slicing tool and G-code generator are implemented to
produce G-code programs responsive to CFD data. Unlike
conventional 3DP practices, this integrated approach
enables the production of environmentally responsive
surface textures, establishing a continuous link between
environmental factors, design generation, and digital
fabrication.

column2:
Martin Bielik, Milan Valasek, Luyang Zhang, Sven Schneider
and Reinhard König
column3:
Floor Plan Affordance Prediction:  Is the floor plan layout
determined by its outline or the architect?
column7:
The process of generating floor plans for residential units
can be a labour-intensive, repetitive, and tedious task. We
argue that if it is possible to determine the
suitability/affordance of an outline for a given program
before engaging into labour-intensive and tedious design
process, significant time and resources could be conserved.

In the present research, we employ deep neural networks to
predict 11 characteristics of a floor plan just from its
outline. The predictive model was trained on an audited
subset (N=20,150) of the open-access Swiss dwellings
dataset (Standfest, et al, 2022). We were able to
accurately predict the number of rooms and the presence or
absence of elements, such as loggia, balcony, open plan
kitchen, natural bathroom ventilation, and 2nd bathroom.
Finally, the model also showed moderate but meaningful
predictive power for features capturing the configurational
properties of a floor plan.

We conclude that the outline of a floor plan does indeed
partially determine the configuration of certain layout
characteristics and that using machine learning models to
predict these characteristics is a viable tool for aiding
the design process of residential units. Additionally,
based on the results we discuss the relevance of our
results for the research into the development of machine
learning tools for automated floorplan generation.

 

Standfest, M., Franzen, M., Schröder, Y., Gonzalez Medina,
L., Villanueva Hernandez, Y., Buck, J. H., Tan, Y.,
Niedzwiecka, M., Colmegna, R (2022) Swiss Dwellings: A
large dataset of apartment models including aggregated
geolocation-based simulation results covering viewshed,
natural light, traffic noise, centrality and geometric
analysis. https://doi.org/10.528/zenodo.7070952

column2:
Martin Bielik, Sven Schneider, Luyang Zhang, Milan Valasek
and Reinhard König
column3:
Bridging the Gap: Enhancing AI-Generated Floor Plans with
Multi-Modal Data Integration
column7:
The rapid growth of AI tools for automated floor plan
generation is becoming increasingly evident. These tools
generally employ variations of deep neural networks trained
on extensive datasets of existing floor plans to create new
ones. Typically, the input for these generative models is
the floor plan outline, with some approaches allowing for
additional specifications such as room type, number, and
entrance location.
However, current generative models often fall short in
practical applications due to multiple factors: A) limited
control over the model, B) high variability in the quality
of generated floor plans, and C) unrealistic user requests.
To address these challenges, we leverage the same large
dataset (N=20,150) used for training generative model
(Standfest, et al, 2022) for search and prediction
functionalities. This paper introduces the "Floor AI"
online platform, integrated directly with CAAD software.
Our user study demonstrates that a multi-modal approach
utilizing the training dataset can mitigate the
deficiencies of current generative models, thereby bridging
the gap between research and practical application.

Standfest, M., Franzen, M., Schröder, Y., Gonzalez Medina,
L., Villanueva Hernandez, Y., Buck, J. H., Tan, Y.,
Niedzwiecka, M., Colmegna, R (2022) Swiss Dwellings: A
large dataset of apartment models including aggregated
geolocation-based simulation results covering viewshed,
natural light, traffic noise, centrality and geometric
analysis. https://doi.org/10.528/zenodo.7070952

column2: Hojung Kim
column3:
Crafting a Participatory Approach towards Traditional
Vietnamese Weaving and Digital Computation
column7:
The braided knot, illustrated by Gottfried Semper,
highlights the deep interconnection between materiality and
craftsmanship, particularly through weaving—a rhythmic
interplay of threads and voids. This concept was
materialized through collaboration with a community of
weavers from Phu Nghia village, Vietnam, resulting in a
modular lighting installation that reflects the region’s
cultural identity. The research aimed to integrate
traditional Vietnamese Bamboo and Rattan Weaving (BRW) with
computational design and digital fabrication, demonstrating
how technology can enhance and preserve craft heritage.
The study focuses on sustainability in material
computation, emphasizing the ethical sourcing of bamboo and
rattan. Bamboo species such as high-density fiber bamboo
grown at high altitudes, Bambuseae (woody tropical
bamboos), and Calamus trees for rattan were used to develop
lightweight, modular objects. Computational tools predicted
weaving outcomes and facilitated the fabrication of
components otherwise impossible by hand.
Preliminary explorations, using Rhino and Grasshopper,
analyzed the structural properties of bamboo rods and
complex weaving techniques. Local artisans provided
feedback, refining these digital models and leading to the
development of twill and plaiting BRW techniques. These
methods were integrated with 3D-printed joinery system,
resulting in a spherical surface of woven panels over an
iron framework.
The research combined qualitative and quantitative
methodologies: a literature review, surveys, and interviews
with artisans, alongside structural testing of 3D-printed
materials like PLA, ABS, Nylon, Carbon Fiber, and PETG
Translucent to assess durability and flexibility. This
hybrid approach highlighted how computational design can
support the preservation and advancement of traditional
weaving crafts.

column2: Jaechang Ko, Sora Key and Mark Clayton
column3: Integrating AI Tools and Methods in the Design Process
column7:
The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI),
particularly through Large Language Models (LLMs) like
MidJourney [1], DALL·E [2], and ChatGPT [3], has brought
significant advancements to creative industries, including
architectural design. These tools excel at generating
ideas, 2D images, and conceptual content. However,
architectural design presents a set of unique challenges;
each project involves shifting design directions,
collaboration dynamics, and evolving communication
strategies[4]. While LLMs are effective in ideation, they
may not fully address architecture's practical, complex
demands.
We conducted a pilot study involving architectural
designers to explore the potential and limitations of
existing LLM tools in practice. Through feedback
collection, we gained insights into three key areas where
LLMs could complement the design process: the visualization
of reference images, the generation of new 3D design ideas,
and the creation of optimized 3D models. Based on these
findings, we selected three additional AI tools to address
these needs: t-distributed stochastic neighbor
embedding(t-SNE) [5], 3D generative adversarial
networks(3DGANs) [6], and Genetic Algorithms (GA) [7]. We
then developed a workflow using these tools, applied to
chair design, and demonstrated it to participants. Their
feedback provided valuable insights into the strengths and
weaknesses of these technologies and directions for how
they could complement existing design processes in the
industry.
This study explored the potential and limitations of
integrating t-SNE, 3DGAN, and GA tools into the
architectural workflow to explore more possibilities beyond
the conventional use of LLMs for image generation. In this
research, we emphasize that, beyond 'design exploration,'
human oversight remains essential in navigating the
practical constraints of real-world projects, and highlight
the need for a more strategic combination of AI tools for
effective integration into the process.

column2: Guy Austern, Moria Schwarz and Boaz Sternfeld
column3:
Comparing different Building representations for
readability by Large Language Models
column7:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are able to generate high
quality text, images and even code from a user request. To
date, they have not been extensively used in architecture
where the basic paradigm of designing building using
Building Information Models (BIM) software remains
unaltered. This research evaluates the ability of LLMs to
understand different representations of building data, so
that it can be used in the design process. We tried
different ways of extracting architectural information from
a BIM file and asked the LLM various questions about its
content. We tested the LLM with images, tabular data
structures, La-belled Property Graphs (LPG), IFC files and
the original Revit format. On all formats, we tried two
approaches: directly uploading the extracted information
into the LLM and asking the LLM to generate code for
querying the data. We compared the correctness of the
results provided and the time it took to process the
queries.
The results of this study suggest that graph-based
representations help LLMs answer complex architectural
questions by increasing their capability to process
geometric relations. The results also indicated the high
potential of running code generated by LLMs within BIM
authoring software, dramatically reducing runtimes and
simplifying the overall process. These findings can be
utilized for developing LLM applications such automated
code compliance, scheduling, de-tailing and generative
design, positioning them as powerful tools in the
architec-tural domain.

column2: Joosun Yum, Ji-Hyun Lee and Yu-Hsiu Hung
column3:
Optimizing Spatial Design and Visitor Engagement in Tourism
Factories: Analyzing Movement Patterns and Feedback at an
Optical Lens Manufacturer
column7:
This study explores visitor behavior and spatial design in
industrial tourism, with a focus on optimizing engagement
at Hwa Meei’s "Eye Fun Vision" tourism factory in Taiwan.
By employing semi-structured shadowing, semi-structured
interviews, and surveys, the research collected data on
visitor movement, engagement, and satisfaction across 21
subareas of the factory. Tools such as customer journey
maps and spaghetti diagrams were used to analyze visitor
flow and identify subareas of high and low engagement. The
findings highlight that subareas fostering creativity and
interactivity, such as "Frames DIY" and "Hand-eye
Coordination Toy," were highly engaging, while zones with
dense textual content and minimal interaction, like "See
Hwa Meei" and "Domestic Eyeglasses Industry," scored lower
in terms of visitor interest.

Visitor feedback also indicated a strong preference for
more child-friendly activities, immersive experiences, and
improved wayfinding throughout the factory. Recommendations
from the study suggest enhancing low-engagement subareas
with interactive features, adjusting spatial layouts to
reduce congestion in high-traffic zones, and improving
signage and instructions to make the visitor experience
smoother and more intuitive.

The study provides practical insights into how spatial
design can be leveraged to enhance visitor engagement in
industrial tourism settings. By balancing interactive
elements with educational content, factory tours can create
more engaging and memorable experiences. The research
emphasizes the value of visitor-centered design in factory
tours, which not only enriches the visitor experience but
also contributes to the growth and sustainability of the
industrial tourism sector.

column2: Minghao Wang, Chi Zhang, Yuchen Qin and Shen Xu
column3:
An Analytical Framework for Urban Morphology to
Synergistically Enhance Outdoor Thermal Comfort and
Building Energy Efficiency
column7:
Urban morphology influences both outdoor thermal comfort
and building energy consumption, however, designs focused
on a single performance ob-jective may inadvertently
undermine another benefit. In response, this study
introduces a framework to examine the synergistic impacts
of urban mor-phology on diverse performance goals,
exemplified by outdoor thermal comfort and building energy
consumption in 25 residential areas in Wuhan. Results show
that winter outdoor thermal comfort is primarily influenced
by floor area ratio (32.10%) and sky view factor (27.83%),
while summer com-fort depends on the aspect ratio of the
plane (24.99%) and building footprint area (17.98%).
Heating energy use is most affected by shape factor
(54.65%), whereas cooling energy use is driven by green
ratio (31.10%) and footprint area (22.97%). Additionally,
summer cooling demand strongly cor-relates with
microclimate. Leveraging these findings, the study
recommends design strategies to achieve synergistic
optimization of outdoor thermal com-fort and building
energy consumption in residential areas.

column2: Zhiyong Dong, Peter Búš, Qi Wang and Maowei Jiang
column3:
Enhancing Robotic Embodiment in Architecture: An
Intelligent Approach Combining Vision Systems and
Generative Neural Networks for Autonomous
Design-to-Production
column7:
As architecture increasingly demands complex geometries and
intricate building environments, robotic systems equipped
with intelligent perception and decision-making
capabilities are crucial for bridging the gap be-tween
design and production. This research uses modular
structures as a case study to integrate vision-based
systems, generative neural networks, and cyber-physical
environments to enhance autonomous assembly processes. The
paper demonstrates how robots, through visual recognition
and optimization algorithms, can identify and assemble
components in dynamic environments with minimal human
intervention. OpenCV is employed to recognize irregularly
arranged components and transfer them into the digital
space, then multi-objective optimization (MOO) framework
generates stable assembly plans, which are further refined
using conditional generative adversarial networks (cGANs)
to produce feasible solutions for robotic execution. The
results highlight the potential of intelligent robots to
improve efficiency and adaptability for architectural
design-to-production.

column2:
Gal Guz, Nikolas Martelaro, Gerhard Schubert and Jonathan
Dortheimer
column3:
Quantifying Architectural Experience Using Visual Language
Models: Does AI Dream of Rendered Spaces?
column7:
Architectural design relies on human intuition and the
personal experience of the architect to assess the
emotional qualities of spaces, posing a challenge since
emotions are subjective. While traditional methods lack
standardized metrics for these subjective experiences,
recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) offer
new possibilities for quantification. This study explores
the potential of visual language models (VLMs) to evaluate
architectural spaces emotionally, bridging the gap between
objective measurements and subjective experiences. We
conducted an experiment using GPT-4o, with vision language
model capabilities, to generate emotional ratings for ten
images depicting various spaces. The model's predictions
were compared to human evaluations obtained through a
survey using the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule
(PANAS). The VLM demonstrated a strong correlation with
human ratings for negative affect and a moderate
correlation for positive affect after excluding
computer-aided design (CAD) images, which showed
discrepancies. The findings highlight the potential of VLMs
to quantify emotional evaluations, offering a novel
approach to integrating emotional metrics into the design
process. This capability could revolutionize architectural
design by enabling optimization based on emotional
prediction.

column2:
Sivan Grodsky, Alex Binh Vinh Duc Nguyen, Panos
Chatzitsakyris, Danut Bidasca, Thanasis Farangas, Andrew
Vande Moere and Davide Schaumann
column3:
Generating Open Office Layouts using Flexible Architectural
Components
column7:
Open office layouts aim to provide a variety of
workstations that accommodate workers’ diverse activities.
However, designing layouts that cater to continuously
changing schedules is challenging. Daily adjustment of
office layouts using flexible architectural components such
as movable desks and partitions could address this issue.
Nevertheless, little is known about how to dynamically
arrange such layouts to meet workers’ needs while
mitigating visibility-related stressors, including privacy
and distractions. This paper proposes a computational
framework to optimize the daily configuration of office
layouts and workers’ allocation to meet workers’ needs for
daily schedules. The framework integrates architectural
knowledge of spatial layout arrangements with generative
design for automated floorplan creation, and agent-based
simulation of human-centered evaluations. Specifically,
architectural knowledge is gathered and processed using a
graph-based representation used by a generative design
algorithm to synthesize, simulate and evaluate office
layouts, ultimately identifying optimized configurations
that meet workers’ needs. The proposed framework involves:
(a) abstracting architectural knowledge into a library of
zones, fully furnished functional areas that compose a
layout; (b) identifying spatial requirements of a daily
activity schedule; (c) assembling zones into full layouts,
(d) allocating people to zones, (e) arranging flexible
partitions based on visibility and activity adjacency
considerations, and (f) evaluating visibility-related
considerations to rank the optimal ones. The framework
underwent iterative testing to refine the generated layouts
based on feedback collected from professional architectural
designers. The joint optimization of daily office layout
arrangement and workers’ allocation could potentially
accelerate the adoption of flexible architectural
components to promote workers’ well-being.

column2: Fei Guo, Eduardo Costa, Feng Dai and Xin-Nan Zhang
column3:
Generative design and modeling of industrial layouts: a
study in semiconductor manufacturing
column7:
Industrial layouts have been investigated for their
potential for cost saving and improving manufacturing
performance. Efficient design depends on the experience and
the suggestions of experts. While generative design has
been applied to conceptualize factory layouts, such
approaches are not yet applied to detailed design work.
Moreover, certain types of factory layouts such as in
semiconductor manufacturing are strictly based on the
respective linear process. Such rule-based systems often
generate layouts packed tightly together on fab and in
subfab with overlapping columns, resulting in complex
design systems that would take designers weeks to detect
and correct irregularities manually. We propose a design
framework supported by a lightweight algorithm to aid
design work efficiently, developed from a real-world case
study from semiconductor manufacturing, and demonstrated
with generative designs and evaluations. As a first step, a
precise manufacturing process that involves hundreds of
iterative operations are encoded into a computational
model, in which the whole fabrication area is automatically
divided into several districts, which are later adjusted by
definite equipment placements. Afterwards, a
constraint-solving optimization algorithm is used to
position processing equipment in bays of sequential regions
in fab and subfab systems areas, reconciling distributed
support systems with column conflicts automatically in 3D
model form. During the generation, evaluation data is
simultaneously collected by geometrical methods for later
multi-objective decisions. This method is expected to be
helpful in facilitating industrial design and decision
making compared with existing methodologies.

column2: Chenyi Cai, Kosuke Kuriyama, Youlong Gu and Pieter Herthogs
column3:
Can a Large Language Model Assess Urban Design Quality?
Evaluating Walkability Metrics Across Expertise Levels
column7:
Urban street environments are vital to supporting human
activity in public spaces. The emergence of big data, such
as street view images (SVI) combined with multi-modal large
language models (MLLM), is transforming how researchers and
practitioners investigate, measure, and evaluate semantic
and visual elements of urban environments.
Considering the low threshold for creating automated
evaluative workflows using MLLM, it is crucial to explore
both the risks and opportunities associated with these
probabilistic models.
In particular, the extent to which the integration of
expert knowledge can influence the performance of MLLM in
the evaluation of the quality of urban design has not been
fully explored.
This study set out an initial exploration of how
integrating more formal and structured representations of
expert urban design knowledge into the input prompts of an
MLLM (ChatGPT-4) can enhance the model's capability and
reliability to evaluate the walkability of built
environments using SVIs.
We collect walkability metrics through existing literature
and categorize them using relevant ontologies.
Then we selected a subset of these metrics, used for
assessing the sub-themes of pedestrian safety and
attractiveness, and developed prompts for MLLMs.
We analysed the MLLM’s abilities to evaluate SVI
walkability sub-themes through prompts with multiple levels
of clarity and specificity about evaluation criteria.
Our experiments demonstrate that MLLMs' evaluative
performance can be significantly influenced by the
integration of expert knowledge, while they are capable of
general knowledge-based assessments. Additionally,
increasing semantic clarity in expert knowledge
representations further improves the consistency and
concentration of MLLM's evaluative performance.

column2:
Karagozaiym Turganbek, Sebastian Wimmer, Martin Hutter,
Alexander Karaivanov, Nicolaj Kirisits and Zeynep
Aksöz-Balzar
column3:
Adaptive Origami: Fabrication of Pneumatic-actuated
Adaptive Folding System
column7:
This research investigates the potential of origami-based
folding systems to function as adaptive architectural
elements that dynamically respond to external stimuli.
These systems have the capacity to alter spatial qualities,
such as acoustics and lighting, in real time to suit
different use cases. The study focuses on overcoming the
challenges of developing a material system that supports
these dynamic transformations. Through a combination of
computational simulations, physical prototypes, and
iterative feedback loops, the research examines material
selection, structural performance, folding mechanisms, and
actuation strategies.
The adaptive system developed consists of a modular
skeletal structure, actuators, and connection joints. A key
aspect of the experiments was exploring the fabrication
possibilities of the Resch trifold pattern. The initial
structure, built using wooden frames, gradually evolved
into a lightweight design, incorporating pneumatic pistons
for actuation. The iterative development process led to the
creation of a flexible skeleton with 3D-printed joints and
actuators that enable real-time transformations.
The modular design ensures scalability, rapid assembly, and
easy part replacement. The system’s potential lies in its
ability to choreograph actuation, allowing synchronized,
complex folding patterns. This opens new opportunities for
kinetic architecture and responsive environments, where
dynamic transformations enhance spatial experiences by
altering forms, light, and sound diffusion based on
real-time inputs.

column2: Igor Pantic, Alvaro Lopez Rodriguez and Carl Barrett
column3:
Augmented Urban Environments: Contextually Aware NPCs
through AI Integration
column7:
The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and
extended reality (XR) is transforming urban environments by
blending physical and digital realities. This study
explores the creation of contextually aware non-playable
characters (NPCs) within augmented urban spaces to enhance
architectural design and user engagement. By embedding
AI-driven NPCs into XR frameworks, we propose a novel
approach to developing dynamic, responsive urban
environments that adapt to user needs.

Our primary objective is to develop a system where
autonomous architectural NPCs act as interactive agents
within urban settings, providing contextually relevant
information and enriching the urban experience. To achieve
this, we combine multiple computational techniques into a
cohesive methodology, integrating movement simulation,
real-time perception, generative visual elements, and
behavior customization using large language models (LLMs)
based on cultural and historical contexts.

We outline a framework where these NPCs adapt their
behavior and appearance in real-time, enhancing user
interaction by offering relevant information and guidance.
Designed for dynamic adaptation to changing conditions,
they provide seamless visual integration within the
environment and culturally informed interactions that
deepen user engagement.

This research highlights the transformative potential of
AI-driven NPCs in urban environments, contributing to more
immersive and adaptive urban spaces. It underscores the
importance of addressing ethical considerations such as
privacy, inclusivity, and bias to ensure equitable access.
The integration of AI-driven NPCs offers a new paradigm for
urban design, where digital and physical worlds interact
seamlessly, paving the way for cities that are more
engaging, responsive, and attuned to the complexities of
modern life.

Core References:

- Manovich, L. 2024. “The Poetics of Augmented Space.”
Accessed June 3, 2024.
- Baudrillard, J. 1994. Simulacra and Simulation. Ann
Arbor: University of Michigan Press.
- Krupat, E. 1985. People in Cities: The Urban Environment
and Its Effects. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
- Castells, M. 2001. The Internet Galaxy: Reflections on
the Internet, Business, and Society. Oxford: Oxford
University Press.
- Mitchell, W. J. 1995. City of Bits: Space, Place, and the
Infobahn. Cambridge: MIT Press.

column2: Oceane Durand-Maniclas and Gulnaz Aksenova
column3:
MATERIAL REUSE IN HERITAGE CONSERVATION:  DEVELOPING A
DIGITAL DESIGN-TO-PRODUCTION CIRCULAR WORKFLOW
column7:
Embracing sustainable strategies, such as the reuse of
building materials, alongside historic building
conservation methods like adaptive reuse, can effectively
preserve material resources and cultural features while
promoting the economic value of buildings. The adoption of
digital approaches within material lifecycle stages offers
a promising opportunity to minimize environmental impacts,
reduce waste streams, and optimize reuse. This supports
digital circular strategies in conservation and heritage.
To foster material reuse strategies in heritage
conservation, this study developed a digital
design-to-production circular workflow that incorporates
Building Information Modelling (BIM), reality capture,
environmental impact assessments such as Life Cycle
Assessment (LCA), and circular material traceability tools
like Material Passports (MP), in addition to digital
restoration techniques. The workflow was implemented and
validated through a case study based in the United Kingdom
(UK), North Wales. Data exchange and datasets are
investigated and reported. The workflow was developed based
on international and UK standards. In addition, the study
addresses the challenges of reusing nonstandardized
components in heritage buildings, contributing to circular
strategies for existing buildings with more complex
features. Finally, the paper develops a novel approach to
improve circular construction in conservation by defining a
digital workflow closing the material reuse loop.

column2: Igor Pantic and Alvaro Lopez Rodriguez
column3:
Architecture in the Augmented Society: Mixed Reality for
the Built Environment
column7:
The convergence of mixed reality (MR) technologies and
artificial intelligence is fundamentally redefining the
built environment, blurring the boundaries between physical
and digital realms. Concepts like the Metaverse are
reshaping societal norms and daily interactions. This paper
explores the significant impact of MR on architectural
spaces, focusing on how digital overlays can redefine
existing environments and influence user perceptions. By
examining themes such as ownership, intellectual property
rights, censorship, and content governance, the research
aims to deepen understanding of MR's role in architecture.

The study analyzes three case studies of MR applications in
architecture, guided by a framework based on three
criteria: Object (type of information presented), Ownership
(content ownership models), and Media (user interaction
levels). The first case examines a consumption-focused MR
platform that enhances user interaction through
personalized digital overlays. The second explores a
user-configurable urban environment that allows
personalization via generative AI, fostering creativity.
The third investigates a community-driven augmented
architecture platform that prioritizes user-generated
content and engagement.

Findings underscore MR's transformative potential to
enhance user engagement, creativity, and interaction within
urban spaces. However, integrating MR necessitates careful
consideration of ethical and social implications, including
risks of bias, censorship, and social isolation. To fully
realize the benefits, it is crucial to prioritize
inclusivity, foster community engagement, and ensure
transparency in content creation and ownership. This
research provides a framework for understanding MR's
potential and challenges in shaping future cities, paving
the way for more creative, inclusive, and responsive urban
environments.

Core References:

- Assange, J., Appelbaum, J., Müller-Maguhn, A., &
Zimmermann, J. 2016. Cypherpunks: Freedom and the Future of
the Internet. New York: OR Books.
- Ball, M. 2020. “The Metaverse: What it is, Where to Find
it, and Who Will Build it.” MatthewBall.Vc.
- Baudrillard, J. 1981. Simulacres et Simulation. Paris:
Galilée.
- Deleuze, G., & Guattari, F. 1987. A Thousand Plateaus:
Capitalism and Schizophrenia (B. Massumi Trans.).
University of Minnesota Press.
- Vlahakis, V., Karigiannis, J., Tsotros, M., Gounaris, M.,
Almeida, L., Stricker, D., Gleue, T., Christou, I.T.,
Carlucci, R., & Ioannidis, N. 2001. "Archeoguide: First
Results of an Augmented Reality Mobile Computing System in
Cultural Heritage Sites." In Proceedings of the 2001
Conference on Virtual Reality Archaeology and Cultural
Heritage (VAST '01). Association for Computing Machinery,
New York, NY, USA, 131–140.

column2: Kurt Neiswender
column3:
Implementing Reality Capture and Extended Reality to
Visualize Spatial Implications of HVAC System Design
column7:
Mechanical systems design is difficult for architecture
students to understand when traditional construction
documents are two-dimensional representations. By
leveraging point clouds and Extended Reality (XR)
equipment, students can better understand the spatial
implications of HVAC systems in architecture. The immersive
capabilities of XR place students in a full-scale virtual
building where the layers of building construction can be
hidden to reveal the integration of the mechanical
components thus reinforcing the complexity of architectural
design thinking and decision-making. Two methods of XR
space creation provide equal educational value to students.
The first is the reality capture of existing buildings to
present point cloud models that can be viewed in XR. The
second is to import students' designs from CAAD software
into the XR space to see firsthand how the integration of
HVAC systems alters their designs.

The widespread availability of XR equipment coupled with
more affordable reality capture equipment now makes it
possible to enhance the physical understanding of building
systems integration within a virtual environment. The
learning outcomes for students are better positive
reinforcement of students’ familiarity with complex
building systems which traditionally can threaten students
from implementing any systems into design projects. Through
this strengthened relationship with architecture and
building systems, students can become better communicators
in practice in their field and with consultants and
contractors. The emphasis of this advanced CAAD workflow
empowers students to emerge into practice with a broader
knowledge of building systems integration and regain
control of the design process.

column2: Danrui Li, Yichao Shi and Yaluo Wang
column3:
(CI) Enhancing Early-Stage Architectural Design with
LLM-Driven Assistant and Knowledge Graph
column7:
While various tools and methods have been developed to
support architects in later design stages—such as energy
cost estimation optimization—assistance for early-stage
architectural design remains an emerging area. Early-stage
design involves the conceptualization of ideas, exploration
of spatial relationships, and the integration of aesthetic
and functional considerations. This phase is marked by
highly creative processes, often occurring without concrete
data or specific constraints, making it difficult for
architects to consolidate their ideas or receive detailed
feedback that guides their design evolution.

Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) provide
a technical foundation for supporting early-stage design.
Through their reasoning capabilities and vast,
language-based knowledge, LLMs can engage in meaningful
dialogue with human users on architectural design topics.
However, these models exhibit significant limitations:
first, they present design concepts in abstract terms,
often lacking direct references to real-world examples.
This limits the utility of feedback, as designers receive
general insights without specific case studies or
contextualized guidance. Second, LLMs may have gaps in
architectural knowledge, as architecture-related content is
less prevalent in the training data, leading to shallow or
incomplete advice in this domain.

To address these limitations, retrieve-augmented generation
(RAG) systems have emerged as a valuable solution. RAG
integrates LLMs with an external knowledge database,
allowing the model to retrieve specific, real-world
examples and domain-specific information from a structured
repository. This combination enhances the model’s capacity
to provide more informed and contextually relevant feedback
to users, making it particularly valuable in creative
fields like architecture. However, applying RAG systems to
early-stage architectural design presents two major
challenges: (1) it remains unclear how architectural
knowledge can be effectively organized and indexed for
retrieval, given the complex, interdisciplinary nature of
design; (2) there is limited understanding of how
architects will interact with such a tool in practice, and
how it can best complement their creative processes.

In this work, we propose an LLM-based assistant with RAG
for early-stage architectural design, aimed at addressing
the two major challenges. First, we construct a knowledge
graph from both textual descriptions and visual
representations of real-world design cases. This knowledge
graph serves as a structured repository, enabling the
retrieval of specific examples relevant to various design
scenarios given by users. Compared to using pure LLMs, the
inclusion of the knowledge graph provides more grounded and
specific advice, moving beyond abstract suggestions. Next,
we design a human-computer interface that leverages this
knowledge graph to enhance the user experience for
architects. The interface allows designers to chat with the
assistant in both natural language and visual inputs, while
the system retrieves relevant cases from the knowledge
graph and presents them in an intuitive and interactive
format. Furthermore, the chat-based interface supports
iterative design processes, enabling architects to
continuously refine their designs, explore alternative
solutions, and draw inspiration from real-world examples in
a seamless and integrated manner.

In conclusion, our LLM-based assistant, enhanced by RAG and
a robust knowledge graph, bridges the gap between abstract
design concepts and practical, real-world examples,
offering architects a powerful tool for seeking design
suggestions or case references in early-stage design. By
addressing the key challenges of knowledge organization and
user interaction, this system has the potential to
significantly improve the quality and efficiency of the
architectural design process, fostering creativity and
innovation in a structured yet flexible environment.

column2:
Danrui Li, Yichao Shi, Yaluo Wang, Ziying Shi and Mubbasir
Kapadia
column3:
ArchSeek: Retrieving Architectural Case Studies Using
Vision-Language Models
column7:
Efficiently searching for relevant case studies is critical
in architectural design, as designers rely on precedent
examples to guide or inspire their ongoing projects.
However, traditional text-based search tools struggle to
capture the inherently visual and complex nature of
architectural knowledge, often leading to time-consuming
and imprecise exploration. This paper introduces ArchSeek,
an innovative case study search system with recommendation
capability, tailored for architecture design professionals.
Powered by the visual understanding capabilities from
vision-language models and cross-modal embeddings, it
enables text and image queries with fine-grained control,
and interaction-based design case recommendations. It
offers architects a more efficient, personalized way to
discover design inspirations, with potential applications
across other visually driven design fields. The source code
is available at \url{https://github.com/danruili/ArchSeek}.

column2: Juan Jose Castellon
column3: CNT Fiber-woven prototypes: Zero weight, infinite span
column7:
The proposed parametric structural system is a novel
implementation of Carbon Nanotube (CNT) Yarns, Galvorn, a
carbon nanomaterial that combines superior strength,
lightweight, conductivity, flexibility, and more,
outperforming GHG-intense alternatives.
The resulting prototype is a parametric structural
component composed of a central hollow mast, 3D-printed
dented spacers working in compression, and a woven pattern
of CNT yarns in tension. The woven pattern is generated
using a robotic arm that places the fibers following a
precise geometrical pattern and post-tensioning the
structure to improve substantially its structural behavior
while using a minimum amount of material. This method
allows the production of customized structural components
using parametric tools and robotic fabrication
technologies. Each structural CNT woven structure has a
different geometric and structural pattern responding to
specific static requirements as well as architectural and
environmental considerations.
Accordingly, the structural prototype works as a column or
beam, with optimum use of material and unique aesthetics.
Additionally, the fiber-woven structural component
integrates lighting and data network systems harnessing the
conductive properties of the CNT yarns. Therefore, it has
the potential to incorporate ecological and infrastructural
capacities such as harvesting photovoltaic energy and
rainwater.
This paper documents the computational tools, fabrication
techniques, and structural implementations resulting in an
experimental prototype as a base for future developments of
the project.

column2:
Yuan Jiang, Boyuan Yu, Jianing Luo, Jiawei Wang and Fang
Zheng
column3:
Innovative Applications of Steel Slag in sustainable
building design and construction: A Human-Machine
Collaboration (HMC) Framework
column7:
Steel slag, a by-product of steelmaking, poses significant
environmental challenges due to its predominant use in
landfills, where it contributes to soil pollution. However,
recent advancements in sustainable material science have
opened pathways for recycling steel slag, particularly in
the construction industry, which traditionally shares the
steel sector’s high carbon footprint. This research
addresses the question: How can steel slag, a waste
material from a carbon-intensive industry, be transformed
into a valuable resource for sustainable construction while
adhering to circular economy principles?

Building on the rapid advancement of computer-aided
architectural design (CAAD) technologies, this study
integrates Ameba and robotic arms to repurpose steel slag
into sustainable construction materials. It introduces a
Sustainable Building Design and Construction (SBDC)
framework, focusing on human-machine collaboration to
transform waste materials into valuable resources. The
framework follows these stages: (a) Conduct experimental
research on combining steel slag with various substances to
determine its potential applications in construction,
particularly for producing bricks and structural
components. (b) Employ Computer-Aided Architectural Design
(CAAD) methods to optimize the resulting structural forms,
integrating steel slag with bitumen to create complex
structural components. (c) Develop a human-machine
collaboration (HMC) framework to translate the optimized
designs into tangible architectural elements.The findings
present innovative strategies for repurposing industrial
by-products, addressing persistent issues such as
non-degradable pollution caused by steel slag. By
emphasizing human-machine collaboration, the study aims to
enhance resource efficiency, minimize waste, and promote
innovation in reusing steel slag within the construction
industry. The study underscores the importance of coupling
technological advances with critical evaluations of
environmental trade-offs to advance toward more sustainable
practices.

column2:
Darcy Zelenko, Isabel Solin, Jean-Paul Rollo, Sahar
Soltani, Camilo Cruz Gambardella and Duncan Maxwell
column3:
Design Quality Housing Assessment Methodology: Supporting
Heuristics with Evidence-Based Decision-Making
column7:
This paper outlines a performance-based assessment
methodology to evaluate the design quality of housing
layouts, to expedite decision-making to inform the spatial
configuration process for designers. The research presents
a novel methodology to holistically assess design quality
in housing layouts by synthesising government policy and
literature-derived design standards to develop factors of
analysis. These are then technically implemented using
computational design methods and data visualisation
techniques are used to articulate the derived spatial
characteristics, with an aim to support designers to make
informed decisions. The assessment methodology is validated
through a case study of two pools of apartment layouts in
the Australian context. The findings demonstrate the
methodology's capacity to corroborate positive design
quality claims and highlight potential shortcomings. This
research validates a design quality-based housing
assessment methodology and future work should aim to refine
outputs and broadening the scope of evaluation.

column2: Ming Tang
column3:
Enhancing Digital Twins with Internet of Things, Large
Language Models: Assessment of DT Development Platforms
column7:
This research explores the integration of Digital Twin (DT)
with Large Language Model (LLM), IoT (Internet of Things),
and Building Information Modeling (BIM) technologies,
aiming to advance the capabilities of digital ecosystems in
manufacturing and architectural domains. Digital Twins,
defined as mirrored virtual models of physical entities,
are pivotal in optimizing system operations, enabling
real-time monitoring, and improving decision-making
processes. Despite advancements in DT technology,
challenges remain in standardization, data integration, and
platform interoperability.
The study evaluates leading DT platforms—Autodesk Tandem,
NVIDIA Omniverse, and Unreal Engine—by integrating
IoT-driven techniques and legacy machine data with modern
systems. Among these platforms, Auto-desk Tandem
demonstrated superior functionality in integrating BIM and
IoT, providing real-time monitoring of building systems and
leveraging cloud-based services for scalability. In
contrast, Unreal Engine excelled in immersive visualization
and avatar-based interaction, particularly for integrating
LLMs. Omniverse is powerful for high-fidelity rendering,
open USD framework, and real-time streamlining with other
software.
Key contributions also include developing and integrating a
multi-agent LLM framework that enhances DT capabilities by
enabling predictive maintenance, fault diagnosis, and
conversational interfaces. These AI agents integrate
diverse datasets, including legacy and smart machine data,
to facilitate decision-making, anomaly detection, and
operational strategy development. The system's practical
application was validated in a case study, a DT based on
the University of XX's Digital Futures Building, showcasing
its scalability for diverse environments, from industrial
plants to smart buildings. Challenges addressed in the
study include integrating heterogeneous data sources,
standardization of protocols, and overcoming technical
limitations of existing platforms. The findings underscore
the potential of combining DTs with IoTs and LLMs to create
intelligent, adaptable systems that foster operational
efficiency and sustainability.

column2: Farnaz Nazarzadeh, David Kroll and Jane Burry
column3:
Review of social sustainability in the interactive
performance of kinetic architecture
column7:
Kinetic structures, known for their adaptability and
interactive capabilities, transform spaces into responsive
environments (Nazarzadeh & Asefi, 2022). By creating
dynamic and interactive designs, such architecture fosters
social sustainability and cultivates a sense of belonging,
happiness, joy, enjoyment, and excitement through playful
interaction. Social sustainability encompasses various
dimensions, including social interaction, architectural
identity, sense of security, flexibility, and social
participation (Kefayati & Moztarzadeh, 2015), all aimed to
fulfill fundamental human needs and enhance the overall
quality of life. While much of the focus in architectural
design has been on economic and environmental
sustainability, this paper emphasizes the importance of
social aspects as a pillar in achieving sustainable
development goals. It aims to review the application of
kinetic architecture in promoting social sustainability.
The research employs a descriptive-analytical methodology
to identify key concepts of social sustainability in
kinetic architecture, drawing from relevant case studies.
The result of this paper reveals that kinetic designs can
foster diversity and adaptability, encouraging playful
interactions that enhance physical, mental, and social
wellbeing. These structures facilitate meaningful
communication, human-centered interaction, collaboration,
and shared activities, promoting social connectedness.
Ultimately, kinetic architecture not only creates iconic
landmarks that enhance public spaces but also evokes
emotions such as happiness and joy. By meeting user
preferences, it significantly contributes to overall life
satisfaction and quality of life. Integrating kinetic
design in interactive environments can profoundly impact
social sustainability by fostering emotional wellbeing and
meaningful human connections.

Kefayati, Z., & Moztarzadeh, H. (2015). Developing
Effective Social Sustainability Indicators In Architecture.

45, 40-56.

Curved Elements and a Constant Perimeter. Journal of
