column2: Daien Liu and Taysheng Jeng
column3:
Catalyzing Creativity in Human-AI Co-creation: A Design
Cognition Approach
column7:
This study investigates how generative AI (Gen-AI)
catalyzes creativity in design workflows, focusing on the
comparative impact of "Sketch-based" approach. Empirical
experiments were conducted with eight architects using
Stable Diffusion, incorporating the ControlNet plugin for
enhanced co-creation. Subjects completed time-restricted
design tasks under varying con-ditions, allowing a detailed
analysis of their cognitive and iterative processes. The
research introduces a modified protocol analysis framework
to catego-rize interactions into "Physical," "Conceptual,"
"Knowledge," and "Venture" actions. Results identify three
co-creation patterns: Machine-Led, Human-Led, and
Human-Led-Machine-Led, each reflecting varying degrees of
crea-tivity and control. Key findings highlight that human
leadership in co-creation ensures task success while
leveraging AI's randomness and diversity enhances
creativity. The study concludes with recommendations for
improv-ing Gen-AI interfaces, fostering seamless
integration of diverse mediums to empower designers. Future
research directions include interdisciplinary com-parisons
and user interface enhancements to optimize
creativity-driven de-sign workflows.

column2: Rodrigo Garcia-Alvarado
column3:
Collaborative Development of Earthquake-Resistant and
Variable 3D Printed Housing
column7:
3D printed construction is a promising technology for
housing, but it must address challenges related to its
application and broader dissemination. This paper presents
the multidisciplinary and multi-institutional development
of a 3D printed housing prototype, incorporating seismic
resistance strategies and flexible design programming,
aimed at promoting the adoption of this technology in a
country prone to earthquakes, climatic variability, and
significant housing demand.
The project leverages automated printing equipment,
structural capacity analysis, and adaptable programming of
architectural forms to suit diverse geographical and
functional conditions, while also integrating with
traditional construction processes. As a result, a
generative design system for 3D-printed housing forms has
been established, alongside a comprehensive workflow for
BIM modeling and the toolpath programming. Additionally,
the project has developed a reliable procedure for material
preparation and verified printing techniques for
residential-height walls, along with strategies for
structural reinforcement, thermal insulation,
transportation, and on-site assembly.
Moreover, the initiative includes a thoroughly a plan for
foundations, roofing, installations, and housing finishes.
Ongoing environmental monitoring and displacement tracking
for seismic performance will provide insights for adjusting
designs to varying geographies and expanding architectural
possibilities.
This work has brought together architects, builders, and
structural, mechanical, and electronic engineers, all
contributing to the design, programming, execution and
management. Collaboration agreements, comprehensive
documentation, product testing, and equipment validation
have been key components of the project, creating new
avenues for university research and advancing the
capabilities of participating organizations and
professionals. Ultimately, this project opens a new horizon
for technological advancement in construction.

column2:
Sida Dai, Yuqing Zhou, Michael Carlos Barrios Kleiss and
Mostafa Alani
column3:
Reinforcement Learning-Based Design Approach for Kinetic
Facades in ICU Rooms: Enhancing Patient Comfort and Visual
Conditions
column7:
An Intensive Care Unit (ICU) is an integral component of
the modern hospital system, offering intensive and
specialized medical and nursing care for critically ill
patients who require prolonged hospital stays [1]. Unlike
outpatient care, ICU patients often endure prolonged stays
in severe physical and mental conditions, making it
essential to create a healing environment that soothes and
stabilizes their emotional state [2][3]. Common
environmental stressors in ICU include noise, ambient
lights, limited mobility, and social isolation [4]. ICU
patients often face challenges with mobility and body
positioning during their stay, making it even more critical
to provide a comfortable, adaptable lighting environment
[5][6][7]. Meanwhile, Kinetic facades have gained
increasing attention in recent years for their ability to
effectively regulate sunlight [8]. However, the complexity
of these facades presents a significant challenge in their
design and implementation [9]. This research proposed a
reinforcement learning-based design method for kinetic
facades to improve the comfort and visual conditions in ICU
rooms. This design method can optimize multiple design
objectives by applying reinforcement learning in the
generative process. The two key objectives are: (1)
reducing direct solar glare and heat for patients, and (2)
maximizing the view of the exterior landscape from the
patients' perspective. The study details the design
method's components, including the design system,
generative algorithm, and evaluation methodology. A case
study at Providence Alaska Medical Center demonstrates the
real-life application of this method and validates facade
performance through simulation. The results indicate that
the kinetic facade generated by the proposed method
successfully achieved the desired goals, significantly
reducing the likelihood of glare and heat for patients.

[1] Marshall, J. C., Bosco, L., Adhikari, N. K., Connolly,

What is an intensive care unit? A report of the task force

[2] Higgins, T. L., McGee, W. T., Steingrub, J. S.,

45-51.
[3] Moitra, V. K., Guerra, C., Linde-Zwirble, W. T., &
Wunsch, H. (2016). Relationship between ICU length of stay

[4] Wenham, T., & Pittard, A. (2009). Intensive care unit

[5] Bazuin, D., & Cardon, K. (2011). Creating healing

column2: Ariel Yakobi, Eran Sharon and Arielle Blonder
column3:
Investigating self-shaping fibre composites: tunning curing
parameters to optimise resulting curvature
column7:
As part of a broader architectural initiative aimed at
moldless fabrication of complex surfaces, this study
investigates the potential of self-shaping mate-rials,
specifically fiber composites. Composed of advanced fibers
such as glass or carbon embedded in epoxy resin, and
structured in controlled un-balanced laminates, these
materials form a Frustrated Composites system. Unlike
industrial practices that minimize displacement and strain,
our re-search aims to harness material properties to
generate curvature from pro-grammed internal stresses and
create controlled complex geometries from flat laminates.
Existing literature primarily focuses on producing balanced
laminates to reduce distortions, necessitating a
re-evaluation of fabrication protocols for Frustrated
Composite laminates. We investigate the effect of variables
such as temperature, curing time, and post-curing processes
over the shaping and post-relaxation curvature of
Frustrated Composites. Our methodology involves two stages:
identifying the effects of curing time and temperature on
uniformly patterned samples by measuring initial and
post-relaxation curvatures, and validating findings over
larger panels with com-plex patterns. Our findings aim to
provide new insights into the potential of self-morphing
composites, paving the way for innovative applications in
architectural design.

column2: Kaan Karabagli and Ethem Gurer
column3:
Co-Creative Urbanism and the Digital Flâneur: Reimagining
Urban Spaces through Mixed Reality
column7:
This study investigates how mixed reality (MR)
interventions can foster participatory urbanism in
small-scale “urban interiors,” reframing these localized
spaces as sites of ecological awareness and collaborative
design. Drawing on Merleau-Ponty’s theory of embodied
cognition, the research employs the concept of the “digital
flâneur” to examine how everyday users move beyond passive
observation by engaging with augmented overlays in
courtyards, atria, and semi-public corridors. Two pilot
workshops—one at a historic university campus and another
on a local island—serve as empirical anchors, enabling
participants to visualize and co-create interior
environments that integrate trees, animals, and local
biodiversity into immersive spatial narratives.
Findings underscore that MR-facilitated, small-scale
interventions can deepen both ecological literacy and
collective agency: participants revised conventional
designs to accommodate multispecies needs and contributed
diverse viewpoints to real-time spatial adaptations. Yet,
these benefits coexist with challenges regarding data
privacy, uneven digital literacy, and potential
commercialization, highlighting the need for transparent
governance frameworks that protect user autonomy and foster
equitable participation. By combining theoretical insights
on non-anthropocentric design with practical applications
in micro-scale experimentation, this paper reveals how MR
can catalyze socially inclusive and ecologically sensitive
transformations before scaling to broader contexts.
Ultimately, the study proposes that when approached with
robust ethical safeguards, MR technologies can cultivate a
new era of co-creative urbanism, positioning urban
interiors as generative microcosms for exploring collective
stewardship and sustainable futures.

column2: Celso Urroz and Shermeen Yousif
column3:
Open-Source Approaches to Integrating Advanced Robotic
Systems in Architecture
column7:
In the rapidly advancing field of computational design,
open-source methodologies and tools have proven to be
pivotal in democratizing knowledge in this discipline.
However, introducing and sharing knowledge of computational
fabrication with lay designers remains limited, with access
to open-source resources often constrained. This study
introduces a developed framework to democratize such
knowledge and provide open access methods, specifically for
integrated end-effector systems in architectural robotic
fabrication. The proposed framework is aimed at enabling
architects to fabricate sustainable architectural
prototypes with natural materials. We developed and
publicly shared customizable workflows that integrate both
software and hardware solutions for combining extrusion
processes—clay and thermoplastic—as well as gripper
applications. This included documentation for integrating
an electronic controller to connect end-effector actuators
(stepper motors or pneumatic valves) to a robotic arm, with
a signal flow from Rhino-Grasshopper ⟶ Robotic Arm ⟶
Arduino ⟶ End-effector Actuation. The central controller
design supports various end-effectors (clay/thermoplastic
extruders, pneumatic grippers), ensuring compatibility for
different tasks. Additionally, we created a library of
Grasshopper definitions for toolpath techniques like
variable speed control, 6-axis non-planar extrusion,
extrusion jumps, and pick-and-place toolpathing. By sharing
these workflows on GitHub, we offer an open-source
collaborative computational design framework, coupling
advanced computation and sustainable architectural robotics.

column2: Qian Cao, Weijing Wang and Rudi Stouffs
column3:
Revealing the Relationship Between Site Planning Strategies
and Sentiment Through Deep Learning: Enhancing Data-Driven
Architectural Design Strategies
column7:
Current architectural design research often overlooks
users' emotional responses in high-density urban
environments, limiting the effectiveness of design
strategies. To address this gap, our study combines deep
learning techniques with user-generated data from social
media to explore the complex relationship between site
functional layout and sentiment. By integrating the content
of images accompanying with textual information that are
collected from social media, we bridge the gap left by
traditional design research, which fails to account for
emotional feedback in decision-making.

We integrate building morphology data, master plan,
satellite imagery, and Points of Interest (POI) data,
utilizing Graph Neural Networks (GNN) to classify building
functions and extract relevant metrics. The site layout is
defined based on five key dimensions: spatial organization,
functional proportion, facility connectivity, physical
environment response, and land use intensity. Emotional
responses are categorized as negative, positive, and
neutral. Through regression analysis, the interaction
between emotional patterns and layout metrics is revealed,
illustrating the complex relationship between emotions and
site functional layout. We apply subjective dimension of
the space as the weight of identified physical dimensions,
constructing a comprehensive matrix for site planning. This
provides a new perspective for better understanding the
impact of functional layout on emotional experiences.

The findings indicate that site functional layout
significantly impacts users' emotional experiences. Highly
connected layouts enhance positive emotion, while areas
with better public facility availability and mixed-use
zones are identified as hedonic hot spots. Conversely,
isolated, single-function areas reduce users' happiness.
This study provides a data-driven design tool, highlighting
the critical role of site functional layout in shaping
subjective well-being and improving urban operational
efficiency.

column2: İpek Geç, Ayşegül Akçay Kavakoğlu and Leman Figen Gül
column3:
Innovative Fabric Formwork Systems: Origami-Based
Deployable Structures
column7:
Concrete is one of the most widely used materials in
architecture and con-struction. Traditional fixed formwork
systems, while common, fail to cap-ture the material’s
inherent fluidity. Exploring alternative production
tech-niques offers opportunities to reflect concrete’s
fluid nature in design. Fab-ric formwork, which allows
concrete to be shaped using its fluidity and makes it not
only a building element but also a part of design, is one
of the creative techniques that have been studied and
realized by many research-ers. Within the scope of this
study, fabric formwork is integrated into a folding mold
system inspired by origami and examined using physical,
dig-ital and computational design tools. Throughout the
process, each design it-eration fed the next model and
contributed to the development of the de-sign, creating a
circular production process. Then, the models designed and
produced in different environments were superposed using
the photogram-metry method and the values that each model
contributed to the design pro-cess were determined. In the
final phase, artificial intelligence-based visual-ization
tools were used to scale and analyse the potential of
folded fabric patterns from multiple perspectives. This
study not only evaluates a multi-stage production process
that occurs in parallel within both digital and physical
contexts but also demonstrates how an alternative,
sustainable, and cost-effective strategy can expand the
possibilities of concrete applica-tions beyond traditional
methods.

column2: Md Zishaan Khan, Halil Erhan and Elif Sezen Yagmur Kilimci
column3:
Design and Development of Interactive Systems for
Integration of Data-Informed Design Democratization
column7:
Engaging communities in design evaluation is essential for
creating built environments that meet stakeholder needs.
Traditional public engagement methods such as in-person
meetings, focus groups, and town halls—often fall short of
democratizing the design process, resulting in unfunctional
or undesirable spaces. Their limitations in time-scope
balance, inclusivity and accessibility can lead to mistrust
in the system, resulting in a lack of motiva-tion to share
opinions. These shortcomings highlight the need for new
tools that foster more inclusive community input. In this
paper, we argue for a de-sign-democratization approach that
invites design stakeholders to share their input informed
by the proposed alternatives and their data. We
demonstrated the implementation of this approach in D-DEM,
a social-media-like platform for data-informed discourse on
design proposals. Developed using design study methodology
and previous research on the existing tools in the
indus-try and academia, D-DEM presents design data to
engage design stakeholders inclusively and transparently.
We evaluated D-DEM’s usability, utility and adaptability
through a formative mixed-method study. Our initial
findings demonstrate the potential of using such platforms
to enhance the feedback loop, fostering a democratic design
discourse.

column2: Antony Pelosi and Tane Moleta
column3:
Establishing Non-Destructive, Data-Driven Design Workflows
for Interdisciplinary First-Year Architectural Studios.
column7:
While computational design has become integral to
architectural education, a notable gap remains in
introducing non-destructive, data-driven workflows during
the foundational year. This paper addresses this gap by
examining how such computational design methods can act as
catalytic interfaces—fostering interdisciplinary
collaboration and enhancing early architectural education
through iterative and flexible design processes.

Drawing on theoretical analysis and educational
observations from foundational courses, this study explores
how integrating non-destructive workflows with parametric
tools, such as Grasshopper, transforms the learning
environment. Implementing these workflows in large
first-year design studios enables students to engage
dynamically with computational principles, including
controlling points, lines, surfaces, and volumes, while
promoting adaptability and innovation.

By comparing two cohorts—one employing conventional
point-and-click workflows and another utilising
non-destructive parametric workflows—this study reveals
significant advantages in engagement, equity, and
computational thinking. Findings demonstrate that early
adoption of parametric tools fosters reflective practices,
enhances collaborative learning, and equips students with
critical skills for advanced architectural studies.
Recommendations for curriculum development highlight the
transformative potential of non-destructive workflows in
preparing students for contemporary architectural practice.
 
By outlining effective strategies and presenting case
studies of student work, we demonstrate how
non-destructive, data-driven workflows can be seamlessly
integrated into foundational courses, serving as catalytic
interfaces between computational design thinking and
architectural practice. Our findings reveal that early
adoption of these methods enhances computational skills and
fosters interdisciplinary collaboration among students. We
conclude with recommendations for curriculum development,
emphasizing the critical role of non-destructive workflows
in preparing students for advanced, interdisciplinary
architectural studies.

column2:
Mehrun-Nisa Raja, Md Zishaan Khan, Halil Erhan and Tina
Bahrouz
column3:
Gamification as a Tool for Enhancing Public Engagement in
Built-Environment Design.
column7:
This research explores the potential of gamification to
enhance public en-gagement in the built environment,
addressing the limitations of traditional methods. We
hypothesize that stakeholder participation in evaluating
alterna-tive designs using spatial and non-spatial data can
be significantly increased by integrating game elements
such as feedback mechanisms, rewards, and pro-gress
in-dictators into task-based systems. We present an initial
prototype that implements a flexible gamification schema,
offering rewards for achieving specific goals, a progress
bar to track advancement, and feedback loops to maintain
user interest. Our findings suggest that gamification can
enhance mo-tivation, engagement, and collaboration by
making tasks enjoyable and inter-active. This approach
leverages the power of digital platforms to democratize
design decisions and foster a more inclusive and informed
public discourse. The research contributes a methodology
for applying gamification to task-guided public engagement
systems, providing valuable insights for developing digital
tools for the built environment.

column2: Yanran Shan and Kam-Ming Mark Tam
column3:
Discovering Pareto-Efficient Urban Networks Through Shape
Grammar, Multi-Objective Optimisation and Machine Learning
column7:
The concept of a “15-minute neighborhood” is a widely
recognized and practiced global initiative that aims to
create walkable cities, improving convenience and reducing
carbon emissions by optimizing the layout of urban street
networks. However, walkability, which broadly describes the
closeness of any combination of points of interest in a
city, can come into conflict with other urban planning
goals, such as infrastructure cost and traffic. Therefore,
a design approach based on multi-objective optimization is
needed to navigate the trade-off of potentially conflicting
urban design objectives.

This work builds on past design approaches combining
multi-objective optimization and shape grammar (Lima et
al., 2022), proposing an AI-assisted design framework that
efficiently leverages the data generated from
multi-objective optimization to expedite and enhance the
design exploration of urban networks according to various
performances. Specifically, the research introduces a
surrogate model that learns to map design into various key
urban design quantities and a generative model that
generates urban networks at the multi-objective
optimization solution space.  Both models use convolutional
neural networks (CNN) as their backbone, while the
generative model leverages generative adversarial networks.
Notably, this work devised strategies to embed constraints
of the urban grammar space into the CNN and operators to
ensure the generation of diverse design solutions. By doing
so, the research developed new insights that clarified the
relationship between urban planning objectives and designs.
Ultimately, this work opens new pathways for the
exploration of efficient urban designs that balance
walkability with other urban planning objectives, fostering
sustainable development and enhancing the quality of life
in urban environments.

References:
Lima, F. T., Brown, N. C., & Duarte, J. P. (2022). A
grammar-based optimization approach for walkable urban
fabrics considering pedestrian accessibility and
infrastructure cost. Environment and Planning. B, Urban
Analytics and City Science, 49(5), 1489–1506.
https://doi.org/10.1177/23998083211048496

column2: Umaru Mohammed Bongwirnso and Christiane Margerita Herr
column3:
IoT-Driven Biophilic Design Strategies for the Operation of
Net-Zero Energy Buildings
column7:
In China, building energy consumption is projected to
increase by 80% by 2050 [1], [2] due to technological
advancement and population growth. Addressing these
challenges requires innovative approaches that combine the
reduction of carbon emissions with a simultaneous increase
in living quality as well as health and well-being. This
study examines how biophilic design strategies can be
employed to improve energy efficiency, reduce carbon
emissions, and create healthier indoor environments [3].
Complementing well-established energy conservation
strategies [4], we employ IoT for real-time monitoring and
data collection, focusing on biophilic elements such as
natural light, ventilation, and greenery for improved
energy management and occupant comfort during the
building’s operational stage, assessed through the Indoor
Environmental Quality (IEQ).
We focus on how IoT-driven systems can enhance IEQ in
commercial buildings during operation while reducing carbon
footprints and advancing net-zero energy goals. IoT serves
as a comprehensive framework for real-time data collection
from building sensors that monitor biophilic and
energy-related factors. IoT-driven systems optimize energy
use and occupant well-being, balancing quantitative metrics
like energy consumption, air quality, and thermal comfort
with qualitative factors like natural light, ventilation,
and material selection. The study utilizes DesignBuilder
v7.3.0 to model a prototype commercial building in a
subtropical climate, comparing energy efficiency and
occupant behavior in scenarios with and without IoT-enabled
biophilic design.
The findings offer new perspectives into sustainable
building practices, showing how IoT-driven biophilic design
strategies can improve indoor environments, reduce energy
use, and enhance occupant well-being. The study advances
current initiatives by illustrating how innovative
technologies combined with biophilic design strategies can
create resilient, low-carbon, and healthier building indoor
environments.


References:
[1]	S. Guo, D. Yan, S. Hu, and Y. Zhang, “Modelling
building energy consumption in China under different future
scenarios,” Energy, vol. 214, p. 119063, 2021, doi:
10.1016/j.energy.2020.119063.
[2]	B. Gao, X. Zhu, J. Ren, J. Ran, M. K. Kim, and J. Liu,
“Multi-objective optimization of energy-saving measures and
operation parameters for a newly retrofitted building in
future climate conditions: A case study of an office
building in Chengdu,” Energy Reports, vol. 9, pp.
2269–2285, 2023, doi: 10.1016/j.egyr.2023.01.049.
[3]	Y. Gong, E. S. Zoltán, and G. János, “Healthy Dwelling:
The Perspective of Biophilic Design in the Design of the
Living Space,” Buildings, vol. 13, no. 8, pp. 1–15, 2023,
doi: 10.3390/buildings13082020.
[4]	Yuchen Wang, L. Liu, S. Sharma, F. A. Awwad, M. I.
Khan, and E. A. A. Ismail, “Integration of internet of
things (IoT) technology in the design model of sustainable
green building spaces,” Environ. Dev. Sustain., no.
0123456789, 2024, doi: 10.1007/s10668-024-04968-w.

column2: Xin Wang and Sam Joyce
column3: MORPHOLOGICAL SECTIONS THROUGH LATENT SPACE
column7:
The design of floor plans is a core task in architecture,
balancing functionality, spatial configuration, aesthetics,
and efficiency. Traditional methods struggle with
complexity and flexibility, limiting rapid iteration during
early design stages. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
offer a novel approach, but controlling GAN outputs to meet
specific design needs remains a challenge.
This study proposes a novel workflow for floor plan
generation using StyleGAN3, replacing traditional segmented
design processes with an end-to-end approach that generates
complete floor plans in one step. By leveraging latent
space control techniques, precise manipulation of
attributes such as geometric features (e.g., proportions,
aspect ratios), drawing styles (e.g., line thickness), and
structural elements is achieved. A dataset of 2,000
high-resolution apartment floor plans was used to train the
model, with Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and GANSpace
methods employed to explore latent space characteristics.
Linear interpolation and attribute vectors further enable
the transformation of layout typologies (e.g., horizontal
to vertical), showcasing the intuitiveness of latent space
exploration and its potential to guide design.
Key contributions of this study are threefold. First, it
establishes a novel GAN-based workflow for full floor plan
generation, enabling the creation of complete and coherent
layouts in a single step. Second, it introduces latent
space exploration techniques to improve control over
GAN-generated architectural floor plans, revealing the
relationships between StyleGAN3 latent space and key
architectural attributes. Third, it provides a theoretical
and practical framework for integrating GANs into
early-stage conceptual design processes, empowering
architects to efficiently generate diverse, optimized
schemes and bridging cutting-edge AI technology with
creative exploration.

column2: Yuchen Wang and Yin-Shan Lin
column3:
AR-Driven Multidisciplinary On-Site Design for Revitalizing
Existing Built Environments with MIMOSA Platform
column7:
This paper explores a novel approach for early-phase design
in the context of urban renewal, focusing on the
revitalization of existing built environments. By
leveraging augmented reality (AR) technology, this method
enables multidisciplinary design teams to conceptualize,
design, and collaborate directly on-site, enhancing
site-specific awareness and facilitating communication
among professionals from different disciplines. The
proposed method is supported by the development of the
MIMOSA platform, which allows users to engage in tasks
related to urban planning, architectural design, and
landscape design through dedicated functional modules. With
dual perspectives, an AR camera lens and a drawing panel,
it provides an integrated interface for on-site design.
Additionally, the platform features built-in real-time
modeling and statistical visualization of design
indicators, highlighting the interdependencies and
constraints between disciplines. Preliminary tests
demonstrate the platform's capability to enable seamless
transitions and synchronization between different
disciplinary modules. However, further improvements are
needed in areas such as model alignment, user interface
optimization, and the level of participation for each
discipline.

column2: Yiting Sun, Hua Chai, Tianyi Gao and Philip F. Yuan
column3:
Developing Stress-Line ribbed Timber Slabs: Laminating
Timber Ribs with Stay-in-Place Formwork
column7:
While the concrete ribbed slabs brought forward by Pier
Luigi Nervi have been widely studied, timber counterparts
are less explored due to the complexity and variety of
their curved form. There have been considerable
difficulties to build curvature with timber in regards of
its identical materiality with current stress line
generation tools and fabrication technologies. This study
introduces a design and fabrication method for ribbed
timber slabs that simulates the principal stress lines. A
weighted Voronoi diagram-based algorithm is employed to
generate the curve patterns that simulate the stress-line
distribution, accommodating various slab geometry and
boundary conditions. The generated pattern involves
simulating the principal stress lines using two types of
curves: radial curves emanating from the supports to
simulate the maximum principal stress curves, and looped
curves encircling the support to simulate the minimum
principal stress lines. Radial components primarily
function as reinforcement ribs for the slab, which are
constructed from multiple layers of wood laminas. Looped
curves are approximated using discrete timber sticks that
serve as stay-in-place formwork. The looped components are
first assembled and fixed precisely according to their
designed positions. Then, continuous laminas are then bent
against these formworks to form the radial ribs, ensuring
continuity in the direction of the major principal moments.
Timber ribs are curved laminated without the need for
custom-made moulds. The integration of computational design
and digital fabrication offers a scalable solution for
creating timber slabs with complex geometries, making it an
attractive proposition for sustainable construction
practices.

column2: Qinhui Yang, Hua Chai and Philip F. Yuan
column3:
Stock-Constrained Design of Irregular Material Based on
Graph Neural Networks
column7:
The application of natural materials and recycled materials
in the construction industry is crucial for reducing
resource consumption and lowering carbon emissions.
However, the irregularity in dimensions, shape, and
physical proper-ties of these materials, coupled with the
constraints of available stock, poses significant
challenges for practical application. Designing with
limited and var-ied material stocks requires precise
matching of materials to specific structural needs, which
is difficult to achieve using traditional methods.
Tradition algo-rithms struggle when applied to irregular
materials, where variability in form and property
complicates the optimization process, leading to less
efficient uti-lization of resources. To address these
challenges, this study proposes an inno-vative method based
on Graph Neural Network (GNN). The proposed GNN method
converts the design scheme of irregular materials into
graph, capturing the intricate relationships between design
scheme and materials. By training on a dataset specifically
generated to reflect real-world conditions, the GNN model
learns to accurately predict optimal matching positions for
each material under stock-constrain. This approach not only
enhances the precision of material al-location but also
significantly improves the efficiency and sustainability of
uti-lizing irregular materials. Moreover, the integration
of a novel Frame+ layer re-fines the feature extraction
process, enabling more accurate predictions of mate-rial
fit. Beam placement in a floor slab are used as a case
study. Consequently, this research provides new ideas and
technical means for the efficient utilization of irregular
materials in the construction industry, offering a
promising ap-proach to stock-constrained design and
promoting sustainable and circular con-struction practices.

column2: Marco Mondello and Fulvio Papadhopulli
column3:
Synaptic Synergies: A Dual Perspective on AI Integration in
Architectural Education and CAAD Pedagogy
column7:
Large Language Models (LLMs) and text-to-image synthesizers
are gaining momentum in academic contexts, challenging
educators to adapt and evolve, and destining the first
generation of students exposed to Artificial Generative
Intelligence (AGI) to become more proficient in AI than
their mentors. In this evolving pedagogical landscape, the
role of educators should be to guide students towards
deeper, more meaningful interactions with AI, rather than
simply allowing the availability of this technology to be
superficially integrated into existing didactical
frameworks.
This paper presents the results of an inter-university
collaboration aimed at developing a replicable workflow to
enhance the interactivity of computational design tools and
integrate AI-driven processes into architectural
education.The aim is to merge data-driven decision making
with the unconscious realms of text-to-image prompting. The
workflow focuses on two core concepts: (1) Design with
Environmental Analysis, which emphasises contextual
sustainability by optimising both public spaces
microclimates and the building's environmental performance;
and (2) AGI-enhanced visions using Stable Diffusion's
ComfyUI interface to enhance diversity with mutiple
AGI-driven design explorations. The methodology involves
two iterations: a week-long intensive workshop and a
semester-long CAAD course, delivered at different
universities, with project sites and programmes freely
chosen by the students. Outcomes are assessed against five
indicators: Conceptual Maturity, Adaptive Agency,
Contextual Resonance, Critical Integration of AI and
Generative Diversity.  Both iterations are analysed
comparatively. The results reveal a tension between
data-driven contextual design and AGI-generated conceptual
visions that can only be resolved through the skilful use
of this new technology.
This research critically examines the benefits and
limitations of AI as a design education tool, contributing
to the wider discussion of AI's role as a co-creator in
modern pedagogy. By encouraging innovative workflows and
interdisciplinary collaboration, this study highlights the
potential of AI to reshape architectural education and
inspire future generations of designers.

column2: Elif Aktas Yanas and Leman Figen Gül
column3:
Empathy in Design Cognition: Examining the Impact of Trait
Empathy on Architectural Outcomes
column7:
In recent years, computer-aided design (CAAD) interfaces
have made it easier to create products that closely
resemble real-world experiences through three-dimensional
visualizations, virtual reality, and simulations. Using
these tools in both the design and final production stages
allows designers to imagine the user experience better.
However, there are concerns that these technologies may
risk alienating and distancing the designer from the real
needs of users by virtualizing materiality, spatial
understanding, and human interaction. As a primary human
faculty, empathy naturally allows designers to envision how
individuals might interact socially, emotionally, and
physically with the designed environment. While empathy is
assumed to impact design outcomes, no conclusive proof
exists (Chang-Arana et al.,2022).
This study investigates the relationship between designers'
empathic engagements and their design outcomes through
think-aloud design protocols conducted with 16 architecture
and interior architecture students. We assessed empathic
engagement through two methods: the 'Feeling AS' empathy
framework we developed and the Empathy Quotient (EQ) test
(Baron-Cohen & Wheelwright, 2004), which was translated
into Turkish by Bora and Baysan-Arabacı (2009). Final
design outcomes were evaluated by an independent jury using
Shah et al.'s (2000) framework, which measures Quantity,
Quality, Novelty, and Variety. By comparing empathy scores
with these metrics, we aim to determine whether empathy
drives more user-centered, innovative design solutions.
Throughout this study, we aim to contribute a broader
discourse on empathy in design cognition and explore how
empathy can shape design practice.

References
Baron-Cohen, S. Wheelwright, S. (2004). The empathy
quotient: an investigation of adults with Asperger syndrome
or high functioning autism and typical sex differences. J
Autism Dev Disord. 34,163-175.

Bora  E., Baysan-Arabacı, l. (2009). Empati Ölçeği Türkçe
formunun üniversite öğrencilerinde psikometrik özellikleri.
Klinik Psikofarmakoloji Bülteni 19 (1), 39-47.

Chang-Arana, Á. M., Surma-aho, A., Hölttä-Otto, K., & Sams,
M. (2022). Under the umbrella: Components of empathy in
psychology and design. Design Science, 8, e20.
https://doi.org/10.1017/dsj.2022.13.

Shah, J. J., Kulkarni, S. V., & Vargas-Hernandez, N.
(2000). Evaluation of Idea Generation Methods for
Conceptual Design: Effectiveness Metrics and Design of
Experiments. Journal of Mechanical Design, 122(4),
377. doi:10.1115/1.1315592

column2: Hayri Dortdivanlioglu
column3:
Computing Beyond the Vitruvian Canon: Ambiguity as a
Catalyst in Computational Design Theory
column7:
This paper reinterprets Vitruvius’s architectural theory to
challenge the canonical view of De Architectura as a rigid,
rule-based system of Classical architecture. Traditionally,
Vitruvius has been positioned as the foundation of
deterministic architectural logic, emphasizing proportional
and formal systems—a logic reinforced by computational
design’s algorithmic formalization. However, this study
uncovers the latent ambiguities within Vitruvius’s
prescriptions, revealing gaps, redundancies, and contextual
flexibility that foster dynamic and adaptive design
processes. Drawing on George Stiny’s conception of
ambiguity in shape grammars, this paper argues that
Vitruvius’s ambiguities align with contemporary
computational approaches, where open-ended rules and
iterative recalibrations enable creativity and
responsiveness to context. By reframing Vitruvius’s
principles as a generative framework, this study bridges
historical and computational design, demonstrating how
ambiguity functions as a catalytic interface for
innovation, adaptability, and interdisciplinary exchange in
architecture.

column2: Marija Mateljan, Seyran Khademi and Georg Vrachliotis
column3:
Reading Between the Lines: Bridging AI and Architectural
Knowledge in Floorplan Understanding
column7:
Architectural drawings are powerful tools for representing
spatial, functional, and relational knowledge about
buildings and environments. Traditionally interpreted by
humans, these drawings are now increasingly analyzed by
learning machines, opening new possibilities for design.
However, machine’s current ability to understand floorplans
is still limited compared to human architectural expertise.
By enabling machines to read and analyze floorplans as
architects do, we unlock new ways to enhance and support
the design process in an era of growing visual data. A key
challenge is enabling machines to interpret geometry,
topology, and architectural semantics with the same depth,
fluidity, and understanding as architects. While architects
instinctively perceive visuals as cohesive wholes, drawing
on tacit knowledge and experience that shape their
perception, machines require formalized relationships
through annotated knowledge representation. Formalization
is crucial for bridging the gap between human perception
and computational analysis in the evolving landscape of
intelligent machines. This study proposes a theoretical
framework for understanding spatial knowledge in
floorplans, addressing the various layers of information
embedded within them. By deconstructing implicit
information using a case study of a house, this research
connects visual features with computer vision tasks such as
detection, segmentation, and classification, while also
associating architectural semantics with existing knowledge
models. The framework outlines 15 information layers that
provide a foundation for future architectural datasets.
This interdisciplinary approach bridges the gap between
human perception and computational analysis, enhancing
transparency and accessibility in architectural reasoning,
contributing to holistic knowledge representation in the
era of multimodal artificial intelligence (AI).

column2: Filipe Coutinho Quaresma, Nuno Rio and Filipe Guterres
column3:
A Detail Shape Grammar Interpreter – the case of generate
grammars to fabricate.
column7:
This investigation shows the construction of a shape
grammar interpreter focusing a specific shape grammar
(Stiny, 1972) that is a shape grammar of detail,
incorporating rules to produce habitable artifacts
manufactured through CNC and FDM. The Detail Shape Grammar
Interpreter (DSGI) proposed, aims to be easy and intuitive
to use (Stouffs, 2022), supporting a constraint number of
rules and its parameters from two different detail
grammars, a Detail Shape Grammar of the Play Shelter
(Quaresma, 2024) e a Residential Structures for the Elderly
Transformation Grammar (Guterres, 2022). A shape
recognition module is being used with promising results,
expanding the possibilities of manipulating a set of rules
generic part. 4 levels of satisfaction are offered at DSGI
(Excellent; Good; reasonable and Weak) serving as a control
mode in the appli-cation of the machine learning (ML)
module, with the prediction being carried out with
non-linear regression, proceeding to change γ according to
those 4 conditions leading to “optimized” design solutions
through rule generation. A User Interface was built using
the Add-on in GH, Human UI, which made possible to expand
the computational component allowing the application of
rules and their parameters in real time leveraging and
facilitating collaboration processes between project teams
(Menges, 2023), promoting co-design to fabricate.

column2: Pok Yin Victor Leung and Yijiang Huang
column3:
Design Validation and Conflict Resolution for Robotic
Fabrication: A Multi-Stage Framework for Complex and
Non-Repetitive Processes
column7:
The use of robotics in construction offers transformative
possibilities but also unique computational challenges,
especially for bespoke and non-repetitive assembly
processes. Fabrication constraints such as robotic
reachability, material grasp stability, collision, and
structural stability have to be validated before
construction begins.
However, validating all constraints are computationally
expensive and the current approach are linear black-boxes
that simply run until detecting a conflict.
When attempting to resolve the conflict, the current
approach provides no indication of which variables to
adjust and how to adjust them.

This paper introduces a multi-stage constraint-validation
and conflict-resolution approach as part of a
computer-aided design process.
The approach is developed and its feasibility is validated
by the robotic construction of a complex timber pavilion
with numerous interdependent design variables.
These variable includes the shapes and position of
individual timber elements, choices of structural joints,
and robotic tools.
Our design approach organizes these variables and their
associated constraints into three conflict-resolution
stages: (1) Assembly Design Stage - where real-time
feedback supports creative exploration, (2) Process Design
Stage - where fabrication decision are made, and (3) Motion
Planning Stage - where collision-free trajectories are
computed.
We introduce the concept of proxy checks to provide faster
feedback and more interpretable results in each stage,
enhancing the iterative design process.
Our approach marks a step toward a more intelligent,
computer-aided design systems that can provide suggestions
to resolve conflicts, advancing the field of computational
design for robotic construction.

column2: Cem Ataman, Bige Tuncer and Simon Perrault
column3:
Enhancing End-to-End Processing, Analysis, and
Visualization of Citizen Participation Data in Urban Design
and Planning
column7:
Analysing citizen feedback in urban practices is critical
for developing re-sponsive, inclusive cities, yet managing
the complex, large-scale datasets generated by digital
participation presents significant challenges. This paper
presents the Digital Participation Data Analysis Toolkit
(DIP-DAT), a web-based platform developed to facilitate the
systematic analysis of large-scale digital participation
data in urban design and planning. As cities increasing-ly
collect extensive citizen feedback on issues like climate,
housing, and public spaces, the need for intuitive tools to
interpret these textual datasets grows. Existing solutions
often lack cohesion, requiring technical expertise for
tasks such as preprocessing, topic modelling, and
visualisation, which limits usability for non-specialists.
DIP-DAT addresses these challenges by integrating automated
preprocessing, customizable hyperparameter tuning, and
interactive visualisation within a unified interface,
streamlining analy-sis for researchers, designers,
planners, and policymakers. Through expert evaluation
across domains, DIP-DAT demonstrates its capacity to
trans-form digital feedback into actionable insights,
enabling more inclusive, da-ta-driven urban practices. This
paper discusses the platform’s design prin-ciples,
workflow, and expert feedback, highlighting its potential
to bridge the gap between complex data analytics and
practical urban applications.

column2: Worawan Natephra, Wadeeya Natephra and Ali Motamedi
column3:
Leveraging BIM-Integrated Cloud-based Data Extraction for
Building Envelope Thermal Performance Assessment
column7:
The assessment of building envelope thermal performance is
pivotal for the energy efficient design process. The
selection of an optimal combination of material options for
building envelopes is considered a crucial strategy to
minimize heat transfer, thereby preventing excessive energy
use for heating and cooling, while maintaining indoor
thermal comfort. However, evaluating the thermal
performance of building envelopes based on Overall Thermal
Transfer Value (OTTV) regulations requires manual
computation, which involves numerous variables and
coefficients. Retrieving thermal properties and related
coefficients from the BIM model can potentially shorten the
time required for OTTV assessment. In this research, a
BIM-based data sharing solution for extracting essential
thermal properties of materials is proposed to facilitate
the computation of OTTV of building envelopes. The proposed
method introduces a semi-automated approach for extracting
relevant variables and coefficients directly from BIM
databases stored on the cloud. This provides
interoperability and facilitates collaboration for
accessing accurate and detailed information of physical and
thermal properties of envelope materials from the BIM
database, leading to precise thermal transfer value
calculation. An interactive data visualization dashboard of
OTTV related variables and coefficients is also developed
to provide feedback on building envelope design in
accordance with OTTV regulations. A BIM model of a
residential building is used as the case study to assess
the feasibility of the pro-posed method. The results
revealed that the proposed method provides crucial
information required for design stakeholder to explore and
choose appropriate envelope material combinations to attain
optimal heat transfer coefficients and OTTV.

column2:
Kyunghyun Cho, Hyun Woo Kim, Jae Yeon Shin, Gisung Han and
Seung Hyun Cha
column3:
Thematic Analysis on the Relationships of Design
Personalization on Work Productivity and Workspace
Satisfaction in Virtual Reality
column7:
This study explored a relationship of design
personalization in virtual reality workspaces (VRWS) with
work productivity and workspace satisfaction, based on
trends among working cultures such as 'Desk-terior' and
'Workation'. It highlights the growing desire for
personalized workspaces and how VR technology can offer
more flexibility than physical offices. Despite existing VR
platforms, the importance of design personalization is
often overlooked, with insufficient research on its effects
on psychological and functional performance. The study
focused on whether personalization of VRWS design is
related to workspace satisfaction and work productivity,
and how varying scopes of personalization influence these
results. The study conducted a Focus Group Interview (FGI)
with nine graduate students following prior experience in a
prototyped VRWS with the four conditions of design
personalization. Participants gained experience working in
VRWS using the Oculus Quest Pro VR device. They
personalized the workspace design across four levels,
ranging from a default condition (not allowed to change) to
a Lv. 3 condition with major alterations (e.g., form and
structure). After that, they conducted a brief language
test, which required the same logical comprehension ability
with knowledge work. They performed FGIs a couple of weeks
later, and all the procedures were recorded and
transcribed. The interview data was thematically analyzed
to draw insights and provide an in-depth comprehension of
the correlation of design personalization to work
productivity and workspace satisfaction. The results showed
that design personalization positively influences workspace
satisfaction, whereas there were no direct relationships
between personalization and work productivity.
Nevertheless, the study found an indirect relationship
between the two through users' positive affect change due
to personalized workspace design and procedure. This
research establishes a solid foundation for VRWS design
research by providing an in-depth understanding of the
relationship between design personalization, work
productivity, and workspace satisfaction. It encourages
further studies on optimal personalization features and
offers guidelines for improving existing VRWS platforms.

column2: Zixi Zhang, Wenjing Li and Waishan Qiu
column3:
Exploring the Relationship between Perceived Geographic
Authenticity and Streetscape Features through Machine
Learning
column7:
In the context of globalization and cultural hybridization,
immigrant communities significantly shape how streets are
perceived. While existing research have utilized machine
learning to create quantitative models that link subjective
perceptions to street features, a quantitative correlation
between geographic authenticity perception and streetscape
visual features remains unexplored, highlighting a critical
research gap.

This research presents a framework to measure geographic
authenticity perception by integrating large-scale Street
View Images (SVIs) with crowdsourcing, machine learning,
and computer vision. Chinatowns of New York City, the most
prominent immigrant communities, are chosen as a case
study. Specifically, (1) With a crowdsourcing survey
platform and TrueSkill algorithm, five geographic
authenticity perception scores associated with Chinatown
were collected from SVIs—sense of Chinatown, sense of
Cantonese, sense of China, sense of Asia and sense of
East—as well as eleven mainstream streetscape quality
perception scores (e.g., attractive, comfortable). (2)
Computer vision models were employed to extract key visual
features from SVIs. (3) Multiple machine learning
algorithms modeled the relationship between each perception
score and features. The correlation between geographic
authenticity perceptions and mainstream streetscape quality
perceptions was also explored.

The results indicate that: (1) Eight out of twenty street
visual features are significantly correlated with five
geographical authenticity perceptions of Chinatown, with
varying impacts on each perception. (2) Perceptions of
mainstream streetscape quality differ in their correlation
with five perceptions of geographical authenticity.

This study extends the existing street perception
categories to geographic authenticity perception that
related to cultural attributes. It inspires the
establishment of geographic authenticity perception
indicators for immigrant communities of other countries or
cultures.

column2: Yalei Zhu, Tianyi Gao, Hua Chai and Philip F. Yuan
column3:
Grasp-to-Mill (GtM) Integrated Workflow for Natural Log
Joint Fabrication Based on Multi-Objective Optimization
Algorithm
column7:
With the growing demand for sustainability and innovative
materials in the construction industry, the use of recycled
wood and natural materials has become a key focus of
research. This study presents an integrated dual-robot
autonomous grasp-to-mill fabrication method for processing
irregular natural logs. By optimizing robotic operations,
the method enables efficient and precise processing of
complex geometries while exploring the architectural
potential of irregular timber. The research involves
developing a parametric model library for reused natural
logs, employing YOLO for vision-based recognition and
positioning, and con-structing grasp-to-mill strategies
based on multi-objective optimization algorithms,
addressing parameters such as gripper posture, robotic
stability, and fabrication efficiency. Two case studies
demonstrate the feasibility of the method: the first is a
reciprocal timber structure prototype composed of 28
interlocking natural logs, and the second is a tower
structure constructed using 27 natural logs and traditional
mortise and tenon joints. The study highlights the synergy
between robotics and artificial intelligence, expanding the
application possibilities of irregular timber in
architectural design and construction.

column2:
Nils Opgenorth, Zhenxiang Huang, Jonas Maria Mertens, Hans
Jakob Wagner and Achim Menges
column3:
Prompt-to-Production: AI-Driven Design and Robotic
Fabrication for Rapidly Reconfigurable Circular Timber
Assemblies
column7:
Confronted with accelerating change, the design of
sustainable environments must align long-lasting
philosophies with hyper-adaptive solutions. This research
introduces a method for rapidly reconfigurable timber
assemblies using AI-driven design and robotic fabrication,
known as prompt-to-production. The approach integrates AI
to generate architectural timber designs from text prompts,
which are then discretized into buildable components for
robotic assembly. These timber elements, designed for
circular reuse, can be disassembled and reconfigured into
new designs, supporting flexibility and sustainability in
construction.

AI technologies like GANs have been widely used for visual
design, while recent advancements include tools that
generate 3D shapes and CAD models from prompts (He, 2024).
However, existing AI models struggle to create coherent,
fabricable building ensembles (Koehler, 2023), and current
fabrication tools are limited to techniques like 3D
printing. Recent algorithms (Tian et al., 2024) generate
feasible assembly plans but are restricted to simple “pick
and place” operations. This research addresses these
limitations by introducing a system that supports broader
fabrication processes and adaptable robotic setups.

The developed tool generates detailed fabrication data,
including pick-and-place sequences, joint connections, tool
changes, and travel paths to avoid collisions. Digital
simulations of the fabrication process ensure the robotic
assembly is efficient and error-free. During a one-week
workshop at Tongji University, participants explored the
system’s potential through projects involving large-scale
architectural designs, human-robot collaboration, and
timber assembly optimization. Several prototypes were
fabricated, culminating in the robotic assembly of two
large-scale structures, validating the workflow.

This research demonstrates how AI and robotics can enable
adaptive, sustainable construction, promoting a circular
economy and advancing architectural practices with
efficiency and environmental consciousness.

column2: Jiaxiang Luo and Tian Tian Lo
column3:
Two-Way Interventive Design and Manufacturing: Real-time
design and materiality visualization through mixed reality
systems based on hand tracking
column7:
Abstract

This research proposes a mixed reality (MR)human-computer
collaboration sys-tem based on a "two-way intervention"
approach, which integrates MR and hand tracking technology
to enhance the design and manufacturing workflow driven by
human creativity. By combining MR devices such as HoloLens2
(MR head-set) with advanced design algorithms, the system
not only effectively copes with uncertainties in the
initial design process, but also simulates the design and
manu-facturing process of architectural materials by
learning the physical properties of real materials. This
improves the flexibility and operability of the entire
process. The system adopts two-way real-time interaction
mode, which breaks through the limitation of traditional
design and manufacturing which is dominated by top-down
linear flow, and realizes the close combination of design
and manufacturing process. With the help of hand tracking
technology, users can intuitively control design elements
in the virtual environment, adjust and optimize the design
in real time, forming a highly collaborative closed-loop
design and manufacturing pro-cess. At the same time, the
system can dynamically respond to the user's design
intentions and changes in material conditions, providing
intelligent and custom-ized design optimization
suggestions. The experimental results show that the
pro-posed method has obvious advantages in dynamic and
adaptive aspects, and can effectively deal with the
challenges in complex design and manufacturing scenar-ios,
while improving material utilization efficiency and
reducing production waste.

column2:
Jessica Bielski, Alejandro Rueda, Ivan Bratoev and Frank
Petzold
column3:
Relevant Data And Its Metrics for the Design Process -
Data-based Design-Decision-Making of Architects Prevalent
During The Sketching Process
column7:
To avoid the misinterpretation of the output of
contemporary machine learning (ML) systems, explainability
(XAI) was introduced. It aims to facilitate a well-informed
design workflow of humanartificial- intelligence-teams
(HATs) of human user and ML. For a HAT for architectural
co-design, the communication between architect and
artificial intelligence (AI) needs to be of situational,
conversational nature
(Situation Awareness, SA). However, the relevant data and
its metrics for architects to make decisions for specific
points in time is insufficiently explored for ML. Thus,
this approach aims to identify the situation during the
design decision-making process, when relevant data and its
metrics are prevalent. A literature review on data-based
designing during the order-less design process is
superimposed on an established sequencing framework. The
results are triangulated through a pilot sketch protocol
study capturing the inquired data and applied metrics by
architects. The relevant data and its metrics are
pinpointed and determined within the architectural design
process. Thus, the architectural design development is
deciphered and formalised for further ML approaches.

column2: Jessica Bielski, Ivan Bratoev and Frank Petzold
column3:
Situational Explainability - Explainability for
architectural decision-making support of artificial
intelligence approaches
column7:
Artificial intelligence (AI) methods, such as machine
learning (ML), can expedite well-informed decision-making
during the impactful early design stages through e.g.,
suggestions. Explainability methods (explainable artificial
intelligence, XAI) are a promising approach to remedy the
miscommunication in human-computer-interaction (HCI). It
facilitates interpretability by the human user, optimising
the performance of ML-based design support. The co-creative
human-AI-teams (HATs) of architects and AI aims to mimic
the common architectural practice of design-decision-making
through discussion. This calls for explanations
complementing design suggestions for the individual
situation during the conversation. However, currently
proper communication within HAT for further design
development fails due to insufficient dialogic nature. This
concept paper proposes HCI and cognitive psychology
research for XAI approaches to improve co-creative design
development of AI-generated autocompletion suggestions and
architects through situational explainability. It aims to
investigate the influence on their respective usefulness to
impact the design decisions of the early stages. Drawing
from HCI research, theory-driven explainability, target
group customization, emotion consideration and affective
design of XAI are employed for improvements in situational
decision-making abilities (situation awareness, SA).

column2: Dezijian Zhou, Anastasia Globa and Rebecca McLaughlan
column3:
Emotional Well-Being in Older Adults: The Role of XR,
Spatial, and Physical Interaction in Remote Multimodal
Communication
column7:
This study explores how integrating spatial communication
and physical interaction systems in Extended Reality (XR)
environments can enhance remote social interactions and
digital storytelling, ultimately improving the well-being
of older adults.  With societal aging and shifting family
structures, many older adults rely on remote communication,
yet traditional methods often fail to meet their emotional,
cognitive, and social needs, leading to isolation and
mental health challenges.  While existing technologies
address some aspects of remote spatial communication, they
frequently overlook the specific needs and experiences of
older users. To bridge this gap, this study employs a
Research through Design and Autobiographical Design
approach, using the Spatial and Physical Component and Slot
Layout System to design and evaluate solutions.  From the
researcher’s internal perspective, it examines how these
technologies can strengthen long-term social and emotional
connections for older adults in remote contexts.  The study
provides practical methods, experiential insights, and
real-world applications for developing immersive multimodal
communication systems.  By focusing on spatial and physical
interaction systems in remote XR environments, this
research contributes to the social experiences of older
users and advances interdisciplinary collaboration in
Computer-Aided Architectural Design, benefiting both
architectural and computational disciplines.

column2: Evangelos Pantazis and Iason Pantazis
column3:
Yfaloid: Generative Design and Fabrication of modular
artificial reef structures
column7:
Artificial reefs present a promising yet underutilized
solution for enhancing biodiversity in degraded marine
ecosystems. These structures create habitats for endangered
marine species and provide substrates for algae growth,
fostering ecological recovery in featureless seafloor
environments. The Yfaloid project combines innovative
design, circular economy principles, and digital
fabrication to develop modular artificial reef structures.
It introduces a novel method for fabricating interlocking
cementitious blocks, using both traditional casting and
additive manufacturing techniques. A dedicated
computational workflow and design tool enable the creation
of optimized module geometries and the aggregation of
larger reef structures. The block geometry is based on a
triply periodic minimal surface, optimized for a high
volume-to-surface area ratio—crucial for promoting marine
life colonization. The modular design supports the assembly
of customizable reef structures of varying sizes,
deployable from small vessels and installable by divers
without heavy machinery. This scalable approach aids the
restoration of degraded marine ecosystems and helps prevent
coastal erosion by leveraging locally available resources
and digital fabrication techniques on a case-by-case basis
for reef construction in various coastal areas.

column2: Le Zhao, Thomas Fischer, Wowei Zhang and Christiane Herr
column3:
Digital Design Support for UAV Delivery Noise Reduction
Strategies in High Density Urban Environments
column7:
Catalyzed by advancements in drone technology and favorable
governmental policies, the emerging "low altitude economy"
in urban China is set to transform urban landscapes and
lifestyles. This study addresses new challenges arising
from the integration of unmanned aerial UAV (unmanned
aerial vehicles) and eVTOL (electric UAV capable of
vertical take-off and landing, typically transporting
passengers) within dense urban contexts. Where previous
design strategies have focused on conventional rooftop
takeoff and landing, we examine the adaptation of building
facades to accommodate vertiports in high-rise office
structures. In response to the acoustic challenges
generated by UAV operation at various heights of buildings,
we propose a digitally supported design strategy that
harnesses the acoustic properties of plant species to
mitigate sound interference for occupants within tall
buildings while at the same time offering a wide range of
ecosystem services.
To this end, this study conducted a detailed evaluation of
the noise impact around delivery points on facades at
different radii, systematically addressing vertical drone
takeoff and landing positions as well as flight
trajectories. The acoustic characteristics of vertical
green elements were simulated and evaluated using the
Grasshopper plugin Pachyderm. After multiple iterations of
optimization, we identified the most effective green
elements to provide drone related noise reduction in
architectural façade design and retrofit. While the study
is limited in scope to surfaces without contextual
consideration, it forms a key contribution enabling
architectural design to respond in sustainable ways to the
introduction of drone delivery systems to dense urban
environments.

column2: Zhiyong Dong and Peter Búš
column3:
(CI) Embodied Collective Robotic Collaboration for
Architecture
column7:
Integrating robotics in architecture greatly enhances the
efficiency of design-to-production workflows, particularly
in complex projects requiring precision, speed, and
flexibility (Gramazio et al., 2014). With advancements in
technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), computer
vision, and environmental sensors, robots are becoming
increasingly capable of performing tasks with strong
embodiment, simulating human-like decision-making and
physical presence in the environment. This research
intention explores the role of robots in architectural
assembly, focusing on their ability to understand and
execute complex construction tasks autonomously. The
central aim is to address robots’ understanding of various
components' hierarchies and complexities and to propose a
strategy for structurally sound assembly utilizing visual
recognition and environmental sensing. This study aims to
answer the key research question: Through robotic
embodiment in production space exploration, is the robot
capable of autonomously understanding and applying design
criteria and structural requirements? Is the assembly
scenario a consequence and a representation of a designer’s
intention, or does it belong to a unique robot’s autonomous
decision?

A practical implementation of this study is on using UR10
robotic arms to autonomously assemble architectural
structures, however not in a single task execution, but to
provide the robots their production space to be explored,
decided on the explored conditions and executed following
their decisions on the spot, during the process itself. The
UR10, a versatile industrial robotic arm, is widely used in
various industries due to its precision, flexibility, and
ease of programming. This collaborative initiative takes
the assembly of a spatial structure as a case study. The
robot is tasked with autonomously detecting irregularly
placed objects, generating an assembly plan based on the
detected components, and creating motion paths for the
automatic assembly of a wooden spatial structure out of the
pre-defined custom-shaped building blocks. The UR10 robotic
arm, through its integration with advanced sensors and AI,
makes autonomous decisions during the assembly process,
considering different hierarchies of the components to
maintain continuous structural stability.

This study will expand by incorporating two or more UR10
robotic arms to explore collaborative robotics in
architectural design and production while the robots are
aware of each other to avoid any collisions. The use of
multiple robotic arms will enable more complex and
efficient workflows, where robots can operate in
coordination, either working on different aspects of the
same structure or performing parallel tasks. This level of
coordination requires advanced communication protocols and
synchronization algorithms to ensure that the robots work
harmoniously without collisions or errors. In a
multi-robotic arm setup, one robot could be responsible for
the placement of components while another robot handles the
structural reinforcement, ensuring a seamless and faster
construction process. Collaborative robotic systems offer
significant potential for scaling architectural projects,
enabling robots to work together to create large, intricate
structures with minimal human intervention when the robot
possesses intelligence, according to which makes its
decisions for certain task execution.

Methodological approach

This study encompasses key technologies in enabling the
UR10 robotic arms to execute construction tasks
autonomously. These include computer vision techniques such
as OpenCV (Mahamkali & Ayyasamy, 2015) and convolutional
neural networks (CNNs) (Alzubaidi et al., 2021), which
allows the robots to recognize, differentiate, and
understand the relationships between various objects in the
assembly process. Computer vision plays a critical role in
detecting objects in real-time, allowing the robot to
adjust its movements based on environmental factors, the
components' orientation, and their structural logic. The
UR10’s vision system enables it to adapt to irregularly
placed or unexpected objects, ensuring it can make
real-time adjustments to its assembly plan.

Additionally, the transmission of architectural data
throughout the process is outlined, utilizing ArUco markers
(OpenCV, 2024) to assist in mapping between the camera view
and digital space. ArUco markers provide a reliable method
for identifying and localizing objects in the workspace,
helping the robot to understand its environment and plan
its actions accordingly. These markers create a bridge
between the physical world and the digital twin —an
integrated representation of the physical world (Jiang et
al., 2024).

A digital twin of the real-world environment is established
in a 3D space, where the robots’ motion paths are
automatically generated based on the components detected in
the environment. This digital twin serves as a simulation
space where potential assembly sequences can be tested and
optimized computationally while being executed in the
physical space. The process of physical decisions during
the execution task is reflected in the digital twin; the
decision processes are modified in real-time, and the
physical robot is informed and constantly updated with its
digital twin and executes the assembly.
Evaluation
The workflow will be evaluated based on several key
performance metrics, including the success rate of object
grasping, the accuracy of the robot’s movements, and the
structural stability of the final assembly. These metrics
provide insights into the effectiveness of visual guidance
and the overall reliability of the robotic system in
performing complex architectural tasks. Early results
suggest that visual guidance significantly improves the
robot’s ability to localize and interact with objects in
the environment, addressing common challenges in robotic
construction such as misalignment or incorrect placement of
components.

Benefits and Prospective Impact
The use of embodied robots, such as the UR10, represents a
paradigm shift in architectural design and production.
Embodied robots will bring intelligence and autonomy to
construction processes, reducing the need for direct human
oversight and intervention. The flexibility and
adaptability of embodied robots also make them well-suited
for projects that require customization or rapid iteration
during the execution process, as they can quickly adapt to
new designs and instructions without significant
reprogramming.
In the context of intelligent buildings; robotics offers
tremendous value by automating the construction phase and
ongoing maintenance and modifications. Buildings that
incorporate robotics during their construction can be
designed with future robotic interventions in mind,
enabling dynamic changes to the structure or environment
over time. This adaptability is especially valuable in
urban environments with limited space, and buildings need
to evolve to meet changing demands. Robotic systems,
combined with AI and sensor networks, can also monitoring
the building’s structural integrity over its lifespan, and
automatically repairing or reinforcing areas that show wear
and tear.

Conclusion
The study examines how visual recognition, environmental
sensing, and intelligent robotic embodiment contribute to
more intelligent architectural design and production in an
informing design-to-execution loop. Future research will
continue to explore the potential of more advanced
multi-robot collaboration and the application of embodied
robots in complex architectural scenarios, to create more
efficient, flexible, and intelligent design-to-production
workflows.

column2: Jingyang Liu
column3:
Programmable Thick Kirigami: A Computational Framework for
the Design and Fabrication of Non-Zero Thickness Kirigami
Structures
column7:
This paper introduces a novel computational framework for
the design and fabrication of thick-panel kirigami
structures. Kirigami—derived from kiri (cutting) and gami
(folding)—leverages strategically placed cuts and folds on
a two-dimensional (2D) sheet material to create
three-dimensional (3D) structures. The introduction of
these cuts significantly enhances geometric flexibility,
allowing for the construction of a broader range of 3D
geometries that cannot be achieved through folding alone.
In the literature, so far, most studies focus on
theoretical models assuming the kirigami structure is made
of flat sheets with zero thickness. However, in real-world
applications,  particularly in the architecture,
engineering, and construction (AEC) domain,  the thickness
of surface panels is not always negligible. Informed by
this gap, this paper presents a systematic computational
framework for the design, simulation, and fabrication of
thick-panel kirigami structures. The framework builds on a
theoretical model that predicts the kinematics and
constitutive behavior of both 2D and 3D thick kirigami
structures.  The model is validated through both numerical
simulations and physical prototyping, with demonstrations
of applications in deployable structures. The computational
toolkit for thick kirigami engineering presented in this
paper will pave the road for the design of flexible,
adaptive, and efficient deployable structures that can be
customizable and scalable across multiple applications.

column2: Han Jin, Hao Wang and Ruifeng Tian
column3:
Augmented Scale Perception: Exploring a Full-Scale
Architectural Education Approach Based on MAR
column7:
Scale perception training is a crucial part in the early
stage of architectural education. However, desktop-based
modeling (DBM), which is widely used by architectural
students today, lacks references to real-world objects.
Mobile Augmented Reality (MAR), on the other hand, utilizes
full-scale models and offers the possibility of
experiencing 1:1 space through lightweight mobile devices.
This may present an advantage in scale perception
education. To explore the effectiveness of MAR in
architectural scale perception education, particularly in
comparison with DBM, a field perception-virtual
reconstruction comparative experiment is conducted. The
experiment compares students' performance in reconstructing
the portico of the architectural department building by
adjusting the model's size on a laptop (DBM) and on a
tablet (MAR) after observing the portico on site.
The results show that the advantages of MAR over DBM in
scale perception education depend on the scale of the
parts. MAR demonstrates significant advantages for
medium-scale parts, moderate advantages for large-scale
parts, and no advantage for small-scale parts. Subjective
questionnaires reveal that students express a high level of
satisfaction with MAR in scale perception education,
although they believe the experience still requires
optimization. Finally, the MAR full-scale design approach
is applied to a house design assignment, which involves
numerous medium-scale parts, resulting in high satisfaction.

column2:
Frederick Peter Ortner, Sezgi Yalcinkaya Hamarat, Chewon
Han, Simon Perrault, Mei Chee Tan, Wei Lek Kwan, Kai Zheng
and Praveen Govindarajan
column3:
Sustainable Social Building Assistant (SSoBA): Transforming
Energy Use via Digital Twins, Environmental Sensing and
Occupant Behaviour Change
column7:
Reduction of building energy consumption is an urgent
priority in the effort to eliminate greenhouse gas (GHG)
emissions and mitigate the effects of the climate crisis.
Improvements in building operations are crucial to reducing
building energy use, and intelligent building systems
increasingly provide centralised real-time energy
evaluation and optimisation in support of this goal.
Centralised building management systems (BMS), however, are
poorly suited to user-controlled buildings where occupants
are enabled to determine ventilation and temperature levels
in an effort to improve comfort and well-being. Building
digital twins, if user-friendly and accessible, can help
non-expert occupants understand building functions and
unseen environmental factors and support them to improve
building energy efficiency. This paper shares results of
the design development and test-bedding of a building’s
digital twin system, the Sustainable Social Building
Assistant (SSoBA), created for use by non-expert building
occupants. To evaluate SSoBA, a six-week field study was
conducted in a university living lab: three weeks without
interface interaction (baseline) and three weeks with
access to SSoBA visualizations and nudges.
The Design Science Research (DSR) method was implemented to
