respond to the research question: ‘What design elements and
functions must be advanced to a building’s digital twin
system to effectively engage occupants in modifying their
behavior to support sustainable operations?’ A detailed
analysis of design element prototypes permitted an
interrogation of the hierarchical and functional
relationship between the presentation of spatial
information in the form of maps and building 3D models, and
the temporal data representing building function,
environmental data, and social relationships among
occupants. While more testing is required, preliminary
results comparing user behaviours before and after use of
the SSoBA interface reveal promising improvements in energy
efficiency. On the basis of the presented results,
recommendations are made for future work in the area of
building digital twins and sustainable behavior change for
the built environment.

column2: Yang Li and Rudi Stouffs
column3:
The Representation of Representation in Computational
Design: A Case Study of the Bank of China Tower in Hong Kong
column7:
This research presents a novel meta-representational
approach in computational design by analyzing the massing
logic of the Bank of China Tower in Hong Kong. The study
transitions from an unconventional representational
strategy to a conventional pattern-based form. Existing
computational meta-representational frameworks, such as
parametric design (Woodbury, 2010) and shape grammar
(Stiny, 2006), rely on constraint-based and rule-based
methodologies, which often constrain flexibility and
universality in diverse design contexts. In response, this
study introduces the concept of "representation of
representation" as a new meta-representational approach,
which decodes existing design patterns and offers
alternative solutions for broader application in design
processes.

The changes of representation (Korf, 1980) offer new
perspectives for analyzing design solutions. This research
aims to demonstrate that the massing form of the tower can
be conceptualized as a transformable pattern (Grabow,
1983). This pattern functions as a generative device for
exploring new design spaces (Woodbury and Burrow 2006).

This study utilizes graph-based and topological operations
(Li and Stouffs, 2023) to construct a pattern-based
representation of the tower's massing. The methodology
emphasizes both the objectification of patterns into forms
as references and the abstraction of forms into patterns as
controlling frameworks. This approach conceptualizes
connectivity between objects as a pattern, where the
objects themselves subsequently evolve into patterns
(Grabow, 1983).

Example:
surface - point - surface
objects - pattern - objects
reference - connectivity- objects

The final design artifact is not a direct result of the
initial stages. Thus, it is essential to understand how
intermediate representations evolve over time, shaping the
design process and informing the final outcome.

Korf, Richard E. 1980. “Toward a Model of Representation
Changes.” Artificial Intelligence 14 (1): 41–78.
https://doi.org/10.1016/0004-3702(80)90033-8.

Li, Yang, and Rudi Stouffs. 2023. “Topological Operations:
A New Method Toward Retrievable Design Operations.” In
Computer-Aided Architectural Design. INTERCONNECTIONS:
Co-Computing Beyond Boundaries, edited by Michela Turrin,
Charalampos Andriotis, and Azarakhsh Rafiee, 1819:579–93.
Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-37189-9_38.

Stiny, George. 2006. Shape: Talking about Seeing and Doing.
Cambridge, Mass: MIT Press.

Woodbury, Robert. 2010. Elements of Parametric Design.
London ; New York, NY: Routledge.

Woodbury, Robert F., and Andrew L. Burrow. 2006. “Whither
Design Space?” Artificial Intelligence for Engineering
Design, Analysis and Manufacturing 20 (2): 63–82.
https://doi.org/10.1017/S0890060406060057.

Grabow, Stephen. 1983. Christopher Alexander: The Search
for a New Paradigm in Architecture. Stocksfield ; Boston:
Oriel Press.

column2:
Tarciana Andrade, José Beirão, Arruda Amilton and Paulo
Carvalho
column3:
Bimetal Biomodules: Prototype Evaluation of Kinetic Façades
in Response to Environmental Temperature Variations
column7:
Coordinating construction with solar exposure and shading
systems is fundamental for planning sustainable
architectural solutions. The Bimetal Biomodule design
proposes a kinetic module bioinspired by the grass
Ammophila arenaria, which has leaf grooves that help
control the reversible movement of the plant. We chose the
smart material, bimetal, that responds to thermal variation
and bends when heated to replicate the behavior. Regarding
leaf morphology, we applied creases to the active layer of
the bimetal. The creases contribute to the opening of the
material when the temperature rises and to its closing when
it cools down (opposite movement of the material without
the creased surface). We developed prototypes of the
modules using laser cutting and crease stamping with a
3D-printed matrix. An experiment in an open and relevant
environment in Lisbon, with high daily temperature
variations, involved exposing five samples to solar
incidence over three days (in summer, fall, and during a
heat wave). Statistical treatment of the data identified
equations that explain at least 73.2% of the overall
behavior of the modules at environment temperatures ranging
from 15.6 to 49.3ºC, proving that they are adaptable to
different climate conditions. The computational algorithm
integrates the equations, generates parametric variations,
and simulates protection by solar incidence. Innovation
lies in the creases; relevance in controlling the bimetals
behavior, enabling the biomodules reversible movement
without needing electrical or mechanical devices. A
full-scale model allowed for wishful thinking the premises
put into the conceptual model. The solution has the
potential to contribute to the energy efficiency of
buildings.

column2:
Hyoung-June Park, Yasushi Ishida and Zachary Ikaika
Bantolina
column3:
Unveiling Pāwehe: Revitalizing Hawaiian Identity Through
Architectural Façades
column7:
This research addresses the growing need to incorporate
Indigenous Hawaiian values into contemporary architecture,
aligning with the broader movement to reinterpret Hawaiian
vernacular architecture. Inspired by the works of
architects like Hart Wood and Vladimir Ossipoff (Hibbard et
al., 2010), this study focuses on integrating traditional
Hawaiian patterns into building façades using computational
design for visual comfort and performance analysis.

The project emphasizes the art form of Pāwehe, a geometric
motif representing Hawaiian stories and identity (Buck,
1957). Guided by a Native Hawaiian architectural-cultural
specialist, the study carefully examines these motifs,
ensuring their authenticity and relevance in modern
architecture. The IBM Building in Honolulu, designed by
Ossipoff, was selected for the façade redesign, symbolizing
a blend of cultural heritage and modern architectural
innovation.

The motifs undergo hierarchical deconstruction into
symbolic elements and are translated into computational
rules for three-dimensional design (Lee et al., 2013). By
treating the geometric properties of the motifs as
variables, dynamic façade components are created to
optimize both aesthetic and environmental performance
(Narangerel et al., 2017; Rezakhani and Kim, 2024). This
process uses multi-objective optimization tools, including
Wallacei and Ladybug, to refine design alternatives.

The resulting façade design prototypes were applied to the
IBM Building and compared with its existing structure. The
findings demonstrate the practical and cultural value of
incorporating Hawaiian motifs into architectural
applications, offering new possibilities for culturally
resonant and sustainable architectural practices. Through
this approach, the research contributes to the ongoing
evolution of contemporary Hawaiian architecture.

column2: Weam Numan, Yuval Kahlon and Haruyuki Fujii
column3:
The Gap: Where users become architects Observing the use of
virtual architecture as a communication medium towards
informing architectural design in virtual space.
column7:
A current trend in architectural design is the integration
of VR technology in the process of design
prototyping[1][2]. As VR enables users to experience space
before their embodiment in physical form, the technology is
used for studying their responses to design alternatives -
a practice which presupposes similarity between the
response of users in physical and virtual spaces.
Questioning this assumption, we explore the disparity
between user behavior in virtual architectural spaces (VAS)
and physical architectural space (PAS) and whether
immersive experiences accurately predict users’
interactions in the real-world. By employing a framework
for modeling how agents understand and act in the world
(Belief-Desire-Intention)[3], we analyze user responses
during gameplay within a controlled IVE, focusing on
interaction with and modification of the environment. Our
findings reveal that users adopt a distinct form of
constructional creativity[4] induced by the perceived lack
of constraints in IVEs[5], where users perceive gaps in the
design, utilizing the virtual architecture as a responsive
interface to correct them. This highlights the limitations
of traditional design methods for predicting behavior in
IVEs. We propose a framework that situates the “Gap” as a
critical component of virtual environments. The extraction
of this element enables architects to leverage data
collected in IVEs for more responsive, user-centered design
practices. By advancing understanding of user experiences
in IVES, this research enhances the potential for dynamic
architectural creation while advocating for a new CAAD
paradigm that considers the unique characteristics of IVEs
and the impact of their application on architectural
environment design.

References

[1] M.J. Kim, X. Wang, P.E. Love, H. Li, S.-C. Kang. (2013)
Virtual reality for the built environment: a critical
review of recent advances. Journal of Information
Technology in Construction, pp. 279-305.

[2] Camburn, B., Viswanathan, V., Linsey, J., Anderson, D.,
Jensen, D., Crawford, R.,
et al. (2017). Design prototyping methods: state of the art
in strategies, techniques, and guidelines. Des. Sci. 3, E13.

[3] Bratman, M. E. (1987) Intention, Plans, and Action,
Harvard University Press.

[4] Hii J. (2003) Actions of Architecture: Architects and
Creative Users. (1st ed.). Routledge. p. 86.

[5] Kien, G. (2009). Virtual environment: the machine is
our world. learning, and support in virtual environments.
Sense Publishers, Rotterdam, pp. 9-22.

column2: Gizem Karaoğlu Çitken and Asena Kumsal Şen Bayram
column3:
A Daylight Optimisation Framework on Building Envelopes
Design
column7:
Most interactions between the indoor and outdoor
environments occur in building envelopes fenestrations.
Therefore, it is essential to have an efficient window
shading system that maintains appropriate visual comfort by
minimizing glare and supplying adequate amounts of
illumination. It is important to make effective use of
natural light in sustainable architectural applications. In
this con-text, vernacular building elements made of
different materials such as mashrabiya and breeze block
respond to parameters such as privacy, thermal comfort and
daylighting performance. The aim of this research is to
propose a design algo-rithm that optimises daylighting
performance by incorporating vernacular build-ing elements
into building envelope design. The mashrabiya and breeze
block patterns commonly used in Türkiye were studied in
detail and square, circular and hexagonal patterns were
included in the scope of the research. These patterns were
analysed in two different sizes, 20x20 cm. and 5x5 cm.
openings. In the simulation model prepared using Rhino,
Grasshopper and Ladybug interfaces, the daylight autonomy
parameter was investigated according to three different
climate types in Turkey, which are Istanbul, Adana and
Erzurum provinces. The results of the research show that
small perforated panels give better results in hot
climates, while large openings are more efficient in
regions with low temperature variations throughout the
year. In cold climates, square geometries were found to
perform better than other geometries. Developing an
algorithmic framework that can provide recommendations for
missing inputs based on given pattern, location and size
inputs is the main objective of this research.

column2:
Adii Shtykov, Ning Gu, Helen Barrie, Veronica Soebarto and
David Kroll
column3:
Evaluating Industry Perceptions of a Digital Twin-Enabled
Tool for Real-Time Environmental and Occupant-Centric
Building Performance in an Urban Mixed-Use Development
column7:
Capturing real-time occupant-centric data is essential in
building performance evaluation. Traditional post-occupancy
evaluations rely on retrospective surveys, often leading to
incomplete assessments of environmental impacts on occupant
well-being. The COVID-19 pandemic has further emphasised
the need for dynamic, real-time evaluation methods.
This study evaluates the usability, visualisation
effectiveness, and adoption potential of a digital
twin-enabled tool for integrating real-time environmental
and occupant-centred data into building performance
analysis. The tool was demonstrated in a series of industry
workshops involving architects, facility managers, and
property developers across Australia, the UK, and Malaysia.
A mixed-methods approach was used, combining quantitative
survey data and qualitative interviews to assess
familiarity with digital tools, ease of use, and
visualisation capabilities, along with barriers to adoption.
Findings indicate that familiarity with BIM and structured
data workflows in-fluenced usability, with architects and
facility managers rating the tool high-er. UK and
Australian participants showed strong adoption potential
than Malaysian participants, reflecting regional
differences in practice. While vis-ualisation capabilities
were well received, concerns about privacy, security, and
cost feasibility emerged.
This study provides practical insights into the
opportunities and challenges of implementing digital twin
solutions in building performance evaluation, showcasing
its potential for real-time, evidence-based decision-making.

column2: Chuheng Tan, Shaopo Huang, Quan Zhou and Haipeng Zhong
column3:
Computing Urban Tissue: Landslide Mitigation Strategy of
Urban Infrastructure Design
column7:
Landslides are a major threat in mountainous regions,
causing severe dam-age and affecting over 8,000 people in
Malong District, Yunnan Province, over the past 20 years.
To mitigate these impacts, urban infrastructure
de-velopment is crucial, with effective prevention measures
like land use re-planning, slope stabilization, drainage
systems, and farmland patterning aimed at reducing
landslide occurrences. However, most current studies fo-cus
narrowly on slope engineering without addressing the need
for a com-prehensive approach that balances protection,
development, and the integra-tion of vernacular building
elements. This study presents an automated ur-ban
infrastructure design and optimization system to mitigate
landslide im-pacts, using Malong District, Yunnan Province,
as a case study. It integrates a Multi-Objective
Evolutionary Algorithm (MOEA), Geographic Infor-mation
System (GIS), and Rigid Body Dynamics (RBD) within Houdini,
forming a comprehensive workflow for urban planning in
landslide-prone areas.

column2: Lei Li, Yixin Hao and Runjia Tian
column3:
Zero-Shot Architectural Style Classification with Large
Language Models
column7:
Accurate architectural style classification is essential
for integrating historical and contemporary design elements
and for educational purposes. Traditional methods often
struggle with complex styles due to intricate details and
inter-style relationships. This study introduces a novel
application of Large Language Models (LLMs), specifically
Vision Language Models (VLMs), for architectural style
classification. VLMs, with their extensive pre-trained
datasets and generalization capabilities, show significant
promise in zero-shot learning scenarios, classifying styles
without prior specialized training on architectural images.
We explore the effectiveness of state-of-the-art VLMs like
GPT-4o in this domain, demonstrating their potential to
match or exceed traditional CNN models without extensive
training (Wu et al., 2024).

The study employs a dataset from Wikipedia's "Architecture
by style" entries, featuring nearly 5,000 high-resolution
images across various styles, from "American Craftsman" to
"Gothic." Two classification tasks are conducted: a
10-class task with distinct styles and a 25-class task with
subtle differences.

We assess GPT-4o using four methods:
1. GPT4o-Vision-DIRECT: Direct classification with a simple
prompt.
2. GPT4o-Vision-TAGS-ONLY: Classification guided by
descriptive tags generated from image features.
3. GPT4o-Vision-PIC+TAGS: Combining the image with
descriptive tags for nuanced analysis.
4. GPT4o-Vision-PIC+TAGS+REASON: Adding detailed
explanations for classification decisions.

Experiments show that GPT-4o, particularly in the
GPT4o-Vision-PIC+TAGS configuration, achieves the highest
accuracy: 86.15% for the 10-class task and 63.44% for the
25-class task. GPT-4o outperforms traditional methods and
other LLMs like Qwen-VL and Claude-3, demonstrating
superior accuracy and generalization. The model excels with
distinctive styles but struggles with similar ones,
suggesting areas for improvement.

This study demonstrates GPT-4o's potential in zero-shot
architectural style classification, offering a
resource-efficient and accurate alternative to traditional
models. Future work will expand the dataset and improve
model interpretability and computational efficiency,
enhancing the model's capabilities.

column2:
Earl Mark, Nancy Cheng, Joseph Ashmore, Nuno Nunes, Ibere
Lopes and Daud Shad
column3:
(CI) Building Resilience: CAAD and Displacement Data in
Humanitarian Architecture
column7:
Question
 
How can the dynamic, expansive, and varied nature of forced
human displacement data be integrated into CAAD modeling
systems to unlock new possibilities in humanitarian design
solutions?

  
Motivation
  
Over 117.3 million people, 1.5% of the world, are forcibly
displaced (UNHCR, 2024). Securing a place to stay in the
aftermath of a crisis has complex objectives for sustaining
life.  Internally Displaced People living in suitable
shelters are twice as likely to achieve financial stability
(IOM, 2023). However, it is often elusive due to such
persistent problems as insecure land tenure, scarce
material resources, protracted environmental events, and
other uncertain risks (GSC, 2021). During a crisis, Shelter
and Settlements assistance must respond to multiple streams
of data that fluctuate dynamically.
  
As advances in data collection, ethics, and analysis
continue, the potential benefits include improving how and
where to shelter displaced communities. CAAD Futures
provides a valuable forum for conceiving adaptive systems
that can help leverage this data to better the built
environment for forcibly displaced people. Drawing on our
team’s experience in humanitarian work, architecture,
academia, and software engineering, we envision a holistic
information modeling system that integrates this forcible
displacement data with design software to better address
Shelter and Settlements needs at local, regional, and
global levels.
 
 
CAAD ‘Present’ and ‘Future’
  
Founding CAAD Futures member Tom Maver highlighted CAAD’s
early role in bridging the gap between objective criteria
(e.g., cost, performance) and subjective factors (e.g.,
comfort, cultural accommodation) in building design (Maver,
2015). Current CAAD systems -- developed in relatively
stable environments -- often depend on cohesiveness of
client information and construction standards. BIM systems,
in particular, have integrated building lifecycle, design,
engineering, construction, maintenance, and management into
a shared and persistent information framework.
  
However, a critical and under-represented context is the
chaotic conditions of humanitarian crises. During a
displacement crisis, rapid decision-making is needed among
diverse stakeholders. These situations demand design
approaches that account for accelerated construction
timelines, dynamic risk responses, insecure land tenure,
limited resources, and climate impacts. There is a need for
integration of such data analysis into CAAD in order to
respond rapidly and effectively.
  
We propose a “Catalytic Interface” at CAAD Futures 2025 to
explore how CAAD can support crisis response by
incorporating data-driven channels to inform responsive
design and planning. Starting with a high-level metadata
review, we will identify core data types and exchanges
needed for a flexible response in the built and natural
environments. Human displacement data could be coupled or
fully integrated into CAAD or BIM systems, with AI used to
parse and identify patterns. (Human displacement data could
also potentially integrate with GIS, digital terrain
modeling, and other civil engineering applications.)
  
Our goal is to create an adaptive system. Since new
challenges and technological advancements will arise, the
task is to envision a loosely integrated software system
that remains ahead of these changes.
  
  
Data Profile
  
Large volumes of data are generally available during a
crisis. The primary data source driving this proposal is an
existing humanitarian agency’s displacement tracking
system. Actively incorporated into this Catalytic Interface
proposal, the system will provide relevant data in terms of
factors like dwelling conditions, population movements,
relief needs, local hazards, and land ownership. While some
integration with other humanitarian data sets exists,
incorporating this data into CAAD or BIM, with potential
expansion to GIS and AI, presents a significant opportunity
for Shelter and Settlements. We view displacement tracking
and interagency data exchanges as integral to dynamic
modeling of rapidly emerging settlements, rather than
separate efforts. The data interface could also add
mechanisms of localizing input and fostering participation.
  
At a global scale, data sources include common humanitarian
datasets, remote sensing, and gridded population estimates.
Integrating with an existing data initiative may allow
interfacing with humanitarian programs for property
safeguards and land rights for displaced people through
participatory evidence collection and communication during
crises. A comprehensive analysis of these sources could
support decision-makers in real time with virtual scenarios
and forecasts integrated into CAAD systems. Our proposal
moves beyond a static analytical model to one that adapts
parametrically to new data, challenging the assumptions of
the existing model.
 
 
“Catalytic Interface” Structure
  
The Catalytic Interface presents an exceptional forum for a
mutually beneficial knowledge exchange. We seek to expand
our team’s collective skills in sustainable design, CAAD
innovation and education, and interdisciplinary design and
planning. We see the potential to learn from and brainstorm
with experts in smart cities, parametric, and rule-based
design. A think-tank approach to envisioning CAAD systems
that addresses the unique challenges of forced migration
and displacement is in our time similar to what motivated
workshops and conferences on standards of practice that
were convened during the early development of BIM
(Eberhard, 1985; Eberhard, 1986;  Christiansen, 1988). Our
goal is to infuse CAAD with a world of information
increasingly generated for humanitarian design practice.
  
Emphasizing displacement data, we start with block diagrams
for analyzing, discussing, and devising metadata interfaces
based on geospatial areas of information exchange.
Resulting mockups would describe the stages in which data
may be used, from the humanitarian Shelter and Settlements
sector to the work of our collaborative partners. Similar
to early BIM workshops, deliverables also include metadata
catalog specifications and simulated data flow
illustrations.
 

Potential Use Case
  
Consider this scenario: a flood displaces rural communities
in a region where land and housing rights are poorly
documented, particularly for tenant farmers and low-wage
workers. A data-driven design interface allows humanitarian
stakeholders to integrate variables like population flows,
damage assessments, land tenure (including community-based
evidence), infrastructure, environmental conditions, and
shelter access. This system enhances coordination between
international actors, local authorities and displaced
people, improves relief prediction and modeling, and
supports balanced rebuilding pathways for returnees,
considering both past and future risks. More dignified and
sustainable shelter solutions thus become achievable for
flood-displaced populations.
  
Overall, this proposal internalizes dynamic displacement
data in CAAD modeling, significantly informing humanitarian
design solutions for sustainable shelter and potentially
improving the lives of millions experiencing forced
displacement.

References
  
1.	Christiansen, P. (1988). "Properties of Future Building
Hyper Documents." In Proceedings of the CIB W74/W78
Symposium on Conceptual Modelling of Buildings. Lund
University, Sweden.
2.	Data Science and Ethics Group (DSEG). (2020). A
Framework for the Ethical Use of Advanced Data Science
Methods in the Humanitarian Sector. Data Science Initiative
(City of The Hague) and Displacement Tracking Matrix (IOM).
https://www.hum-dseg.org/dseg-ethical-framework
3.	Eberhard, J., et al. (1985). The 1985 Workshop on
Advanced Technology for Building Design and Engineering.
National Academy of Sciences, Building Research Board.
4.	Eberhard, J., et al. (1986). The 1986 Workshop on
Integrated Database Development for the Building Industry.
National Academy of Sciences, Building Research Board.
5.	Global Shelter Cluster (GSC). (2021). Shelter Projects
Essentials. www.shelterprojects.org
6.	Humanitarian Standards Partnership (HSP). Interactive
Handbook. Sphere. https://handbook.spherestandards.org/
7.	International Organization for Migration (IOM). (2023).
Periodic Global Report on the State of Solutions to
Internal Displacement (PROGRESS). Geneva: International
Organization for Migration. https://dtm.iom.int/progress
8.	Maver, T. (2015). How CAAD is Changing Society’s Role in
Architecture. Mackintosh School of Architecture, Glasgow
School of Art, Glasgow, United Kingdom.
9.	Maver, T., & Petric, J. (2016). CAAD: Four Decades That
Transformed Architecture and Building Engineering, SPOFA
International Conference.

https://www.unhcr.org/refugee-statistics/

column2:
Earl Mark, Nancy Cheng, Joseph Ashmore, Nuno Nunes and Daud
Shad
column3:
Building Resilience: CAAD and Displacement Data in
Humanitarian Architecture (CAAD Futures 2025 Catalytic
Interface Complement Paper Proposal)
column7:
Every five seconds, a family loses its home [1]. Could a
stronger data framework improve emergency shelter planning,
making it more responsive to site and resource constraints
and better adapt to long-term outcomes? A collaborative
data-driven framework for design and planning in
displacement settings is urgently needed. In a historic
precedent, the birth of building in-formation modeling
(BIM) had expanded 2D computer-aided architectural design
(CAAD) to coordinate more stakeholders into 3D building
design, engineering, construction, and lifecycle
management. Still, BIM’s current focus limits its
practicality in crisis contexts involving mass
displacement, mobile resources, and complex shelter
options. As forced displacement rises worldwide, we
consider the context for more dynamic interfaces for
describing how the built and natural environments affect
crisis response and recovery. Humanitarian organizations
already build daily datasets on resident needs, combining
remote sensing, terrain, and population models. Integrating
CAAD into fluctuating data streams could enable stronger 3D
visualization analysis. Accordingly, spatial
decision-making could be informed by da-ta-driven
simulations and parametric options where changes to
underlying assumptions can repropagate shelter and
settlement solutions. Such systems, accessible to affected
communities, could actively support participatory
approaches. This paper – complementing our intended
engagement at CAAD Futures 2025 – describes the need and
opportunity for greater interdisciplinary collaboration in
responsive shelter and settlements data systems within a
more fluid, expanded, and integrated technology
environment. Drawing inspiration from early BIM colloquia,
we envision a workshop to examine case studies and consider
how real-time and CAAD-integrated displacement data can
reshape humanitarian architecture within a changing global
context.

References
1. Global Shelter Cluster: “Shelter Projects Essentials.”
https://www.shelterprojects.org/essentials/shelter-projects-essentials-2021-screen.pdf,
p. 4, based on 2019 data (March 2021)

column2: Şevval Deniz Kılıç and Asena Kumsal Şen Bayram
column3:
THE EFFECT OF VIRTUAL REALITY EXPERIENCE ON SPATIAL
PERCEPTION: A STUDY ON EXHIBITION SPACES
column7:
This study aims to examine the user’s perception of space
through exhibition spaces and to present a comparative
experiment by addressing the perception of physical space
and the perception of virtual reality spaces. The main
reason for keeping the research within the scope of
exhibition spaces is the presence of ex-hibition elements,
another parameter that is integrated with the perception of
the space while examining exhibition spaces. The analyses
conducted to compare the participants’ exhibition
experiences in the physical space and the virtual reality
environment revealed the effects of the two different modes
of representation on spatial perception, artifact knowledge
and memory. While exhibition experiences in the physical
space created a more defined route and artifact-oriented
perception for the participants, the virtual reality
environment was more exploration-oriented and
boundary-defined. In terms of memory, the physical space
was characterized by a more intense acquisition of
information and the association of experiences with past
memories, while virtual reality experiences created more
abstract and emotional associations. These findings suggest
that the concrete elements of the physical space have
stronger effects on memory and perception, whereas the
vir-tual reality environment offers an experience-oriented
process based on exploring spatial boundaries.

column2: Richa Gupta and Alexander Htet Kyaw
column3:
Insights Informed Generative AI for Design: Incorporating
Real-world Data for Text-to-Image Output
column7:
Generative AI, specifically text-to-image models, have
revolutionized interior architectural design by enabling
the rapid translation of conceptual ideas into visual
representations from simple text prompts. While generative
AI can produce visually appealing images they often lack
actionable data for designers  In this work, we propose a
novel pipeline that integrates DALL-E 3 with a materials
dataset to enrich AI-generated designs with sustainability
metrics and material usage insights. After the model
generates an interior design image, a post-processing
module identifies the top ten materials present and pairs
them with carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) values from a
general materials dictionary. This approach allows
designers to immediately evaluate environmental impacts and
refine prompts accordingly. We evaluate the system through
three user tests: (1) no mention of sustainability to the
user prior to the prompting process with generative AI, (2)
sustainability goals communicated to the user before
prompting, and (3) sustainability goals communicated along
with quantitative CO₂e data included in the generative AI
outputs. Our qualitative and quantitative analyses reveal
that the introduction of sustainability metrics in the
third test leads to more informed design decisions,
however, it can also trigger decision fatigue and lower
overall satisfaction. Nevertheless, the majority% of
participants reported incorporating sustainability
principles into their workflows in the third test,
underscoring the potential of integrated metrics to guide
more ecologically responsible practices. Our findings
showcase the importance of balancing design freedom with
practical constraints, offering a clear path toward
holistic, data-driven solutions in AI-assisted
architectural design.

column2:
Michael Dieffenthaller, Hallie Fischman, Christine Angelini
and Karla Saldana Ochoa
column3:
Generative Design for Coastal Resilience: A Computational
Approach to Living Shorelines
column7:
This study delves into computational methods to develop a
generative design tool intended for the creation of living
shorelines, which are natural coastal buffers constructed
from organic materials such as plants, sand, and rock. In
contrast to conventional hard structures like concrete
seawalls that disrupt ecosystems, living shorelines are
dynamic, fostering biodiversity and ecosystem service
provisioning while providing protection. Historically, the
capacity of estuarine shorelines to sequester carbon and
nitrogen from water systems, which can mitigate impacts of
eutrophication such as algal blooms, has yet to be
appreciated. We present a visual tool that enriches
scenario planning for shoreline design by integrating
computational design with environmental engineering. The
tool incorporates data on nitrogen and carbon storage in
oyster tissue and shells while simulating interactions with
typical shoreline vegetation, including saw palmetto, sabal
palm, wax myrtle, and others. Leveraging parametric
generative algorithms, the computational tool produces
diverse ecosystem scenarios. It offers insights into the
nitrogen and carbon assimilation capabilities of these
simulated living shorelines, predicting nutrient separation
equivalent to removing bags of fertilizer from the water.
This research yields data-driven insights to assist
decision-makers in guiding restoration investments or
formulating policy decisions, such as regulations on
shellfish harvesting. By joining design and environmental
engineering, this project acts as a "catalytic interface"
for interdisciplinary collaboration concerning the future
of resilient shoreline ecosystems.

column2: Fulvio Wirz, Rasti Bartek and Deborah Benros
column3:
Trillium – Canopy structure – Human and AI design
collaboration
column7:
This paper presents the design of "Trillium," an
architectural canopy using AI-driven design exploration and
digital tools for structural optimization and
manufacturing. AI and digital fabrication methods are
employed to adapt structural design principles from housing
units to the design of a timber pavilion, aiming for
modularity, sustainability, and ease of assembly.
AI, using platforms like Midjourney, facilitates
exploration of pavilion design concepts, while tools like
Rhino and Grasshopper are used for optimizing structural
components and connections. Digital fabrication methods,
such as CNC routing, are leveraged for precision in cutting
timber and crafting complex elements, with AI further
streamlining the process by reducing the complexity of
design nodes in Grasshopper.
The iterative workflow integrates AI for Python code
refinement, enhancing design efficiency and reducing the
number of nodes in the computational process. The project
focuses on resource optimization and cost-effective
material use, showcasing AI's role in modern architectural
challenges.
Ultimately, the "Trillium" canopy demonstrates AI's
transformative impact on the design process, emphasizing
sustainable and innovative practices in architecture. The
project was manufactured using digital techniques,
assembled and erected by the students and displayed at the
London Festival of Architecture in June and in the Open
House Festival in 2024.

column2: Ziyu Tong and Changxi Li
column3:
A new framework for CIM construction based on graph
databases
column7:
Urban complexity demands innovative tools for design,
planning, and management. The concept of City Information
Modeling (CIM) has captured the attention of scholars
worldwide. The backbone of CIM's functionality lies in its
database, which is pivotal for data storage and service
provision. However, current CIM databases are more inclined
to serve general basic CIM platforms, and there are
relatively fewer for the renewal scenarios of old
residential areas. In addition, the usual relational
databases are also not capable of expressing and managing
the complex "people, housing, land" relationships. In this
regard, this study identified the data requirements and
functionalities necessary for a CIM framework based on
graph databases. It has systematically categorized the
basic data types into subjects, entities, and
relationships. The first two are expressed as nodes in
graph and the last one is expressed as edges. The subject
and entity database employs JSON format to capture
geometric information and feature attributes. The
relationship database further refines spatial and social
relationships. Taking the Yinhongyuan neighborhood in
Nanjing, China as an example, this study organized the
original CAD and Excel data and built the graph database in
Neo4j. For the convenience of architects and urban
designers, the study realized the development of data
extraction, storage, and query functions for entity,
subject, and relationship objects on the Rhino and
Grasshopper platforms, and tested the spatial distribution
query of property rights and the entity query based on
relationships.

column2: Milica Vujovic, Djordje Stojanovic and Gabriel Wurzer
column3:
Design and Science in Architectural Education: Learning
from a Case Study
column7:
This paper explores the ongoing challenge of integrating
scientific knowledge and methods with critical thinking and
creative design processes, which are central to the
architectural profession and, specifically, architectural
design education. The aim of this case study is to explore
how teaching research methods that support evidence-based
design and employ sensor devices for data collection that
can be explored with computational means or other emergent
computer-aided design processes can be improved in an
established educational setting. The study is based on
analysing student work, an outcome of a specific
educational course module, part of the graduate
architecture program, tasked with developing experimental
design skills and achieving learning outcomes that balance
scientific knowledge and creative work. The analysis of
student work draws out practical findings to serve future
efforts in designing and enhancing curricula in
architectural education by placing more emphasis on
collecting, structuring and analysing data.

column2: Haoyang He, Han Li, Wanyu Pei, Shuyang Li and Rudi Stouffs
column3:
A Graph-Based Prediction Model for Sustainable Urban
Renewal: Integrating Graph Convolutional Networks for
Concrete Recycling Potential Evaluation
column7:
Understanding the complex temporal-spatial patterns of
recycling construction material at the urban scale requires
substantial data on buildings and material stock. Although
several methods were developed to supplement architectural
information for urban-scale material stock calculation and
analysis, few studies quantified the material recycling
potential in a data-driven approach based on urban
features’ spatial and non-spatial homogeneity. Instead of
starting from detailed individual building data, this study
employs Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) to evaluate the
building concrete recycling potential (CRP) by extracting
temporal and spatial similarities of both urban and
buildings. Specifically, the land uses, protection
policies, and spatial agglomeration are set as edge
attributes, and attributable plots are identified as vertex
points, forming a spatial weight connection matrix for CRP
calculation. The central area of Shanghai was chosen as the
study case, and three different GCN model structures,
including basic GCN, Graph Attention Networks (GAT) and
GraphSAGE, were compared for prediction performance. The
result shows that the GraphSAGE structure, which
incorporates the influence of surrounding temporal-spatial
relationships, offered relatively high accuracy in CRP
prediction. Through expert validation, this experiment
further identified the key factors for CRP prediction,
including building density, historical urban policies,
government documents, and site conditions. This enhances
the interpretability of the model for material recycling
potential quantification, offering a valuable resource for
evaluating urban material recycling, particularly in the
context of complex urban backgrounds and building
data-scarce scenarios.

column2: Weiheng Hu, Yuval Kahlon, Momoko Nakatani and Haruyuki Fujii
column3:
Rethinking Participatory Architectural Design: Harnessing
Immersive Environments & AI for Facilitating
Designer-Stakeholder Collaboration
column7:
Participatory Architectural Design (PAD) offers a promising
framework for inclusive and context-sensitive spatial
design. However, its implementation in practice continues
to be hindered by communication breakdowns between
designers and stakeholders. Based on a systematic review,
we identify a key shortcoming of current
technology-facilitated PAD practices - while immersive
technologies such as Extended Reality (XR) and generative
AI enhance stakeholder perception and engagement, they do
not adequately support stakeholders in contributing to the
design process. For example, stakeholders are rarely
involved in the process synthesis (i.e., creating a design
solution) hands-on. To increase the range of contributions
from stakeholders, we develop a theoretical framework
grounded in communication theory to model the interaction
between designers and other stakeholders in PAD. Using this
framework, we examine how technology can support more
substantive stakeholder engagement across the different
phases of design (this includes both current and future
technological scenarios). As illustrative cases, we present
two exploratory studies: a case study applying immersive
sketching in participatory design workshops, and an
AI-supported voxel sketching system developed by our team.
The proposed framework serves as a map for localizing and
conceptualizing new support systems within PAD, while
considering design-stakeholder interaction.

column2: Namdev Talluru, Dominik Reisach and Mathias Bernhard
column3:
Form Follows Fields: An Adaptive Geometric Representation
Utilizing a Multi-Field Integrative Workflow
column7:
This paper investigates field-driven design in
architecture, focusing on the efficient integration of
performance simulations and geometric modeling through
effective data translation. Traditional design workflows
often rely on iterative loops of form generation and
analysis, where differences in data structures and
languages exist between these processes, leading to
inefficiencies and delays. This study hypothesizes that
field-driven workflows, which align their data structures
and languages, can streamline and accelerate design
adaptations.

We propose a computational framework where geometry and
fields interact, presenting geometry-to-field,
field-to-field, and field-to-geometry translations. Various
geometrical techniques are employed to facilitate seamless
data translation. The hypothesis is tested through a case
study of a specific building, applying these methods to
real-world simulations.

The results demonstrate that aligning data structures and
languages between geometry generation and simulation allows
for faster complex data translation into actionable
geometric representations, facilitating a more responsive
design process than traditional methods. By combining
artificial illuminance, acoustics, and glare simulations,
this paper illustrates how effective data translation can
guide design decisions, enabling geometry to adapt based on
environmental factors.

This framework impacts design practices within the
architecture, engineering, and construction industry,
empowering practitioners to develop adaptable, efficient,
and innovative solutions that harmonize functionality and
aesthetics while fostering more responsive architectural
design.

column2: Oscar Gamez Bohorquez
column3:
Fostering new design strategies in architectural
engineering education (Bio-inspired reverse
parameterization of itinerant timber pavilions)
column7:
Introduction & contribution

At the intersection of knowledge between architects and
engineers lies the concept of architectural engineering
(AE)[1]. A design studio (DST) on architectural typologies
(ATYP) for  AE, in Sweden, uses reverse design (RD) to
introduce AE students into designing bio-inspired
architectures[2], where RD stands for extracting design
constraints from shapes found in nature to create a
sketch-based design, later optimized through computation[3].
The main goal is to create innovative ephemeral
architectures using empiric morphogenesis as catalyst for
design iteration from organic shapes. The outcome consists
of four prototypes for an equal number of pavilions
inspired by icons unique to the Swedish Lapland.

Methodologies

Using RD, morphogenesis is achieved through hand-made
mock-ups that turn the sources of inspiration into tangible
matter. The strategy aims at building new design skills as
an alternative to geometrically based design methods. The
DST is split into two stages:
1) A manual iterative design process (IDP), based on
morphological associations, allows students to produce
shape deconstructions and shape aggregations.
2) Input from stage one is used for an algorithmic
environment to improve form-finding and create geometry for
rapid prototyping.

Results.

Conversely to standard AE education, this RD-based
architecture DST did not seek a single correct answer[4].
Instead, the ill-structured problem[5] -characteristic of
architectural design- led to a range of architectural
choices produced during DST stage two, allowing AE students
to make informed designed decisions prior to prototype
manufacturing. The result appears as four pavilion
prototypes with different tectonic approaches[6].

column2:
Christiane M. Herr, Christian Lange, Farahbod Heidari,
Yiming Liu, Sihao Chen and Umaru Mohammed B.
column3:
(CI) Digital Design for New Types of Bio-Integrated
Building Facades:  A Proposal for Collaborative Exploration
column7:
1. Research Context

The building engineering and construction industry, as the
leading source of harmful greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions,
consumes 40% of the world's energy (Ascione et al., 2021).
Additionally, buildings are responsible for 38% of all CO2
emissions and usage of 40% of the world's raw materials,
indicating the urgent need for regenerative solutions in
designing climate-resilient structures (Webb, 2022). Façade
systems, as the multi-functional interface between
buildings and the ecosystems buildings are embedded in, can
provide various ecosystem services by performing a critical
role in adapting daylight radiance, enabling natural
ventilation, regulating heating and cooling loads,
contributing to energy efficiency, and supporting HVAC
systems (Sandak et al., 2019). New types of bio-integrated
facades, are utilizing the remarkable properties of
biological systems for developing novel living building
components with structural features that can enhance the
quality of environmental parameters beyond reducing human
carbon footprints (Pozzobon, 2024a; Shameri et al., 2011;
Zhou & Herr, 2023). These systems incorporate dynamic
interaction and regeneration with the environment, such as
self-healing and adaptation, carbon sequestration, air
purification, nitrogen fixation or bioremediation, and
energy generation through internal biochemical complex
computation (Mercader-Moyano et al., 2021). Over the past
decade, innovative concepts for bio-integrated facades have
emerged for synergies evolving between building performance
and environmental regeneration, including living walls,
microalgae biofacades utilizing photobioreactors (PBRs),
bio-receptive facades that incorporate fungi or bacteria,
green facades featuring trees integrated into the
structure, and biocrusts composed of molds and lichens
applied to the surface (Pozzobon, 2024b). However, these
systems experience challenges in the intelligent monitoring
and controlling of biological functions and decision-making
over the facades' biocomponents, which are essential for
operating optimized behaviors that respond effectively to
changes in environmental conditions and specific
applications in architectural design and construction (Lee
et al., 2021; Sandak et al., 2019; Ünlütürk & Kazanasmaz,
2024). Moreover, existing CAAD-based multi-objective
optimization systems rely on static databases that overlook
real-time datasets reflecting environmental changes,
indicating imperatives for a new CAAD pattern language to
define decentralized bio-facade systems (Jalali et al.,
2020; Lu et al., 2016). These challenges have limited the
future development of these systems and have constrained
the integration of material-based living systems and
building facades to a laboratory scale. This topic area
proposal aims to conduct deep investigations into the next
generation of bio-integrated building facades research
zones to address ongoing concerns at the intersection of
AI-oriented tools and techniques, regenerative design, and
biological systems that can support a transformative shift
towards intelligent self-adaptive bio-integrated facades.

2. Collaborative Digital Design Directions
We aim to study the integration of performance-oriented
computer-aided design with AI-oriented tools and behavior
control methods (intelligent self-regulating systems),
behavioral intelligence of the biological organisms in
biofacades, and the synergy between biocomponents and
environmental regeneration to formulate a new class of
research grammars towards AI nexus of bio-integrated
building facades. The proposal's CAAD areas of focus
include:

1. AI-assisted bio-integrated design: The impact of
computer vision, machine learning, and deep learning
techniques including supervised, unsupervised,
semi-supervised, and reinforcement learning alongside
data-driven strategies such as low-shot, few-shot,
zero-shot, and one-shot learning, on the optimized design
of bio-integrated facades.

2. Data-driven feed-back loops and decision support systems
(DSSs): The role of real-time data mining, monitoring, and
predictive analytics for the creation of self-adaptive
bio-integrated façade systems, supporting intelligent
real-time decision-making processes.

3. Intelligent UAV systems: The integration of drones'
capabilities with deep learning and computer vision AI
tools for data collection, information processing and
feature extraction, and physical installation and
controlling.

3. Research Questions

1. How will the evolution of bio-integrated building
facades unfold in the future, and what role will AI-driven
tools play in shaping their advancement?
2. How can AI-oriented tools and techniques be effectively
integrated into the design and implementation of
bio-integrated facades to enhance their adaptive behaviors
in response to real-time environmental changes?

4. Outputs

The proposed research explores future integrated research
domains between AI-driven tools, biological systems, and
environmental performance within bio-integrated building
façades as the programmable interface for real-time
responding to evolving ecological challenges and indoor
environmental quality. The core of this framework
introduces a novel paradigm that enables circular,
self-sustaining systems reliant on biological resources,
aiming for a balance between creation and utilization. This
framework transcends mere sustainability, engaging in the
active restoration and regeneration of its energy and
material sources in the frame of bio-integrated facades
that dynamically interact with the environment. This
proposal defines the capabilities of harnessing the
inherent biological intelligence, enabling a synergistic
relationship between incubated bio-integrated facades'
biocomponents and the environment. The integration of
AI-driven tools with data-driven decision-making can guide
and optimize the design process to intelligent,
self-adaptive bio-integrated façade systems based on
evidence-based solutions for strategic management of
natural resources in the context of bio-integrated facades
and urban ecosystem.

5.Shared Exploration and Potential Directions

With the proposed collaborative research, we aim to address
the existing challenges in bio-integrated building facades
by exploring interdisciplinary approaches, specifically the
role of AI tools in the future development of intelligent
next-generation bio-integrated façade systems, and finding
new strategies for their design. Findings resulting from
such collaborations can pave the way towards future
bio-integrated building façade systems, enabling a
transformative shift towards intelligent bio-informative
and self-adaptive façades that effectively integrate
AI-driven tools and regenerative design principles. The
future of bio-integrated facades lies in the continued
fusion of AI technologies with biological systems to create
intelligent, self-regulating, and regenerative building
components. As AI and machine learning tools evolve, they
will enable more precise, adaptive, and environmentally
responsive facade systems that can seamlessly integrate
into urban infrastructure. The integration of real-time
data mining, UAV systems for monitoring and maintenance,
and AI-driven decision-making will lead to more
decentralized, scalable, and resilient solutions. This core
proposal topic and its related subfields hold the potential
to significantly advance the design and development of
bio-integrated façades, shifting the boundaries of
architectural innovation while addressing critical
environmental challenges such as carbon sequestration, air
purification, and energy generation. Through this
collaborative proposal, we aim to explore novel strategies
and the future directions of bio-integrated facades design
based on the proposal's CAAD areas of focus.

column2: Kieron Cook and Benay Gursoy
column3:
A Fabrication Grammar for Robotic Sand Packing:  From
Precise Actions to Emergent Shapes and Patterns
column7:
This paper presents a fabrication grammar to formalize the
process of ro-botically packing sand to achieve emergent
shapes and patterns on the sand surface for casting
concrete panels. The study explores the use of 6-axis
ro-botic arms and custom sand mixtures in the development
of a reusable and reconfigurable sand formwork system for
casting concrete architectural pan-els with unique and
variable features. A key challenge of working with dy-namic
materials, such as sand, is their unpredictable behavior
when manip-ulated. By establishing a fabrication grammar
for robotic sand packing, we aim to create a logical
framework that formalizes the emergence of shapes and
patterns on the sand surface, revealing cause-and-effect
relationships between specific actions and material
outcomes in the generation of custom formworks. The robotic
arm operates following toolpaths generated using the
grammar, where each action is governed by predefined
parameters. Addi-tionally, fabrication parameters, focused
on changes in the material rather than the robot’s
behavior, influence how the sand responds to these
ac-tions. This paper presents the fabrication grammar and
exemplifies the emerging patterns and shapes developed
through this process, culminating in cast concrete panels
that demonstrate the potentials of this reconfigura-ble and
reusable formwork system.

column2: Yilun Jiang, Daniel Chad McKee and Kaicong Wu
column3:
Klotski-Solver for Hong Kong Homes: Customized 3D Indoor
Furniture Arrangements using Machine Learning
column7:
Indoor furniture arrangement is crucial for high-density
residential space, significantly impacting the daily
spatial experience of the residence. Hong Kong has one of
the highest density living conditions in the world, recent
research has highlighted the physical and mental health
challenges of long-term immersion in such environments
(Wong et al. 2016; Chan et al. 2021). Such compact living
presents challenges to residents lacking proper design
training to arrange their home space properly.

The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and extended
reality (XR) have expanded residents’ engagement in the
design processes, offering new insights into home
arrangement in the public perspective. Recent research in
indoor scene synthesis (ISS) has explored different machine
learning (ML) methods in generating indoor furniture
arrangement at various scales. Ranging from example-based
synthesis of computer desk set and
simulated-annealing-based living room arrangement (Fisher
et al. 2012; Yu et al. 2011), to the generations of
user-specified furniture in both singular and partitioned
space through Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) and
Reinforcement Learning (RL) (Yang et al. 2020; Di and Yu
2021; Hsu et al. 2022). While the research focuses on
evaluating the algorithmic performance, it overlooks user
accessibility and practical design factors, such as
occupant diversities, efficiency of spatial occupation in
3D and regional constraints. This research aims to explore
ISS applications in Hong Kong’s compact households,
focusing on multi-occupant schemes and emphasizing 3D
spatial efficiency. Using machine learning approaches such
as genetic algorithms (GAs) and reinforcement learning
(RL), we create a new ISS framework tailored to Hong Kong’s
regional character. A reward function transfers user
preference into ranked weights in ISS. Additionally, we
propose mobile user interaction interfaces to further
validate intuitive AI-XR-aided furniture planning.
Preliminary GAs-based experiment shows the framework
outputs effective designs that respond to both singular
room and full partitioned home with multi-occupant
preferences. Future work will expand furniture types and
enhance the interactiveness and efficiency of the framework
using RL.
