column2: Yuhong Wu and Tiantian Lo
column3:
tPACS: Phygital-Aided Construction System based on Modular
Customizable Timber Fabrication
column7:
As construction complexity increases in the architecture,
engineering and construction (AEC) industry, traditional
paper plans struggle to clearly and conveniently provide
adequate installation information, and they suffer from
poor interactivity and limited feedback guidance. This
paper proposes a Phygital-Aided Construction System(PACS),
which combines AR and embedded sensing technologies to help
unskilled workers build complex structures. The system is
based on an AR user interface and spatially anchored
virtual models to help participants review information
before construction and provide real-time feedback to
unskilled workers on assembly location, assembly method and
assembly results during various steps of construction. We
designed modular structures called "capsules" to house
embedded hardware. The hardware combination (pressure
sensors, magnetic sensors, etc.) and placement can be
selected according to different sensing needs. The capsules
merge with the structural components into a unified whole,
which provides long-term condition tracking to meet
building maintenance needs. We use HoloLens as the display
device and Unity as the customized AR environment carrier,
allowing the experiencer to assemble a wooden Dougong model
composed of 16 components. The experiment shows that
participants can master the use of the system after simple
and quick training. This system reduces assembly time and
assembly errors compared to paper instructions. In
addition, the results of the questionnaire indicate that
the system helps improve users' sense of participation and
concentration in the assembly process. PACS has the
potential to reduce the construction threshold of complex
buildings, shorten construction time and reduce
construction errors.

column2: Shirla Sin Ling Tse, Shuo-Te Chien and Yu Chieh Victor Lin
column3:
RECONSTRUCTING A PATTERN LANGUAGE: EMERGENT ASIAN CITIES
AND AIR-PORTS TRANSFORMATION, ANALOGY WITH AMERICAN AND
EUROPEAN CITIES
column7:
This paper explores the transformation of Aviation
Urbanism, a notion extending beyond Airport Urbanism  [Max
Hirsh, 2016] by integrating emerging technologies, such as
AI, blockchain, electric planes and drones, and more
importantly, prioritising civic spaces [Jane Jacobs, 1961]
for a more sustainable, livable, and social future.
Leveraging the post-digital paradigm's capacity for big
data collection and advanced analytics, this research
employs data visualisation to meticulously represent urban
information.

Drawing on "A Pattern Language"  [Christopher Alexandar,
1977] for semantic understanding of urban forms and human
needs in relation to air-ports, the study utilises Shape
Grammars  [George Stiny, 1980] to define the syntax of
urban elements, including neighbourhoods, streets, plots,
runways, terminals, blocks, and buildings. Space Syntax 
[Bill Hillier & Julienne Hanson, 1984 & 1987] analysis,
through DepthmapX and GIS software, quantifies spatial
relationships and reconstructs patterns based on
accessibility to air-ports. This methodology examines the
impact of air infrastructure on urban morphology, analysing
changes in connectivity, intelligibility, and social
behaviours.

By overlaying visualisations derived from Space Syntax and
Alexander's patterns, the research reveals the
geomorphological shifts in Asian cities experiencing
current air-port expansions or second air-ports
constructions, with a comparative study to their European
and American city counterparts (Bangkok, Hanoi, Shenzhen +
Hong Kong, and Tokyo vs London, Paris, Las Vegas + Los
Angeles, and New York). Analysing data pre- and post-
air-port development, the study investigates the potential
for both prosperity and marginalisation of a city resulting
from Aviation Urbanism, thus contributes to a nuanced
understanding of its implications for contemporary cities
and their stakeholders.

column2: Zhiyong Dong, Zhiqian Liu, Qi Wang and Peter Búš
column3:
Augmented Assembly: an Exploration of Modular Design to
Fabrication based on Extended Reality
column7:
Extended reality (XR) brings immersive interactions that
can integrate digi-tal information with physical
environments to design on a 1-to-1 scale, tak-ing
architecture design from two-dimensional to holographic.
This paper presents an in-depth exploration of the
integration of extended reality (XR) into the modular
design-to-fabrication process in architecture, focusing on
how XR can enhance the efficiency and accuracy of
architectural produc-tion. By leveraging XR's immersive and
interactive capabilities, the research aims to address key
challenges in bridging the gap between digital models and
real-world construction, particularly in terms of spatial
accuracy, real-time simulation, and object positioning
during assembly. A key case study involves the construction
of a modular pavilion, demonstrating the entire workflow,
from collaborative design and structural analysis to
optimiza-tion and augmented assembly using ArUco markers
for precise object alignment. Throughout the process, XR
technologies are shown to improve design precision,
fabrication efficiency, and team collaboration by
provid-ing real-time feedback and visualization. The
results reveal that XR has the potential to revolutionize
architectural design and construction, enabling designers
to make more informed decisions and facilitating a more
seamless transition from digital models to physical
structures. This study highlights the growing significance
of XR in computational architecture, contributing both to
theoretical discussions and practical applications, and
underscores its transformative impact on modern
architectural practices.

column2: Smaro Katsangelou and Heather Ligler
column3:
Learning from the Local: On the Rediscovery of Cultural
Heritage through Artificial Intelligence
column7:
The elements of which context is comprised include time,
locality, culture, and mood. This local intelligence is
intricate and challenging to replicate. Given that the
built and natural environments are viewed as a cumulation
of data, one could deduce that artificial intelligence
workflows might fragmentarily start to process, interpret,
and generate data that can simulate local intelligence to
inform design decisions for new projects that respond to a
natural or man-made environment. From text-to-image
generation to customized Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), the
permeation of AI in architecture has been explored manifold
through workflows spanning from very high to very low
Application Programming Interfaces (APIs). However, it can
be challenging to assess this landscape of emerging
architectural workflows that are influenced by the
ever-evolving technological advancements. The scope of this
research considers the current discourse in AI-driven
architecture alongside a deeper insight and understanding
of cultural connotations, spatial regulations, and, above
all, preservation theory and practice. More precisely, this
literature review seeks to identify current and recent
research projects of the last ten years (since 2014)
dealing with the use of AI in any part of the design
process on projects that focus on a specific era, style, or
region of architectural heritage, including adaptive reuse.

column2: 启惠 张 and 昀松 韩
column3:
Exploring the dynamic thermal perception and physiological
responses during indoor-outdoor walking in summer based on
facial thermal image analysis
column7:
Improving people's comfort requirements for outdoor
activities has stimulated the research demand for outdoor
thermal comfort. The layout of buildings, the form of
facades, and the planting of vegetation all affect people's
thermal perception during outdoor walking. However, many
cities focus on walkability by functionality, with little
regard for thermal comfort. The facial temperature infrared
recognition method is a non-invasive strategy that could be
used during human movement. In this study, we designed a
field experiment so that the subjects could experience the
different environmental stimuli of the natural environment.
Synchronously, the temperature features of different facial
regions were extracted from facial thermal images. Results
reveal that the adaptation time of people in a hot
environment is approximately 8 minutes. The buffering
effect of UEB (underneath an elevated building) is superior
to shaded in moving from indoors to sunlit, which can
effectively alleviate the thermal discomfort caused by
direct sun exposure. While walking from the sunlit to the
room, the conclusion is reversed. The thermal overshoot is
observed to persist for eight minutes following a change in
the thermal environment. Both the psychological and
physiological data also indicate that cold stimulation
caused by wind is a more effective method for inducing
thermal pleasure in hot summer. Considering thermal
alliesthesia, dynamic thermal environments may facilitate
the attainment of higher levels of thermal comfort. The
research can provide guidance for designers in improving
the thermal environment of urban walking spaces.

column2: Jinbao Zhong and June-Hao Hou
column3:
Enhancing Architectural Cognition: Augmented Reality’s Role
in Spatial Reasoning
column7:
This paper investigates how surreal Augmented Reality (AR)
experiences can enhance spatial reasoning and architectural
cognition. The research builds on pri-or findings that
emphasize the importance of visualizing and manipulating
three-dimensional (3D) structures. We use a practice-based
approach to develop two AR prototypes for the Meta Quest 3.
Unlike standard CAD or BIM tools that present
photorealistic overlays, these prototypes rely on
video-textured surfaces mapped onto real-world objects and
walls. This method creates “dream-like” en-vironments that
provoke users to traverse the fantasy, challenging their
predictive models and fueling deeper engagement.

The first prototype applies animated materials to each face
of tables or boxes, ac-centuating the tension between
expected shapes and lively textures. The second prototype
merges multiple walls into a unified visual canvas, where a
single loop-ing video encloses the room in a seamless
boundary. Preliminary observations show heightened spatial
awareness, a desire to explore, and a disorienting effect
when toggling illusions off.

These results align with embodied cognition theories by
highlighting how sen-sorimotor interactions can amplify
one’s sense of agency and reflection. The dis-cussion
underscores AR-driven fantasy as a catalyst for creative
thinking, while also illustrating how these illusions can
promote a more thorough understanding of real-world
constraints. Architectural education and practice may
benefit from this approach, which encourages an
interactive, flexible engagement with space. Through
surreal AR interventions, designers and clients alike can
traverse the fantasy, expanding their perception and
appreciation of built environments. These experiences offer
an innovative route to bridging embodied imagination and
prac-tical design considerations.

column2: Daria Smakhtina
column3:
Tracing The Wild: Creating Interfaces Between Humans and
Nature
column7:
Tracing The Wild is a data-driven art project dedicated to
the dynamics of biosocial interactions between predators
and human communities in the Maasai Mara region of Kenya,
where human settlements are spread along the invisible
borders of the protected territories of the Masai Mara
National Reserve.

In this art series, data (satellite GPS collars tracking)
on the movements of three lionesses living in the research
region is re-encoded into digital ‘portraits.’ These
spatiotemporal sculptures are created by combining
in-formation on the animal’s coordinates with the timeline
of their activities using a generative toolset: mapping
techniques in geographic information system software QGIS
are combined with the visual coding instruments in 3D
computer graphics software Blender. The resulting objects
depict the key patterns in predators' territorial
movements, allowing viewers to analyse animal behaviour and
identify time periods and areas of potential risks.

By incorporating the developed generative workflow with
real-time data input and augmented reality tools, these
digital sculptures have the potential to operate as a
real-time interface of human-nonhuman interactions and
represent ecosystem parameters as a dynamic artwork. Placed
in the natural conditions of the research area as updatable
AR sculptures, they can pro-vide local communities and
researchers with valuable insights, conduct design
decisions, inspire architectural design practices aligned
with natural processes, and enhance harmonious co-living.

column2: Yu-Hao Chen, Mi-Chi Wang and Yang-Ting Shen
column3:
Shadow Drift: The Development of Activity-based VR Game for
Heat Risk Awareness and Assessment
column7:
Climate change and urban heat islands significantly
challenge outdoor thermal comfort and public health. To
address these issues, this study em-ploys the virtual
reality game Shadow Drift as a tool to explore the
poten-tial for enhancing residents’ heat risk awareness and
promoting climate ad-aptation actions. The game integrates
real-world site data with object detec-tion and thermal
environment simulation to reconstruct behavioral patterns
in public spaces and thermal environmental characteristics.
Through partic-ipatory shading design tasks, players
experience the process of environmen-tal improvement.

In the game, players analyze high-activity and high-solar
radiation zones, plant trees to optimize thermal comfort
conditions, and evaluate the effec-tiveness of thermal
environment improvements using simulated virtual
res-idents’ behaviors and exposure assessments, with
survival rates serving as a quantifiable indicator. The
study uses Autodesk Insight to obtain solar radiation data
and employs the YOLOv8 model to identify pedestrians from
surveillance footage. After calibrating the data, the
planar coordinates are integrated into the Unity platform.
The results demonstrate that this learning process improves
residents’ understanding of heat risks and their capacity
for action. Participants' performance in virtual reality
scenarios, combined with their real-life experiences,
showcased effective adaptive ca-pabilities. This research
framework highlights the potential of bottom-up climate
adaptation actions and offers an innovative approach to
heat risk awareness and environmental education.

column2: Hani̇fe Sümeyye Taşdelen and Leman Figen Gül
column3:
Aesthetic “Dissensus” in Public Architecture: Computational
Analysis of Contextual Strangeness and Place Appropriation
column7:
Architecture has the potential to stimulate thought and
engagement by challenging conventional forms and functions,
which is rooted in Rancière's concept of "aesthetic
dissensus." This paper investigates how architectural forms
that deviate from expected norms within a specific urban or
cultural context affect social integration in public
spaces. Although significant attention has been directed
toward functional performance in public architecture, there
is limited understanding of how formal deviations influence
appropriation. Using a two-phase approach, we first examine
architectural aesthetics using computer vision algorithms
after conducting a literature review on Rancièrean
dissensus in design. In the second phase, we combine
spatial analysis with crowdsourced social data and
behavioral heat maps generated by computer vision to track
user interactions with space and create an "inclusivity
index" for the selected architectural space. These
computational methods objectively measure physical
engagement, while crowdsourced social data assesses public
sentiment and participation. The findings propose a
technique for correlating formal deviations with
inclusivity and new strategies for architects to create
socially engaging environments. This paper demonstrates how
aesthetic dissensus can foster place appropriation in
public architecture by combining computational analysis
with social data.

column2: Wenqian Yang, Anton Savov and Benjamin Dillenguber
column3:
Virtual Space Design Through Physical Object Recognition,
HoloLens-Based Furniture Tracking and AI-Driven Real-Time
Layout Generation
column7:
This paper presents a workflow that bridges mixed reality
(MR) interactive editing with AI-driven floor plan
generation, creating
an interface for architectural design. The system
integrates physical ob-
ject tracking, hand gesture input, and immersive
visualization to enhance
user interaction. Using MR glasses paired with a computer,
the applica-
tion combines MR’s real-time capabilities with the
generative power of
AI, to deliver user-friendly and accessible design
experiences. The work-
flow involves object recognition via Vuforia, enabling
accurate and stable
tracking of 3D-printed furniture models, and uses Photon
Unity Network-
ing for seamless communication between AR and AI
components. AI
processes floor plan data from tracked physical objects and
user-defined
parameters to generate responsive house layouts.
Visualization is pro-
vided through holographic overlays in AR and a shared
monitor view,
offering immersive and collaborative design experiences.
Tested by over
100 participants including non-experts, the system
demonstrated reliable
performance, though challenges such as multi-object
tracking and real-
time feedback were identified. This work paves the way for
further inter-
disciplinary applications of MR and AI in design, making
floor plan cre-
ation more accessible, engaging, and intuitive, especially
for non-expert
users. Future improvements include optimizing AI processing
speed and
enhancing multi-object recognition for a smoother user
experience.

column2:
Mahdi Jandaghimeibodi, Mostafa Hosseini Vajari, Morteza
Behzadnasab and Soheil Dariushi
column3:
Predicting Stress-Strain Characteristics of 3D Printed BCC
Lattice Structures with Variable Grid Gradation Using
Neural Networks
column7:
This paper presents a novel computational methodology to
predict the mechanical behavior of 3D-printed body-centered
cubic (BCC) lattice structures with varying grid gradation
using an artificial neural network (ANN). The BCC lattice
structure is one of the most widely used and researched
lattice typologies, allowing for lightweight designs that
maintain strength, enable complex geometries, and
facilitate material optimization. BCC lattices are commonly
employed in lightweight structures due to their high
strength-to-weight ratio, but their mechanical response,
especially stress-strain characteristics, can vary based on
structural parameters such as grid gradation.
Evaluation methods, such as experimental compression tests
or 3D simulations of these behaviors, are time-consuming
and resource-intensive. To address this, we employ a
data-driven approach by utilizing an ANN to predict
stress-strain responses as a function of grid variation in
BCC lattices. By systematically varying grid parameters,
such as the spacing of lattice nodes, we generated and
3D-printed a lattice set. Our experimental data was
obtained by conducting physical compression tests on the
lattices. This data was used to train the ANN, allowing it
to capture the complex relationships between lattice
configuration and mechanical performance.
The trained neural network demonstrates a high degree of
accuracy in predicting stress-strain curves of lattice
configurations, reducing the reliance on experimental
testing. Validation against physical experiments confirms
the robustness of the model, showcasing its potential as a
powerful tool for design optimization. These findings are
expected to facilitate the development of optimized
structures for applications in architectural design,
aerospace, automotive, and biomedical fields.

column2: Theodoros Dounas and Wassim Jabi
column3:
Topology Driven Graph Grammars for Generative Artificial
Intelligence in Architecture
column7:
The emergence of new models of generative machine learning
(ML) with the significance and impact of transformer models
has reinvigorated the research space of artificial
intelligence (AI) in architectural design (Vissers et al
2024). Still, generative AI generative AI of the same
breadth that deals with three-dimensional data is not yet
performing at the same level, due to efforts focusing on 2d
output or due to lack of datasets.
In parallel the emergence of light-weight frameworks such
as Topologic [Jabi et al 2021] have enabled the rapid
creation of three dimensional datasets that can be used for
graph machine learning, lending themselves to the massive
potential of the topologic library to produce vector based,
coordinated,  3d geometric,  topologic and semantic models.
[Jabi et al 2022].
Our paper presents  a topology-driven graph grammar to
generate  geometric, topologically correct, semantically
enriched architectural 3d models, that contribute to
datasets for gen-AI training. Our methods operate at the
level of the graph and generation of shape transformation
rules that procedurally allows the generation of the 3d
dataset.
Our systems allows the creation of the 3d models starting
from simple graphs, via the application of grammar rules.
Additionally, we showcase how graph-isomorphism is used for
style transitions, where different grammars rules are
applied to the same graph, or used for part-model
substitution, where we create variant 3d architectural
models, by substituting parts of the models recognised
under the same graph, which are shown to be novel. Our
system is significant in bridging shape grammars with
graphs and topology to develop a generative system that
maintains semantics, topology while being able to generate
new novel solutions. Our system can have direct impact unto
the creation of rich datasets for  generative AI operating
in three dimensions.

column2: Igor Pantic, Soomeen Hahm, Peter Búš and Zhiyong Dong
column3:
(CI) Augmentation in Design and Fabrication: Expanding the
Role of AR and Human-Machine Collaboration
column7:
The future of architectural practice is increasingly shaped
by the integration of digital technologies that augment
human capabilities, particularly in design and fabrication.
As boundaries between human craftsmanship and computational
precision continue to blur, Augmented Reality (AR) is
transforming from a visualization tool into a powerful
means of human augmentation. This research explores how AR
enhances human abilities in real-time fabrication processes
and introduces a broader vision of human-machine
collaboration, where both humans and machines work together
in a seamless, augmented environment.

Our research is rooted in the idea that
augmentation—through the use of AR, AI, and robotics—has
the potential to revolutionize architectural workflows by
creating more efficient, adaptive, and collaborative design
and fabrication processes. By focusing on how these
technologies empower humans to work in concert with
machines, we present a vision of architecture where
creativity is elevated, tasks are optimized, and innovation
thrives.

AR as a Tool for Human Augmentation

AR has evolved into a critical technology for automating
and augmenting human actions in fabrication. It provides
real-time guidance, enabling workers to perform complex
tasks with increased precision, significantly reducing
error rates. Our research highlights how AR can simplify
advanced fabrication techniques, making them accessible to
both skilled and less-skilled workers. This democratization
expands the role of AR from a supplementary tool to a key
technology that elevates human craftsmanship.

In fabrication processes such as timber construction, AR
offers real-time visualization of assembly sequences,
ensuring accuracy even in non-standard designs. This
ability to guide and adjust in real time means that AR is
not just a tool for execution but also a platform for
problem-solving and decision-making on-site, allowing for
greater flexibility during the design and construction
phases. The precision achieved through AR integration
reduces material waste, enhances safety, and enables
complex geometric assemblies that would otherwise require
higher levels of manual skill.

Our position is that AR not only augments human physical
capabilities but also enhances cognitive processes by
offering immediate feedback and reducing the mental burden
of managing complex workflows. AR empowers designers and
fabricators to engage in more creative processes while
handling the technical precision of construction, ensuring
higher quality outcomes with fewer resources. This dual
role of AR as a cognitive and physical augmentation tool
makes it indispensable in the modern architectural practice.

Human-Machine Collaboration: Expanding the Scope

As AR’s role expands, the next frontier is human-machine
collaboration. We propose that AR can act as an interface
that coordinates the actions of both human workers and
robotic systems. This interaction enhances the adaptability
of fabrication processes, with robots handling repetitive
tasks while humans focus on creativity and decision-making.
AR enables this symbiotic relationship, allowing for fluid
workflows where humans and machines complement one
another's strengths.

Human-machine collaboration offers the potential to reshape
construction workflows by streamlining processes and
increasing productivity. Robots can be tasked with
executing high-precision, repetitive operations, while
human workers take on roles requiring judgment, creativity,
and adaptability. AR facilitates this partnership by
providing the human worker with a dynamic interface that
offers real-time feedback and instructions, ensuring that
the robotic elements of the workflow are performing as
expected and are aligned with the overall design vision.

In this scenario, the combination of AR, AI-driven systems,
and robotics provides the best of both worlds: the
technical reliability and speed of automation, paired with
the creativity and contextual understanding that only human
workers bring to the process. This hybrid approach allows
for complex, custom designs that would be challenging to
achieve with either humans or machines working
independently.

Our thesis is that by integrating AR, AI, and robotics, the
architectural field can advance toward a future where
augmentation optimizes both creative and technical
processes. We aim to push the boundaries of what
augmentation can achieve, transitioning from isolated
digital tools to fully integrated human-machine systems.

Pushing the Boundaries of Augmentation

The future of augmentation lies in its ability to blend
traditional craftsmanship with digital technologies. AR, as
a tool for real-time interaction, enables the exploration
of more complex geometries and customized designs,
expanding the possibilities for architects and fabricators.
Our research envisions a future where augmented humans and
machines collaborate to bring more complex and creative
designs to life.

By applying AR and human-machine collaboration to the
design and fabrication process, we can expand the creative
possibilities available to architects, allowing for
dynamic, adaptive workflows that respond to both design
intent and real-time environmental factors. The ability to
engage with a project at multiple levels—conceptual,
technical, and physical—provides a new framework for
iterative, flexible design. In this way, AR not only
improves the execution of designs but also empowers
designers to experiment, refine, and iterate more
effectively.

We propose that this expanded view of augmentation will
foster collaborative, interdisciplinary workflows where
architects, engineers, and fabricators can interact with
digital models and processes in real-time. By integrating
AR, AI, and robotic systems, our work pushes the boundaries
of design and fabrication, offering new methods for
realizing innovative and sustainable architectural
solutions.

Ethical and Social Implications of Augmented Fabrication

While the technological advancements in AR and augmentation
hold great promise for the future of architecture, they
also raise important ethical and social questions. As more
tasks are automated and augmented, the role of skilled
labor in architecture is likely to change. Traditional
forms of craftsmanship may give way to more digitally
augmented methods, leading to shifts in how skills are
valued and how labor is distributed across the design and
construction industries.

We recognize that augmentation technologies present both
opportunities and challenges for the future of labor in the
architecture and construction fields. As AR and robotic
systems become more integrated into workflows, there is the
potential for a loss of traditional, manual craftsmanship.
However, we argue that augmentation is not about replacing
human labor but about enhancing human roles by shifting
focus toward creative and strategic tasks that benefit from
the real-time insights provided by AR.

We also emphasize the importance of ensuring inclusivity
and accessibility to these technologies. While AR can
democratize access to advanced techniques, there is a need
to ensure that these systems are designed in a way that
allows all individuals—regardless of skill level or
socioeconomic status—to benefit from these advancements. By
addressing these concerns, we aim to develop equitable
augmentation systems that balance innovation with
inclusivity.

Conclusion: The Future of Augmented Design and Fabrication

In summary, this research positions AR and human-machine
collaboration at the forefront of the future of
architecture. Our thesis is that augmentation—through AR,
AI, and robotics—offers a transformative framework for
enhancing human capabilities in both design and
fabrication. By pushing the boundaries of traditional
workflows and exploring new methods for human-machine
collaboration, our research seeks to redefine architectural
practice, ensuring that augmented humans and machines work
together to shape a more creative, efficient, and
sustainable built environment.

column2:
Matias del Campo, Sandra Manninger, Alexandra Carlson and
Dansih Syed
column3:
(CI) Robotic Recycling of Demolition Debris for Sustainable
Construction
column7:
Introduction

The construction industry is a leading contributor to
global carbon emissions and waste, particularly through
demolition debris. Most of this waste, comprising materials
like concrete, stone, and metal, is discarded rather than
recycled. This proposal focuses on utilizing robotics,
artificial intelligence (AI), and machine vision to
reimagine how demolition rubble can be processed and
reused. The project introduces two distinct yet
complementary concepts: automated rubble sorting and
robotic rubble masonry.

The first method involves industrial robots autonomously
sorting construction debris to prepare it for reuse in
future construction. The second method applies AI
puzzle-solving techniques to reassemble broken rubble into
new walls, inspired by the ancient Roman construction
method called rubble masonry. Both approaches aim to reduce
the environmental impact of construction while offering
innovative architectural possibilities.

Background and Rationale

As urbanization accelerates, the frequency of demolition
and reconstruction is increasing, which results in large
amounts of waste being sent to landfills. Though some
materials from demolition sites are recycled, the process
is inefficient, requiring human labor and considerable time
to sort and process debris. However, much of this rubble
could be reused, minimizing the need for new raw materials
and reducing the construction industry’s carbon footprint.

Historically, rubble masonry was a highly efficient
construction method that used irregularly broken bricks and
stones set in mortar. While this method has largely fallen
out of favor due to modern preferences for standardized
materials, revisiting it with advanced robotics and AI
could create a sustainable alternative. Furthermore, the
irregular nature of rubble opens up new possibilities for
creative architectural designs.

Research Objectives

This interdisciplinary research proposal seeks to:

1.	Develop an AI-driven robotic system that autonomously
sorts and prepares
        construction rubble for reuse in future projects,
        improving the recycling
        process.
2.	Design an AI puzzle-solving system that enables robots
to reassemble rubble
        into structurally sound walls, modernizing the
        ancient technique of rubble
        masonry through precision robotics.

Concept 1: AI-Powered Rubble Sorting

Methodology

The first approach automates the sorting and categorization
of demolition debris through industrial robots equipped
with sensors, cameras, and AI-based algorithms. Using
machine vision and deep learning, the system will
autonomously identify and classify rubble types—such as
concrete, brick, and metal-based on material properties,
size, and shape.

•	Machine Vision and Deep Learning: The system will rely on
convolutional neural
        networks (CNNs) for object detection and material
        classification, trained on
        large datasets representing different types of
        rubble.
•	Robotic Sorting: Robots will be equipped with flexible
grippers to handle
        debris, separating it into material-specific
        categories, making it easier to
        reuse or repurpose.
•	Sensor Integration: LiDAR and ultrasonic sensors will
enhance the robots’
        ability to detect cracks, weaknesses, or structural
        anomalies in the rubble,
        ensuring that the selected materials are suitable
        for reuse.
        Algorithms and Technologies
•	Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs): For recognizing
different materials and
        sorting them accordingly.
•	Reinforcement Learning: To optimize the sorting process
by improving the
        system's performance over time.
•	Clustering Algorithms: These will group similar materials
for efficient reuse.

Expected Outcomes

•	Reduction in labor costs and increased efficiency in
sorting construction
        debris.
•	A significant waste reduction, as more materials will be
reused rather than
        discarded.
•	Improved accuracy in material selection, leading to
better quality in
        recycling processes.

Concept 2: Robotic Rubble Masonry

Methodology

The second concept leverages robotic construction
techniques to reassemble broken rubble into new walls. This
method draws inspiration from Roman rubble masonry but
integrates modern technology, allowing robots to
autonomously scan, select, and precisely place rubble
pieces.

•	AI Puzzle Solver: This algorithm analyzes irregularly
shaped rubble pieces and
        tries to fit them together like a puzzle. The
        solver optimizes the placement
        of each piece, considering factors such as
        structural integrity and design
        goals.
•	Rubble Scanning: Robots will use 3D scanning technology
to capture the
        geometry of each piece of rubble. This data will
        then be fed into the puzzle-
        solving algorithm, which will calculate the optimal
        placement for each piece.
•	Robotic Arm Placement and Mortar Application: Once a
piece is identified, the
        robot will pick it up and place it in its
        designated position, applying mortar
        as needed. The mortar placement will be managed by
        an AI algorithm that
        ensures it is applied correctly to maintain
        structural stability.
        Algorithms and Technologies
•	Shape Analysis Algorithms: These will analyze the
irregular shapes of the
        rubble pieces and determine how they fit together.
•	Path Planning Algorithms: Used to optimize the movement
of robotic arms during
        the construction process, reducing time and energy
        use.
•	Mortar Application Algorithm: To precisely calculate
where and how much mortar
        to apply for each piece of rubble.

Expected Outcomes

•	The construction of new, structurally sound walls using
entirely recycled
        materials.
•	A creative exploration of architectural possibilities, as
robots can use
        irregular materials to form unique and innovative
        designs.
•	A significant reduction in the costs and energy typically
associated with
        traditional rubble masonry.

Interdisciplinary Approach

The success of this project requires collaboration across
multiple disciplines: architecture, robotics, artificial
intelligence, and sustainability science. The project
offers a unique intersection of ancient construction
techniques and modern technological innovations. Expertise
in computer vision, robotic engineering, machine learning,
and sustainable design will be essential to meet the
project's goals.
The interdisciplinary team presenting this proposal, with
members from Robotics, Computer Science, and Architecture,
will allow the team from various fields to contribute their
knowledge, catalyzing new discussions and ideas that can
enhance the research. This approach will foster the
interdisciplinary and collective design that the CAAD
Futures conference promotes.

Challenges and Solutions

•	Sorting Complexity: Sorting heterogeneous materials with
high accuracy is a
        difficult task. However, advanced machine learning
        models trained on extensive
        datasets will allow the system to generalize well
        across different types of
        materials.
•	Structural Integrity: Building structurally sound walls
from irregular rubble
        requires careful placement and mortar application.
        The use of AI puzzle-
        solving and mortar algorithms will ensure that the
        resulting walls are both
        stable and innovative.
•	Time and Cost: Initial setup costs for robotic systems
can be high, but the
        long-term savings in labor, material reuse, and
        energy consumption make this
        approach cost-effective. (Sidenote: The team has
        access to all the necessary
        hardware (Robots, Sensors etc.) and Software (Coded
        on GitHub, Data Collection
        on AWS and training on Google Colab) to conduct the
        proposed research.

Impact on CAAD Topics

The project contributes to several key CAAD Futures 2025
topics:

1.	Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning in Design:
Applying AI to automate
        rubble sorting and puzzle-solving demonstrates a
        sophisticated use of machine
        learning in architectural design.
2.	Sustainable and Green Design: The project promotes
sustainability by recycling
        construction materials and reducing the need for
        newly manufactured resources.
3.	Robotics in Architecture & Construction: The development
of robotic rubble
        masonry advances the integration of robotics in the
        building industry,
        allowing for more complex and sustainable
        construction processes.
4.	Interdisciplinary and Collective Design: This project is
inherently
        interdisciplinary, requiring input from AI
        researchers, architects, engineers,
        and sustainability experts. It promotes
        collaborative design, aligning with
        CAAD Futures' focus on collective innovation.

Conclusion

This interdisciplinary research proposal aims to
revolutionize how demolition debris is processed and reused
in the construction industry. By developing AI-driven
robotic systems for rubble sorting and masonry, the project
will significantly reduce the carbon footprint of
construction while expanding creative design possibilities.
Through collaboration within CAAD Futures’ Catalytic
Interfaces, this research will contribute to a more
sustainable future for architecture and construction.

column2: Giacomo Montiani, Matthias Helmreich and Achilleas Xydis
column3: Optimized Acoustics for Meeting Pods
column7:
Open-space offices are an architectural typology widely
used in modern working environments. These spaces often
lack privacy, and their constant background noise and
distractions can negatively affect occupants' well-being
and productivity. Meeting pods can provide the required
privacy and acoustic comfort. However, the acoustic design
of existing meeting pods focuses primarily on noise
reduction and often overlooks room acoustic quality. This
research proposes a computational workflow for designing
and producing small meeting pods, focusing on improved room
acoustic performance. The proposed workflow integrates
acoustic simulations within the design process, optimizing
the pod's geometry and controlling the acoustic qualities
of its inner surfaces. It combines two parallel design
strategies: the parametric design of irregular prismatic
volumes and the creation of geometric patterns for resonant
absorbers. Several resonant absorbers are designed and
fabricated using a CNC milling machine and then physically
tested to assess their acoustic performance. The acoustic
test results inform the simulation model used in the
computational workflow to optimize the placement of these
resonant absorbers, thus optimizing the pod’s acoustics.
Computer simulations and a 1:1 scaled physical demonstrator
are used to evaluate the proposed workflow, understand its
limitations, and identify future work.

column2: Sara Codarin and Masataka Yoshikawa
column3:
Fabricated Combines: Integrating Generative AI and Digital
Fabrication in Architectural Design Workflows
column7:
Generative AI is revolutionizing architectural design by
enabling designers to explore new visual and spatial
possibilities through text-based diffusion models and image
generation. The research project *Fabricated Combines*
examines how AI-generated 2D images, despite their
limitations in 3D coherence, can inspire speculative design
processes. Drawing from Robert Rauschenberg’s "combines"
concept, the study merges digital and physical media,
fostering iterative workflows from ideation to
model-making. AI-generated images are converted into 3D
models, refined through manual and digital sculpting, and
fabricated into physical models using 3D printing. This
cyclical process, informed by architectural fragments and
historical narratives, creates a dynamic feedback loop
between digital and physical realms.

The research is structured around four key
objectives—processual, aesthetic, digital, and
material—aiming to challenge traditional notions of space
and materiality while exploring new workflows in
architectural design. The integration of AI tools, such as
Midjourney and Google Colab, facilitates real-time
collaboration and iterative refinement. While AI
accelerates idea generation and enhances creativity, human
intervention remains crucial in refining and realizing
architectural concepts.

The study also highlights the evolving role of AI in design
pedagogy, advocating for hybrid drawing techniques and
AI-enhanced workflows to enrich architectural
representation. As AI technology advances, its potential to
generate more accurate 3D models will grow, emphasizing the
need for educational programs that equip architects with
the skills to harness AI effectively. Ultimately, the
research envisions a future where AI becomes an
indispensable tool in architectural practice, blending
creativity, innovation, and human authorship.

column2: Zixi Zhang, Wenshuo Zhang and Runjia Tian
column3:
Text-to-Siheyuan: LLM-based Multi-Agent Procedural
Generation System of Vernacular Architecture in Beijing
column7:
Rule-Based Procedural Content Generation (PCG) methods have
been instrumental in exploring the mathematical principles
underlying traditional Chinese vernacular architecture
(Wang et al. 2020). However, they often require detailed
architectural knowledge to understand and use the
procedural systems, creating a high barrier to usage.

This research presents an LLM-based multi-agent procedural
generation system(Wu et al. 2023)  for traditional Chinese
vernacular architecture, enhancing efficiency in analyzing
design requirements and facilitating accurate
decision-making while maintaining cultural fidelity.
Siheyuan, a quintessential example of traditional Chinese
architecture, is chosen as a case study (Ma 1999). Our
methodology comprises three steps:

1. Component-Based Disassembly of Traditional Design
Principles: We divided Siheyuan planning principles into
four components—Architecture, Entrance, Veranda, and Wall.
Each component serves as a foundation for our procedural
generation system, managed by specialized agents.

2. Collaborative Multi-Agent Procedural Modeling: Four
GPT-4-based agents (Courtyard Planner, Courtyard Divider,
Depth-Width Planner, and Component Manager) were employed,
each with a specific role in synthesizing parameters. Users
input design requirements through natural language, and the
bot, guided by questions, generates a regularized
fixed-format procedural DSL (Domain-Specific Language),
ensuring the Siheyuan layout aligns with traditional design
principles.

3. Real-Time Interaction and Visualization in 3D Modeling
Platforms: The bot's API was integrated with Grasshopper,
converting design parameters into our Siheyuan DSL
represented in JSON data. The JSON data is processed by the
Grasshopper Python API to generate a 3D Siheyuan model,
reflecting traditional Chinese architectural structures.

This approach offers designers an intuitive and efficient
method for generating vernacular architecture models,
lowers the professional threshold for public engagement,
and enhances participation in cultural heritage
preservation and appreciation for the historical value of
traditional architecture.

References:
Y. Wang, A. Agkathidis, and A. Crompton, “Parametrising

design framework for the digital representation of Siheyuan
iterations based on traditional design principles,”
Frontiers of Architectural Research, vol. 9, no. 4, pp.
751–773, Dec. 2020.

Q. Wu et al., “AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications
via Multi-Agent Conversation,” arXiv.org, Oct. 03, 2023.

University Press, Tianjin, 1999.

column2: Maryam Badiei, Abolhassan Pishahang and Milad Heiranipour
column3:
From Tradition to Computation: Adaptive Ceramic ‎Façades
Inspired by Persian Ice Caves (Yakhchals) for ‎Passive
Cooling
column7:
This study investigates the adaptation of Yakhchal-inspired
passive cooling strat-‎egies into modern ceramic façade
systems. Yakhchals, ancient Persian icehouses, ‎utilized
conical geometries, thermal mass, and natural ventilation
for effective ‎cooling in arid climates. Inspired by these
principles, modular cone-shaped ce-‎ramic tiles were
designed to optimize shading and airflow, reducing solar
heat ‎gain and improving building energy performance. Using
Rhinoceros 3D for de-‎sign and ClimateStudio for
simulation, five façade configurations were evaluated,
‎including a benchmark flat surface and tile
implementations on south, west, east, ‎and three façades
simultaneously. Results showed a 19% reduction in energy
use ‎intensity (EUI) and a 19.8% improvement in thermal
comfort with the three-‎façade configuration. The east
façade alone achieved a 60.5% reduction in solar ‎radiation
absorption, demonstrating the tiles' effectiveness in
managing solar gain. ‎Fabrication employed 3D-printed molds
and hand-built clay tiles to test structural ‎integrity and
aesthetic potential. These experiments provided a
foundation for fu-‎ture work using advanced techniques like
robotic arms and 3D clay printing to ‎create lightweight,
geometrically optimized designs. This research bridges
ver-‎nacular architecture and computational innovation,
demonstrating how traditional ‎knowledge can inspire
sustainable, energy-efficient solutions for modern façade
‎design. The Yakhchal-inspired tiles offer a promising
approach to reducing ener-‎gy consumption and enhancing
thermal comfort in hot climates.‎

column2: Gernot Riether
column3:
Public Space Spectacle: Using Extended Reality (XR) to
Transform a Street into a Cultural Hub
column7:
How can Extended Reality (XR) interventions in urban public
spaces foster cultural exchange and transform physical
environments into dynamic, interactive spectacles?

This study examines a design studio collaboration between
[XXX] University and [XXX] Art Organization, conducted in
[XXX] during Summer 2024. The studio aimed to activate a
public street, transforming it into a cultural hub through
small-scale, XR-driven urban furniture interventions. Three
key projects: (1) Interactive Wayfinding System, (2) Public
Space as Museum, and (3) Infrastructure for Art in Public
Space serve as case studies. These projects utilized XR
technologies and Interaction Design Technologies (IxD) to
enhance public space by introducing digital overlays,
immersive storytelling, and cultural programming. The
analysis explores how physical and digital spaces intersect
to create a dynamic, multi-layered urban experience.

The research illustrates XR’s potential to redefine public
spaces by merging physical environments with digital
narratives. XR interventions enhance the performative,
interactive nature of public spaces, allowing for richer
social interactions and fostering new layers of cultural
engagement. However, the study also highlights challenges,
such as the risk of over-commercialization. Additionally,
concerns about the loss of tactile and sensory elements
intrinsic to traditional public spaces are addressed.
Despite these limitations, the projects demonstrate how XR
can activate urban spaces, creating new forms of social
infrastructure that reflect the diversity and complexity of
contemporary urban life. The integration of XR in public
spaces presents opportunities for urban designers to create
inclusive, engaging environments that foster communal
living in the context of a rapidly evolving digital culture.

References
- Carta, S. (2022). “Machine Learning and the City” Wiley
Blackwell.
- Mitrašinović M. and Mehta V., (2021). “Public Space
Reader” Routledge.
- Imdat, A., Basu, P., Talwar, P, (2022). ‘Artificial
Intelligence in Urban Planning and Design:
Technologies, Implementation, and Impacts” Elsevier.
- Jan Kolko (2007) “Thoughts on Interaction Design” Brown
Bear.
- Costa C., Mastoureh Fathi M., García-Esparza J. (2023)
“Dynamics of Placemaking Volume 1 Placemaking in Practice –
Experiences and Approaches” Brill, Leiden I Boston
- Eren I., Aktuglu Ö., Altanlar A. (2024) Enhancement of
socialization in urban public space through digital media,
Proceedings of the International Conference on Research in
Social Sciences

column2:
Ahmed M. Abuzuraiq, Esmaeil Mottaghi, Halil Erhan, Marcelo
Bernal, Victor Okhoya, Spyridon Ampanavos and Cheney Chen
column3:
Integration of Performance Assessment and Parametric
Analysis through Design Analytics Interfaces in the Early
Phases of Design
column7:
This paper presents D-Predict, an integrated design
analytics tool we developed to support setting up and
generating alternatives while conducting performance
assessments in the early phases of building design. The
system uses ML-based surrogate modelling for rapid
performance analysis, providing real-time feedback to
designers through interactive interfaces. D-Predict
supports both parametric and non-parametric design
approaches, offering various design exploration strategies,
including trial-and-error, sensitivity analysis, and design
space sampling with visualizations. It aims to help
designers make informed decisions based on quantitative
performance metrics like daylight autonomy and energy loads
without requiring expert assistance or running
labour-intensive simulations. To demonstrate the tool's
utility, we present a case study on a real-world project
and illustrate its capabilities for iterative and
parametric exploration of design alternatives leveraging
the speed and reasonable accuracy of an ML-based surrogate
model for daylight autonomy and algorithmic energy load
computation.

column2: Tina Behrouz, Halil Erhan and Elif Sezen Yagmur Kilimci
column3:
Evaluating Augmented Reality as a Tool for Democratizing
Built Environment Design
column7:
Public engagement in urban planning and architectural
design is crucial for creating spaces that reflect the
diverse needs and preferences of the community. Yet,
traditional methods often fail to engage a broad range of
stakeholders effectively. This limitation impacts the
democratization of design processes, where decisions are
frequently dominated by a limited group of decision-makers
or those with specialized knowledge. To address these
challenges, we introduced the D-ARE (Design Democratization
through AR-based Evaluation) system, an innovative approach
that employs augmented reality (AR) technology. This system
enhances public participation and ensures that a broader
and more diverse range informs design decisions of
community insights. The D-ARE system offers an immersive,
augmented, and contextual visualization platform that
facilitates the in-situ sharing of both spatial and
non-spatial design data, making complex data accessible and
understandable to stakeholders, regardless of their
technical expertise.
Our evaluation of D-ARE involved a mixed-method user study
with 20 participants, assessing the system's ease of use,
the clarity of the information presented, and its
effectiveness in engaging stakeholders. Findings indicate
that AR can significantly improve public engagement by
helping users visualize design alternatives within the
actual context of their implementation. However, the study
also identified the need for more engaging data
presentations and raised safety concerns about users
becoming overly immersed in the AR environment. These
findings highlight the potential of AR in democratizing the
design processes of built environments, indicating that
improvements in data visualization could enhance its
effectiveness. Future research should persist in advancing
digital public engagement tools to foster more inclusive
design practices.

column2:
Matias del Campo, Joseph Kenny, Eleni Vasiliki Alexi,
Sandra Manninger and Dr. Daniela Mitterberger
column3:
Toward AIXR: Designing a Framework for AI-Informed
Human-Robot Collaborative Assembly of Nonuniform Material
in Extended Reality
column7:
This paper presents AIXR, a framework for artificial
intelligence (AI) informed, extended reality (XR) guided
human-machine collaboration in rubble-based construction.
Addressing the dual challenges of material irregularity and
automation gaps, the research proposes a hybrid workflow
that integrates AI-driven material classification, robotic
sorting and assembly, and augmented reality (AR) interfaces
for real-time human-robot coordination. By leveraging
multimodal sensing, graph-based task distribution, and
adaptive AR interactions, the system enables construction
workers to engage directly with algorithmically optimized
layouts while retaining control over aesthetic and
structural decisions. The approach reframes demolition
waste as a site of architectural potential, demonstrating
how human-in-the-loop (HITL) systems can foster
sustainable, responsive, and materially intelligent
construction practices.

column2: Hyeokjin Choi, Jun Seo Lee, Jae Yeon Shin and Seung Hyun Cha
column3:
A Framework for Virtual Windows to Enhance Indoor Spatial
Experience in Extended Reality
column7:
In modern indoor space, not everyone can enjoy windows with
good views. Moreover, extended indoor hours and windowless
spaces can hamper occupant physical psychological health.
Conventional solutions, like digital windows, face issues
with fixed viewpoints and high cost of installation.
Meanwhile, advanced XR devices have made real-time tracking
and high-fidelity rendering feasible, enabling the creation
of virtual windows that replicate and enhance the
experience of physical windows. This paper proposes a
framework for designing XR-based virtual windows aimed at
enhancing indoor spatial experience. The framework consists
of three core components: (1) Window Position Analyzer,
which calculates feasible window placement by analyzing the
physical environment and user movements; (2) Window
Configuration Manager, which defines parameters for the
window frame and glazing; and (3) Virtual Scenery
Generator, which creates immersive views through object
arrangement and motion simulation. By synthesizing recent
advancements in computer graphics, sensing technologies,
and neural rendering, this study discusses how to achieve
naturalistic scenes and realistic lighting effects without
major architectural modifications. We then present a
proof-of-concept scenario focusing on residential contexts,
highlighting the key technical considerations and design
choices required. The findings illustrate that XR virtual
windows can provide a flexible, personalized, and
psychologically beneficial alternative to traditional
windows, representing a promising direction for the future
of indoor space experience.

column2:
Hongyi Chen, Haojun Wang, Yulin Chen, Jingyi Guo and Runjia
Tian
column3:
Text-to-Motif: Computational Design of Motif Patterns with
Shape Grammar and Latent Diffusion Model
column7:
This research introduces a computational framework
combining shape grammar and deep learning to generate
patterns from Southwest China, integrating them into
contemporary design (Jiang et al. 2022). Building on prior
works in computational motif generation (Situngkir, 2008)
and the fusion of shape grammar with neural networks for
pattern creation (Hu et al., 2021), the study advances
computational design methodologies.

Leveraging recent developments in text-to-image generation
models like Stable Diffusion (Ramesh et al. 2021), Low-Rank
Adaptation (LoRA), and ControlNet, the framework enhances
efficiency and control in image generation. The methodology
comprises four computational stages: data collection, unit
pattern extraction, pattern evolution using shape grammar,
and color filling.

Fieldwork from 2022 to 2024 provided a dataset of
traditional motifs categorized as animal, nature, or
geometry. These motifs were digitized and used to train
LoRA models within the Stable Diffusion framework. Shape
grammar, combined with templates developed in Grasshopper,
evolved unit patterns into complex, coherent designs. The
final stage applied color schemes specific to five minority
groups—Yi, Shui, Miao, Dong, and Yao—integrated into the
models for automated colorization.

The generated patterns were evaluated through
questionnaires distributed to designers, minority groups,
the general public, and non-Chinese individuals, focusing
on model accuracy, structural complexity, color
consistency, innovation, and applicability. Feedback
highlighted the framework's effectiveness in producing
intricate designs, demonstrating the potential of advanced
computational techniques in modern design practices. Future
research will expand the dataset to include more patterns
from additional groups and refine machine learning models
for greater context.

References

Hu, Tao, Qingsheng Xie, Qingni Yuan, Jian Lv, and Qiaoqiao
Xiong. "Design of ethnic patterns based on shape grammar
and artificial neural network." Alexandria Engineering
Journal 60, no. 1 (2021): 1601-1625.

Jiang, Wenxi, Yang Qin, Wei Guangbo, and Wu Yin. 2022.
"Research on the Extraction and Remanufacturing Methods of
Miao Embroidery Patterns Based on Shape Grammar." Software
Engineering and Applications 11 (2): 411-424.

Ramesh, Aditya, Mikhail Pavlov, Gabriel Goh, Scott Gray,
Chelsea Voss, Alec Radford, Mark Chen, and Ilya Sutskever.
"Zero-shot text-to-image generation." In International
conference on machine learning, pp. 8821-8831. Pmlr, 2021.

Situngkir, Hokky. "Deconstructing Javanese Batik motif:
when traditional heritage meets computation." Available at
SSRN 1312789 (2008).

column2: Chen-An Lee and June-Hao Hou
column3:
Improving Architectural Form Classification through
Salingaros’ Metrics and Topological Data Analysis
column7:
This study explores challenges in contemporary
architectural classification, particularly in machine
learning models processing vast, high-dimensional geometric
datasets. The irregularity and complexity of such data
often limit the effectiveness of traditional classification
methods. To address these issues, this research adopts
Salingaros’ theoretical framework, conceptualizing
architectural forms using form temperature (T), a measure
of visual intensity, and harmony (H), a measure of symmetry
(Salingaros, 2006). By isolating key geometric features,
these metrics reduce dataset complexity and enhance
classification accuracy.

In addition to Salingaros’ metrics, computational
algorithms were developed to measure T and H quantitatively
from architectural geometry. These metrics are integrated
with Topological Data Analysis (TDA) (Chazal & Michel,
2017), specifically Persistent Homology (PH) (Otter et al.,
2015), to extract essential geometric structures from
complex architectural datasets. TDA, known for its
robustness to noise, effectively manages data
irregularities (Saul & Tralie, 2019). Persistent Homology,
through persistence diagrams, captures and visualizes
fundamental geometric properties, improving machine
learning models’ efficiency and accuracy in architectural
classification (Tauzin et al., 2020; Hensel et al., 2021).

The proposed method was validated by analyzing Greek
architectural orders and classifying Modernism and
Metabolism architectures, demonstrating superior accuracy
and efficiency compared to traditional point cloud
classification using deep learning models for 3D model
classification (Guo et al., 2019). By integrating
Salingaros’ metrics with TDA, this study enhances the
scalability and precision of machine learning models for
architectural classification.


References

Chazal, F., & Michel, B. (2017). An Introduction to
Topological Data Analysis: Fundamental and Practical
Aspects for Data Scientists. Frontiers in Artificial
Intelligence, 4.
Guo, Y., Wang, H., Hu, Q., Liu, H., Liu, L., & Bennamoun
(2019). Deep Learning for 3D Point Clouds: A Survey. IEEE
Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence,
43, 4338-4364.
Hensel, F., Moor, M., & Rieck, B.A. (2021). A Survey of
Topological Machine Learning Methods. Frontiers in
Artificial Intelligence, 4.
Otter, N., Porter, M.A., Tillmann, U., Grindrod, P.M., &
Harrington, H.A. (2015). A roadmap for the computation of
persistent homology. Epj Data Science, 6.
Salingaros, N. A., & Mehaffy, M. W. (2006). A Theory of
Architecture. Umbau-Verlag Harald Püschel.
Saul, N., & Tralie, C. (2019). Scikit-TDA: Topological Data
Analysis for Python. Zenodo.
http://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.2533369
Tauzin, G., Lupo, U., Tunstall, L., P'erez, J.B., Caorsi,
M., Medina-Mardones, A.M., Dassatti, A., & Hess, K. (2020).

Learning and Data Exploration. J. Mach. Learn. Res., 22,
39:1-39:6.

column2: Xinru Li and Kam-Ming Mark Tam
column3:
Encoding Performance in Digital Weave Design Using AI and
Optimisation
column7:
The use of bitmaps to represent patterns has a long
history, originating with the Jacquard loom, where they
efficiently encoded the interlacing of warp and weft
threads (Ping Zhong et al., 2017). While effective, this
representation creates a complex design space that is
challenging to navigate, as arbitrary pixel adjustments
often result in disordered patterns and undesirable
mechanical properties. Most research on weave patterns
treats the input weave as fixed, focusing on analysis
rather than developing intuitive strategies for exploration
and modification.
This research proposes a computational pipeline that
integrates machine learning and computational geometry to
explore weave patterns in both aesthetic and functional
dimensions, with Navajo patterns serving as a case study
(Laura Devendorf et al., 2023). The pipeline comprises four
key components: (1) generation, (2) transformation, (3)
mixing, and (4) optimization. This iterative framework
allows flexible entry points for pattern development and
synthesis.
The workflow introduces AI-driven techniques for initial
pattern ideation, leveraging text-to-image synthesis tools.
In parallel, a comprehensive set of operators is developed
to generate and manipulate bitmap patterns using image
processing and machine learning methods (Kalyanmoy Deb et
al., 2002). A novel approach utilizing constrained
NURBS-based modeling is introduced to represent the
high-dimensional space of bitmap weaves, reducing the
complexity to a few intuitive parameters (Muhammad Arslan
Rauf et al., 2022). This approach facilitates the creation
of symmetrical, geometrically uniform patterns suitable for
design. Additional operators support the synthesis of new
patterns from existing bitmaps (Noreen Akram et al., 2024).

Multi-objective optimization methods are employed to
fine-tune these operators based on custom metrics that
account for the feasibility of hand weaving (Alsaid Ahemd
Almetwally, 2020). Finally, this research leverages
generative dimensionality reduction techniques to model the
solution space of weavable bitmap patterns, enabling the
direct, performance-driven synthesis of weave patterns that
meet specific weavability criteria (Xiaopei Wu & Li Li,
2024).
This pipeline, incorporating both pre-trained and
scratch-trained AI models, empowers designers to produce
diverse, intricate patterns while maintaining control over
key design constraints. Its applicability extends beyond
weaving to other fields of visual pattern generation.

column2: Chao Tang, Kam-Ming Mark Tam and Christiane Margerita Herr
column3: Interactive BIM Modelling Assistant with Multi-Agent LLM
column7:
The integration of Geographic Information Systems (GIS),
Building Information Modeling (BIM), and multi-agent Large
Language Models (LLMs) offers transformative possibilities
for generating localized and regulation-compliant
architectural designs. Previous research has applied LLMs
in BIM workflows for tasks like code compliance checking,
floor plan generation, parametric modeling, energy
simulation enrichment, and command-based modeling. However,
most studies focus on open-ended tasks, with limited
emphasis on integrating site-specific constraints and
structured knowledge bases, which are crucial for practical
usability. This study introduces a novel framework
combining GIS data, BIM automation, and multi-agent LLMs to
address these gaps. It employs a hybrid Retrieval-Augmented
Generation (RAG) strategy, integrating multi-perspective
vector search and semantic knowledge retrieval to process
site-specific GIS data and regulatory guidelines, enhance
retrieval and align designs with HK's unique site
conditions, spatial, performance, and compliance
objectives. Specialized agents and designers collaborate
iteratively, using ChatGPT 4o and o-1 as the backbone, to
create massing models and refine them into spatial models
while addressing conflicting design factors, with Revit
Parametric Refactoring transforming refined data into IFC
models. Additionally, the framework adopts a Hierarchical
Data Approach to organize design and compliance information
at multiple scales (plot, massing, building, and detail)
and utilizes Parallel Data Flows to concurrently refine
massing- and building-level data, ensuring real-time
synchronization among specialized agents.  This approach
accelerates regulation-adapted ideation, advancing human-AI
collaborative design workflows that balance creativity,
localization and compliance, offering scalable and
practical solutions for site-specific architectural design.

column2:
Davide Schaumann, Andrew Vande Moere, Yuval Kahlon,
Farahbod Heidari, Alex Binh Vinh Duc Nguyen, Yiming Liu,
Umaru Mohammed Bongwirnso, Sihao Chen, Thomas Fischer and
Christiane M. Herr
column3:
Buildings as Symbiotic Systems: Cybernetic Adaptation
between Technical and Biological Systems in Architecture
column7:
Contemporary architectural design increasingly integrates
biological and technical systems that interact with – and
adapt to – their surrounding environments. Biological
systems encompass living organisms such as humans, animals,
plants, and bio-based materials, while technical systems
include adaptive building components, materials, and
technologies. These interactions present new challenges and
opportunities for designers who need to consider new
temporal and spatial dynamics as part of architectural
design. The successful interaction of mutually adaptive
biological and technical systems can be characterized as
symbiotic, potentially fostering long-term sustainability,
biodiversity, and well-being. Despite their increasing
integration, biological and technical systems often operate
through distinct forms of agency – self-sustaining
imperatives versus programmed objectives – which can
generate conflicts when their regulatory mechanisms are
misaligned. To achieve symbiotic interactions, this paper
proposes a conceptual framework for designing symbiotic
architectural systems that mediate the agency of biological
and technical elements. Drawing on cybernetic theory, it
examines adaptive feedback mechanisms that continuously
regulate these interactions, balancing the competing goals
and needs of each system. By reframing buildings as
constantly changing (eco)systems rather than static
containers, this approach supports the design of resilient
environments striving to sustain dynamic equilibria toward
human, ecological, and environmental health.

column2: Yu Li, Jiapan Sun, Yixuan Liu and Bingbing Fan
column3:
Design and manufacture of waste timber composite panels:
sustainable and innovative use of recycled timber
column7:
In the context of the growing global demand for sustainable
building materials, timber has gained significant attention
from architects and manufacturers as an efficient and
sustainable construction material. However, the current
handling of waste wood in forest production is concerning,
with data showing that a large amount of waste wood is
deteriorated and does not realize its full potential value.
This paper examines how digital technologies can enhance
the efficient use of waste wood and achieve zero waste in
the timber construction manufacturing process, using the
"Adaptive Assembly Roof" project as a case study.
The project aims to develop composite roof panels made from
reclaimed materials such as bark, waste timber, and
sawdust. Through material testing and computational design,
the project enhances the performance and structural
strength of these materials, maximizing the value of waste
materials in the manufacturing process. Additionally, the
project introduces an adaptive assembly node system that
allows the panels to be repeatedly assembled and
disassembled at various angles, meeting different user
needs and extending the life cycle of the materials. This
paper further discusses how digital technologies can
promote the sustainability of timber architecture and
effectively address challenges related to misinformation
and resource waste in the forestry sector.

column2:
Bin Li, Bingbing Fan, Jiaxiang Luo, Zujian Liu, Yixuan Liu
and Jiapan Sun
column3:
The Resonance of the Chenghuang Culture: Recreating the
Memory of Zhengzhou Chenghuang Temple with Mixed Reality
Technology under the Digital Twin Paradigm
column7:
This study proposes a more comprehensive and accurate
approach to the conservation and reuse of architectural
heritage, focusing on the City God Temple in Zhengzhou,
China, built in the early 16th century. For this
architectural heritage, the study adopted high-precision
laser scanning technology (TLS), and the 3d model generated
by the FARO Focus 3d S120 scanner can comprehensively
capture the texture, structure, spatial distribution and
landscape planning of the City God Temple, thus laying a
solid foundation for the creation of the digital twin. In
terms of mixed reality experiences, the collected scanning
data will be used as the basic data, combined with HoloLens
2 and Fologram technology, to combine the scanned 3D model
with the realistic map, providing visitors with a
multi-scale immersive experience. Through accurate data
collection and technical execution, this study ensures
accuracy and stability in empirical research, can stably
present the cultural history and spatial perception of City
God Temple, and provides technical support for the revival
of cultural memory.

column2: Zhining Wang, Ningyuan Wang, Yue Chen and Zhe Guo
column3:
Research on Modular Generation and Construction Methods of
Layered Wooden Structures from the Perspective of
Traditional Building Techniques: A Case Study of Tang-Style
Dougong
column7:
The construction logic of traditional dougong (bracket sets
in traditional Chinese architecture) exhibits a high degree
of logical coherence and modularization, making it possible
to translate and reproduce its construction patterns
digitally. By systematically examining the construction
logic of layered wooden structures found in traditional
building methods, this study selects the dougong of Foguang
Temple from the Tang Dynasty as the research object,
attempting to explore a computational generative design and
intelligent construction model for layered wooden
structures based on a digital strip system. Firstly, this
research provides a detailed analysis of the riveting
types, individual component characteristics, and connection
parameters of the Tang Dynasty dougong, with the corner
bracket set of Foguang Temple serving as a representative
example. Secondly, utilizing the WASP algorithm in
conjunction with a design concept based on discrete
combinations, a set of assembly logic codes is developed to
reorganize the original components. Thirdly, the assembly
methods and milling paths are programmed into a robotic arm
plugin for simulated construction processes. Finally, a
freely reconstructed structure embodying the aesthetics of
dougong, controlled by the principles of discrete
combinations, is produced. This provides a meaningful
reference for the popularization and reinterpretation of
the style and connotations of dougong, a traditional
element. This study ultimately establishes a dataset of
information on layered wooden structure construction based
on a visual coding platform, which includes methods for
generating layered wooden structures prototyped from
traditional dougong, discrete combination construction
methods, and technical pathways supported by robotic arms.
It demonstrates the charm of traditional Chinese
construction methods and expands the feasibility of
contemporary reconstructions of traditional wooden
structures. The innovation of this research lies in the
development of a computer language that captures the
assembly logic of dougong, introducing the parameterized
concept of discrete combinations to modernize traditional
assembly practices. The use of robotic arms for physical
construction allows for the flexible reproduction of
complex dougong forms within digital environments,
deepening the understanding of their underlying
construction logic and providing valuable insights into the
digital translation and reproduction of time-honored
building techniques. This research has important
theoretical and practical significance for promoting the
inheritance and development of traditional architectural
culture, as well as expanding the ideas and techniques of
contemporary architectural design.

column2: Chee Meng Chan and Frederick Kim
column3: Perceptual Urban Form
column7:
Enabled by growing repositories of urban data, a growing
body of research presents promising techniques for
analysing the visual perception of urban spaces. While much
of the existing research focuses on understanding and
predicting perceptions of existing urban spaces, there is a
notable gap in the exploration of methods for generating
urban environments specifically curated to evoke desired
visual perceptions. Our research seeks to bridge this gap
by extending such analysis and prediction techniques into
the third dimension. We aim to establish foundations in
data encoding and analysis methods such that future
research can more readily work with perception and
morphology directly in three dimensions. Our methods
involve the following steps: (1) urban scale 3D scene
reconstruction from widely available image and map data,
(2) evaluating the performance of 3D data encodings, and
(3) predicting the visual perception of urban spaces
directly from their morphologies. Through our techniques,
we perform further analysis to bridge the gap between human
and machine understandings of morphology and perception to
demonstrate how our techniques may be applied in designing
for visual perception. The proposed methods open up new
avenues for urban design, serving as a step closer to
creating urban spaces that are intentionally designed to
evoke specific responses from their inhabitants.

column2: Taiyang Wang, Peng Luo and Rudi Stouffs
column3:
The optimization of visual perception factors in badminton
sports environment applied virtual reality and machine
learning
column7:
In the realm of public health studies, the sports
perceptions of individuals are influenced by both
environmental factors and their emotional experiences.
Previous research investigating the impact of environmental
factors on sports perception and emotions has predominantly
relied on subjective questionnaire assessments, lacking
objective data verification. Furthermore, the practical
application of research findings in design remains limited.
This study focused on the visual environment of badminton,
employing an eye tracker and a semantic differential
questionnaire to validate the feasibility of virtual
reality (VR) technology. It aimed to characterize sports
gaze patterns and identify environmental factors
influencing sports perception. We explored key
environmental factors, including illuminance (IL), height
(Ht), roof saturation (RSa), roof slope (RS), backwall
saturation (BSa), and natural materials proportion on the
backwall (BN). These factors helped organize orthogonal
experiments in an immersive virtual environment. We
unveiled the influence of these factors on emotional
components like pleasure (P), arousal (A), and dominance
(D) in sports perception. Additionally, we examined the
interplay of P, A, and D with sports perception scores (W).
After training and comparing four surrogate prediction
models of sports emotions, a genetic algorithm combined
with an artificial neural network was applied in
optimization and renovation. The optimized thresholds were
IL: 778.32lx–874.43lx, Ht:15.27m–19.60m, RSa: 95.23–96.20,
RS: 14.03°–18.07°, BN: 95.23%–96.20% and BSa: 58.01–76.51.
When the P, A and D (ranged 1–5) increased by 0.85, 0.75
and 1.9 respectively, the W (ranged 1–5) improved from 3.75
to 4.60 in the renovation.

Li Zhang, Jiawei Wang, Zhicheng Wang, Yuetong Wu, Han Li,
Qi Zhang and Bo Gao
column3:
Evaluation Method of AI-Generated Architectural Facade
Images Based on DCNN
column7:
Abstract. In recent years, Generative Artificial
Intelligence has been extensively applied in the field of
architectural design, emerging as a powerful tool that
significantly reduces designers’ workload, particularly in
simple and repetitive tasks. Notably, the advent of the
Stable Diffusion model has markedly enhanced the efficiency
of architectural facade design. However, in practical
applications, the selection of optimal design schemes
remains heavily dependent on the professional expertise and
experiential judgement of designers, with subjective bias
posing a significant challenge that undermines overall
efficiency. To address this challenge, this study proposes
a novel evaluation approach based on a Deep Convolutional
Neural Network (DCNN). The DCNN evaluation model is trained
via supervised learning to extract and interpret key
features from AI-generated architectural facade images,
thereby enabling accurate quantitative analysis.
Experimental findings demonstrate that the proposed method
successfully achieves automatic prediction of AI-generated
facades, thereby opening a promising new research avenue
and offering valuable methodological insights for future
studies and practical applications in this domain.

column2:
Matthias Hornung, Markus Renner, Diellza Elshani, Mathias
Niepert and Thomas Wortmann
column3:
Augmenting IFC-Based BIM Models for Graph Neural Network
Training of Non-Orthogonal Spatial Typologies: A
Context-Informed Design Methodology
column7:
Building Information Modeling (BIM) and Industry Foundation
Classes (IFC) data are valuable resources in architecture,
offering detailed and structured information on building
elements.
However, using such resources to develop artificial
intelligence (AI) models that are capable of learning and
generating spatial and geometrical suggestions remains a
challenging problem.

This study presents a systematic method for converting
real-world BIM/IFC projects into graph representations,
suitable for training Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), which
overcome the limitations inherent to conventional AI
techniques based on pixel and 3D voxels in architecture.

First, a custom schema was defined to encode each building
element and spatial relationship as triplets, allowing for
the generation of heterogeneous graphs that capture
geometry, topology and semantic labels.
Using models provided by multiple architecture offices, we
extracted over 180,000 subgraphs that represent diverse
non-orthogonal spatial typologies.
Next, each subgraph was annotated with multi-label
classifications (element type) and continuous attributes
(e.g. dimensions, orientation) to support both
classification and regression tasks.

Finally, to demonstrate the utility of the dataset, we
trained a custom neural network (NN) to complete partial
spatial graphs, producing non-orthogonal room layouts based
on the existing building context.
The custom NN suggests that the dataset has the capacity to
support advanced 3D generative tasks in architecture and
could lay the groundwork for future studies on automated
design synthesis.
